# Overview



This page introduces **plm_interp**, a research codebase accompanying the paper *"Mechanistic Interpretability of Protein Language Models Reveals Encoded Structural and Functional Properties of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins"* (bioRxiv, 2026), authored by Lauren Naworski, Lydia Good, Rob Scrutton, and Tuomas P. J. Knowles. Here you will learn what the repository investigates, how its scripts are organized into four analysis branches, what software environment it requires, and the engineering conventions that make its results reproducible. No prior experience with protein language models is assumed — every concept is introduced from first principles, with deeper treatment deferred to later pages in this guide.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L6)

## What Is plm_interp?

Proteins are not always rigid, folded machines. A large class — **intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs)** — function while remaining structurally flexible, and they are heavily implicated in human disease and cellular organization such as liquid–liquid phase separation. ESM-2 is a pretrained protein language model (specifically the 650M-parameter `esm2_t33_650M_UR50D` variant, with 33 transformer layers and 1280-dimensional embeddings) that learns representations of amino acid sequences from millions of evolutionary sequences. The central question of this repository is whether the *attention patterns* inside ESM-2 — the internal maps showing which amino acid positions the model "looks at" when processing a sequence — encode measurable structural and functional properties of IDPs, such as disorder, contact geometry, compactness, and disease relevance.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L6), [scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L29-L31)

The repository does not ship a library or package. Instead it provides a collection of standalone, sequentially-run scripts that consume committed datasets, execute GPU-heavy model inference, and emit figures matching those in the publication. A mapping table in the README links each paper figure to its exact reproduction commands, which is the fastest way to understand which scripts belong together.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L96)

## The Core Idea: Reading the Model's Attention

For a beginner, the key mental model is this: when ESM-2 processes a protein sequence, every attention *head* (there are 20 per layer, across 33 layers) produces an **attention matrix** — an N×N grid where entry (i, j) quantifies how strongly position i attends to position j. The scripts request these matrices directly from the model with `need_head_weights=True` and save them to disk in compressed chunks, because the full set of matrices for hundreds of proteins is far too large to hold in memory at once. A follow-up script condenses the per-head matrices into a single interpretable summary per protein via **attention rollout**, and analysis scripts then compare these summaries between ordered proteins (from the PDB structural database) and disordered proteins (from DisProt).

Sources: [scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L54-L58), [scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L42-L50)

Disorder is quantified with **IUPred2A**, an external third-party tool that predicts per-residue disorder probabilities from sequence alone. It is the one dependency the conda environment cannot install for you: after installing it manually, you must point the `iupred_filepath` variable at your local copy in `scripts/attention_functions.py`. This function library is the shared heart of the codebase — nearly every analysis script imports its attention-loading, rollout, and disorder-extraction helpers from it.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L18-L18), [scripts/attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L18-L25)

## Repository at a Glance

The project follows a flat layout: all executable code lives in `scripts/`, all input and summary data in `data/`, raw model outputs in `attention_matrices_chunks/` (generated, not committed), and final plots in `figures/` (generated). A single serialized model file, `mlp_final.pt`, holds the trained radius-of-gyration predictor, and `publication.mplstyle` defines the shared plotting theme used by every figure-producing script.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L22-L32)

```
plm_interp/
├── data/                          # committed inputs + derived summary data
│   ├── protein_input_sets.csv     # master list: ProteinID + Sequence for PDB & DisProt sets
│   ├── pdb_disprot.fasta          # exact filtered sequences used in the study
│   ├── disprot.fasta              # raw DisProt release 2025_06 sequences
│   ├── clinvar_sequences.csv      # disease variant sequences (ClinVar-derived)
│   ├── idrome.fasta / idrome_clustered.fasta  # IDRome ensemble sequences
│   └── ...                        # perplexities, contact-map batch info, CD-HIT cluster files
├── scripts/                       # all analyses (16 standalone scripts)
├── attention_matrices_chunks/     # generated: raw ESM-2 attention tensors (joblib chunks)
├── figures/                       # generated: publication figures
├── environment.yml                # conda environment "torch-gpu"
├── mlp_final.pt                   # trained Rg-predicting MLP
└── publication.mplstyle           # shared matplotlib theme
```

The architecture forms a hub-and-spoke pattern: `attention_functions.py` provides shared utilities, and four largely independent analysis branches fan out from the committed datasets in `data/`. Each branch corresponds to one or two figures in the paper.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    DATA["data/<br/>committed datasets<br/>(DisProt, PDB, IDRome, ClinVar)"]
    EXT["esm2_interp_data.py<br/>downloads live external data"]

    subgraph B1["Branch 1 · Attention vs. Disorder → Figures 1–2"]
        A1["get_esm2_attention_matrices.py<br/>per-head ESM-2 attention"] --> CHUNK[("attention_matrices_chunks/<br/>22 joblib chunks")]
        CHUNK --> A2["get_esm2_attention_rollout.py<br/>attention rollout"]
        A2 --> A3["attention_rollout_analysis.py<br/>PDB vs DisProt statistics"]
    end

    subgraph B2["Branch 2 · Disease Residues → Figure 3"]
        C1["clinvar_expanded.py<br/>attention at ClinVar variant sites"]
    end

    subgraph B3["Branch 3 · Contact Maps → Figure 4"]
        D1["get_contact_maps.py<br/>categorical Jacobians"] --> D2["md_variable_cutoff.py<br/>MD trajectory contacts"]
        D2 --> D3["md_contact_maps_analysis.py"]
    end

    subgraph B4["Branch 4 · Rg Prediction → Figure 5"]
        E1["rg_mlp.py<br/>train MLP on IDRome Rg"] --> CKPT["mlp_final.pt"]
        CKPT --> E2["es_ablation2.py<br/>attention-head ablation"]
    end

    DATA --> B1 & B2 & B3 & B4
    EXT --> DATA
    PPL["esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py<br/>perplexity vs. disorder"] --> B1
    FIG["figures.py + publication.mplstyle"] --> OUT["figures/"]
    B1 & B2 & B3 & B4 --> FIG
```

> [!TIP]
> The chunking pattern in Branch 1 is the repository's most important engineering idea: attention tensors are written to 22 numbered `joblib` files (chunk size 200 proteins) so that downstream scripts can load and process one chunk at a time with explicit `del` statements — the only practical way to work with hundreds of gigabytes of attention data on a single GPU machine.

Sources: [scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L42-L48), [scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L36-L56)

## The Four Analysis Branches

Each branch tests a different hypothesis about what ESM-2 attention encodes. The table below maps scientific questions to scripts and paper figures, exactly as documented in the README's reproduction table.

| Branch | Hypothesis Tested | Core Scripts | Paper Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Attention vs. Disorder** | Attention rollout patterns distinguish ordered (PDB) from disordered (DisProt) proteins | `get_esm2_attention_matrices.py` → `get_esm2_attention_rollout.py` → `attention_rollout_analysis.py` | Figures 1–2 |
| **Disease Residues** | The model attends more strongly to known ClinVar disease-variant positions | `esm2_interp_data.py` → `clinvar_expanded.py` | Figure 3 |
| **Contact Maps** | Categorical Jacobians from ESM-2 predict residue contacts validated against MD trajectories | `get_contact_maps.py` → `md_variable_cutoff.py` → `md_contact_maps_analysis.py` | Figure 4 |
| **Rg Prediction & Ablation** | Attention-derived embeddings can predict radius of gyration; ablating electrostatics-associated heads degrades prediction | `esm2_interp_data.py` → `rg_mlp.py` → `es_ablation2.py` | Figure 5 |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L96)

Two branches deserve brief unpacking for newcomers. The **Rg branch** trains a small MLP regression head (hidden dimension 512, dropout 0.3) on layer-33 ESM-2 embeddings, using MD-derived Rg values from the IDRome database for training and experimental SAXS measurements as an out-of-sample check; fixed seeds (`SEED = 42`) and deterministic cuDNN flags make retraining bit-reproducible. The **ablation script** then zeroes out up to 50 attention heads identified with electrostatics-related statistics and measures how the MLP's Rg predictions degrade — a causal test of *which* attention heads carry physical meaning.

Sources: [scripts/rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L22-L57), [scripts/es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L22-L40)

The **contact-map branch** adapts published methodology (credited to Zhang et al., *PNAS* 2024) that perturbs each residue through all 20 amino acid substitutions and measures how output logits respond — producing a *categorical Jacobian* whose high off-diagonal entries indicate residue–residue contacts. The README explicitly flags which functions are adapted third-party code and notes they fall outside the repository's MIT license.

Sources: [scripts/get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L16-L57), [README.md](README.md#L82-L84)

## Environment and Dependencies

Reproducibility starts with a fully pinned conda environment named `torch-gpu`, created with `conda env create -f environment.yml`. The stack combines GPU-enabled deep learning, scientific Python, and domain-specific IDP tooling:

| Package | Version | Role in This Project |
|---|---|---|
| `torch` | 2.5.1+cu121 | GPU model inference and MLP training |
| `fair-esm` | 2.0.0 | Loads ESM-2 and exposes per-head attention matrices |
| `transformers` | 4.55.2 | Auxiliary masked-LM utilities in analysis scripts |
| `scikit-learn` / `scipy` / `statsmodels` | 1.7.1 / 1.16.1 / 0.14.5 | Statistics: logistic regression, UMAP, correlations, FDR control |
| `matplotlib` / `seaborn` | 3.10.5 / 0.13.2 | Figure generation under `publication.mplstyle` |
| `mdtraj` | 1.11.1 | Parses MD trajectories for contact-map validation |
| `cd-hit` | 4.8.1 | Sequence clustering to remove homologous redundancy |
| `idptools-starling`, `localcider`, `metapredict` | — | IDP sequence analysis tooling |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L16), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L553-L561), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L486-L495), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L287-L290)

> [!TIP]
> One practical prerequisite trips up most first-time users: the IUPred2A disorder predictor must be installed separately from its academic site, and the hard-coded `iupred_filepath` string at line 25 of `scripts/attention_functions.py` still points to the authors' HPC cluster — you must edit it before any disorder-related script will run.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L18-L18), [scripts/attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L25-L25)

## Data Philosophy: Committed Derivatives vs. Live Sources

External biological databases (PDB, DisProt, ClinVar, RefSeq, IDRome) are *living* databases — they change constantly, so a naive re-download today will not reproduce the paper. The repository resolves this tension with a deliberate two-track design: the exact filtered sequences used in the study are committed under `data/` (for example `protein_input_sets.csv`, `pdb_disprot.fasta`, `clinvar_sequences.csv`), while `esm2_interp_data.py` documents and automates download of the raw upstream sources for users who want the most current versions. A single boolean flag (`derived = True`) in `clinvar_expanded.py` switches between these two modes. Notably, the massive raw attention tensors are *never* committed — they must be regenerated with the Branch 1 scripts.

Sources: [scripts/esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L1-L34), [scripts/clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L20-L27), [README.md](README.md#L44-L48)

Licensing follows the same care: the code is MIT-licensed, but committed third-party datasets (DisProt under CC BY 4.0, PDB under CC0 1.0, IDRome under GPL-3.0, ClinVar-derived data in the public domain) remain under their original licenses, with a full attribution table in the README.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L67-L78)

## Shared Engineering Conventions

Three patterns repeat across all sixteen scripts, and recognizing them will make every deep-dive page easier to follow. First, every script anchors its paths with the two-line idiom `SCRIPT_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent` followed by `BASE_PATH = SCRIPT_DIR.parent`, so scripts work regardless of your current working directory. Second, figure-producing scripts activate the shared theme with `plt.style.use(f'{BASE_PATH}/publication.mplstyle')` and use consistent group colors (orange for PDB, steelblue for DisProt), while the dedicated `figures.py` assembles multi-panel layouts on a millimeter-precise 183 × 170 mm canvas matching journal column geometry. Third, GPU-related scripts print device diagnostics and manage memory explicitly (batch size 2 for attention extraction, `save_interval` chunking, aggressive `del` + garbage collection), reflecting the reality that per-head attention tensors dominate the memory budget.

Sources: [scripts/attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L15-L16), [scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L32-L33), [scripts/figures.py](scripts/figures.py#L26-L39), [scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L19-L27), [scripts/get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L13-L14)

If you want hands-on results quickly, go straight to installation and the first run; if you want conceptual grounding first, the biology primer is the gentlest entry point.

1. **[Quick Start](2-quick-start)** — install the `torch-gpu` environment and verify your GPU setup end to end.
2. **[External Data Acquisition](3-external-data-acquisition)** — deep dive into `esm2_interp_data.py` and the derived-vs-live data strategy.
3. **[ESM-2 and IDP Biology Primer](6-esm-2-and-idp-biology-primer)** — the conceptual background for everything above.
4. **[Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction)** — the first stage of Branch 1, where raw attention tensors are born.

For the intellectually curious, the [Research Questions and Hypotheses](7-research-questions-and-hypotheses) page formalizes the scientific logic connecting the four branches, and [Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management) expands on the chunking strategy highlighted above.

# Quick Start



This page takes you from a fresh clone to your first complete ESM-2 attention analysis. `plm_interp` is the companion codebase for the paper *Mechanistic Interpretability of Protein Language Models Reveals Encoded Structural and Functional Properties of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins*: it extracts per-head attention matrices from ESM-2, compresses them via attention rollout, and compares the resulting signals between ordered (PDB-derived) and disordered (DisProt-derived) protein sets. By the end of this guide you will have a working `torch-gpu` environment, the single required manual configuration (IUPred2A), and the three-stage "Figure 1" workflow running end to end.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L6)

## The Pipeline You Are About to Run

Everything in the Quick Start revolves around one core data path. A single CSV of protein IDs and sequences feeds ESM-2 (the 650M-parameter `esm2_t33_650M_UR50D` checkpoint), which emits raw attention tensors; those are chunk-saved to disk, rolled out into per-protein summary matrices, and finally analyzed as ordered-vs-disordered sets with figures written as SVGs. Two auxiliary dependencies hang off this path: the IUPred2A disorder predictor (invoked as a subprocess during analysis) and the ESM-2 weights (auto-downloaded on first run).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["data/protein_input_sets.csv"] --> B["get_esm2_attention_matrices.py"]
    W[("ESM-2 650M weights<br/>(auto-downloaded)")] --> B
    B --> C[("attention_matrices_chunks/<br/>attention_matrices_labeled_*.joblib")]
    C --> D["get_esm2_attention_rollout.py"]
    D --> E[("attention_matrices_chunks/<br/>attention_rollout_comb_original.joblib")]
    E --> F["attention_rollout_analysis.py"]
    I["IUPred2A<br/>(manual install)"] -. subprocess -.-> F
    F --> G[("figures/*.svg")]
```

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L29-L36), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L36-L56), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L40-L64)

## Prerequisites and Hardware

Before touching the terminal, confirm you have the following. The environment pins PyTorch `2.5.1+cu121` (CUDA 12.1 wheels), so an NVIDIA GPU with compatible drivers is strongly recommended; the scripts do fall back to CPU automatically, but per-protein attention extraction over the full committed dataset is GPU-bound work. Python 3.11 is the pinned interpreter (`cpython=3.11.13`).

| Requirement | Details | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|
| Conda (Anaconda/Miniconda) | Any recent distribution | `environment.yml` is a conda env spec, not pip-only |
| NVIDIA GPU + CUDA driver | Drives pinned for CUDA 12.1 (`torch==2.5.1+cu121`) | Matrices script prints GPU name/memory at startup; CPU fallback exists but is slow |
| IUPred2A | Separate download from `https://iupred2a.elte.hu/` | Disorder segmentation; the only manual code edit in this guide |
| Internet access | For ESM-2 weights + external databases | Model checkpoint downloads on first forward pass; external datasets via download script |
| Disk headroom | Raw attention tensors are large | 22 joblib chunks (up to 200 proteins each) plus the rollout artifact |

Sources: [environment.yml](environment.yml#L1-L7), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L553), [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L23-L27), [README.md](README.md#L18)

## Step 1 — Install the Environment

Three commands reproduce the authors' exact runtime. The environment is named `torch-gpu` and pulls from five channels (`conda-forge`, `bioconda`, `nvidia`, `defaults`, `pytorch`), mixing conda packages with a pip layer that carries the GPU-enabled PyTorch build and `fair-esm` (the package providing `esm.pretrained.esm2_t33_650M_UR50D`).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/lnaworsk/plm_interp.git
cd plm_interp
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate torch-gpu
```

Key packages resolved by this spec:

| Package | Version | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `python` | 3.11.13 | Interpreter |
| `torch` (pip) | 2.5.1+cu121 | Tensor engine with CUDA 12.1 |
| `fair-esm` (pip) | 2.0.0 | ESM-2 model loading and batch tokenization |
| `transformers` | 4.55.2 | HuggingFace models used by the analysis stage |
| `biopython` | 1.85 | FASTA parsing (`SeqIO`) |
| `cd-hit` | 4.8.1 | Sequence clustering (via bioconda) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L16), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L1-L7), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L486), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L553)

## Step 2 — Configure IUPred2A (The One Manual Edit)

This is the step beginners most often miss. The shared utility module `scripts/attention_functions.py` shells out to IUPred2A via `subprocess` to compute per-residue disorder probabilities, and the path to the predictor is a **hardcoded absolute path** pointing to one of the authors' HPC home directories — it will not resolve on your machine. Download IUPred2A from `https://iupred2a.elte.hu/`, then edit line 25:

| | `scripts/attention_functions.py`, line 25 |
|---|---|
| **Before (as committed)** | `iupred_filepath = '/rds/user/ln399/hpc-work/llps/DeePhase_LN/__PREDICT_LN/tools/iupred2a.py'` |
| **After (your machine)** | `iupred_filepath = '/home/<you>/tools/iupred2a.py'` (wherever you unpacked IUPred2A) |

The functions that consume this path, `extract_IDR` and `extract_IDR_profile`, invoke `python <iupred_filepath> <tmp_fasta> long` as a subprocess — so both the path *and* a working `python` on your `PATH` are required at call time.

> [!TIP]
> Because every pipeline stage imports from `attention_functions.py` (`get_esm2_attention_rollout.py` imports `safe_load`/`attention_rollout`; `attention_rollout_analysis.py` uses a wildcard import), fixing line 25 **once** repairs the entire pipeline. The import itself is harmless — the path is only resolved when disorder-extraction functions actually execute.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L18-L25), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L45-L51), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L10), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L8), [README.md](README.md#L18)

## Step 3 — Create Output Directories and Fetch External Data

Two runtime directories are referenced by the scripts but are **not present in the cloned repository** (they are excluded from git because they hold large generated artifacts). Both stages write files directly into these paths with no `os.makedirs` call, so the first run will crash on a missing directory unless you create them first:

```bash
mkdir -p attention_matrices_chunks figures
```

For input data, the repository uses a **two-tier data model**: derived datasets used by the paper are already committed under `data/` (e.g. `protein_input_sets.csv`, `pdb_disprot.fasta`, `clustered_input.fasta`), while large external downloads (NCBI gene2refseq, GRCh38 RefSeq proteome, IDRome tables, experimental SAXS data) are fetched on demand:

```bash
python scripts/esm2_interp_data.py
```

| Data Tier | Examples | How You Get It |
|---|---|---|
| Committed (derived) | `data/protein_input_sets.csv`, `pdb_disprot.fasta`, `clinvar_sequences.csv` | Already in your clone |
| Downloaded (live) | `gene2refseq`, `GRCh38_latest_protein_copy.faa`, IDRome DB | `python scripts/esm2_interp_data.py` |
| Never committed (regenerable) | Attention matrices, rollout matrices, figures | Produced by the pipeline below |

> [!TIP]
> The scripts resolve all data paths via `BASE_PATH = SCRIPT_DIR.parent`, so they work regardless of your current working directory — but the *output* directories are assumed to pre-exist. If you ever see `FileNotFoundError` on a `.joblib` dump or a figure `.svg` save, the cause is an absent `attention_matrices_chunks/` or `figures/` folder, not a code bug.

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L9-L10), [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L76-L87), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L64), [README.md](README.md#L36-L48)

## Step 4 — Run Your First Analysis (the Figure 1 Workflow)

This is the minimal end-to-end run recommended in the README's *Reproducing Results* table for Figures 1–2. Execute the commands in order; each stage consumes the previous stage's joblib output.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S1["1. python scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py<br/>ESM-2 forward passes → 22 joblib chunks"] --> S2
    S2["2. python scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py<br/>Rollout over all chunks → single rollout joblib"] --> S3
    S3["3. python scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py<br/>Ordered vs disordered analysis → SVG figures"]
```

What each stage actually does:

| Stage | Script | Behavior to Expect |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Attention extraction | `get_esm2_attention_matrices.py` | Loads ESM-2 650M to GPU, reads all proteins from `data/protein_input_sets.csv`, runs batches of 2 with `need_head_weights=True`, prints progress indices, saves a compressed `.joblib` chunk every 200 proteins |
| 2. Attention rollout | `get_esm2_attention_rollout.py` | Streams chunks 0–21, computes rollout per protein with `discard_ratio=0.9` and `head_fusion="mean"`, writes `attention_rollout_comb_original.joblib` |
| 3. Analysis | `attention_rollout_analysis.py` | Loads the rollout artifact, applies `publication.mplstyle`, splits proteins into PDB (ordered) vs DisProt (disordered) sets by ID substring, and saves figures (e.g. `figures/input_sets_seqlen_distribution.svg`) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L96), [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L36-L55), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L36-L56), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L32-L45)

## What Success Looks Like

After the three stages complete, your repository gains the artifacts below alongside the committed files. Stage 1's chunks are named `attention_matrices_labeled_{chunk}_{model_type}.joblib` where `model_type` is always `'original'`; the rollout stage expects exactly chunks 0 through 21, matching the committed dataset size at a save interval of 200.

```
plm_interp/
├── attention_matrices_chunks/        # ← you created this
│   ├── attention_matrices_labeled_0_original.joblib
│   ├── ...
│   ├── attention_matrices_labeled_21_original.joblib
│   └── attention_rollout_comb_original.joblib
├── data/                             # committed inputs + downloaded externals
├── figures/                          # ← you created this; SVG outputs land here
│   └── input_sets_seqlen_distribution.svg
├── scripts/                          # all analysis code
├── environment.yml
├── mlp_final.pt                      # pretrained Rg predictor (used by rg_mlp.py)
└── publication.mplstyle              # matplotlib style, auto-applied by analysis
```

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L78-L87), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L56), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L64), [README.md](README.md#L23-L32)

## Tuning Knobs and Troubleshooting

The pipeline exposes a small set of hardcoded-but-editable constants. For beginners, `batch_size` is the one worth knowing first — the authors' own comment marks it as a memory-budget dial.

| Knob | Default | Location | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `batch_size` | 2 | `get_esm2_attention_matrices.py` (line 45) | Proteins per forward pass; raise if GPU memory allows, lower if you hit OOM |
| `save_interval` | 200 | `get_esm2_attention_matrices.py` (line 42) | Proteins per joblib chunk; changing it breaks the rollout stage's fixed 22-chunk loop |
| `discard_ratio` | 0.9 | `get_esm2_attention_rollout.py` (line 48) | Fraction of lowest-attention tokens dropped during rollout |
| `head_fusion` | `"mean"` | `get_esm2_attention_rollout.py` (line 48) | How per-head attention is combined before rollout |
| `device` | auto | both GPU scripts | `cuda` if available, else `cpu` |

Common first-run failures and fixes:

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `FileNotFoundError` when dumping `attention_matrices_labeled_*.joblib` | `attention_matrices_chunks/` missing | `mkdir -p attention_matrices_chunks figures` (Step 3) |
| Script hangs or errors inside `extract_IDR` | IUPred2A path still points to the authors' HPC | Edit `iupred_filepath`, line 25 of `scripts/attention_functions.py` (Step 2) |
| `torch.cuda.is_available()` prints `False` | CPU-only torch build or missing CUDA 12.1 driver | Verify driver supports CUDA 12.1; the pinned wheels are `torch==2.5.1+cu121` |
| CUDA out of memory during stage 1 | Batch too large or long sequences | Reduce `batch_size` (line 45); the script already calls `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` each batch |
| Rollout stage fails loading chunk *i* | Stage 1 interrupted mid-run, or `save_interval` changed | Re-run stage 1 unchanged; chunk indices 0–21 must all exist |

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L42-L45), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L48), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L553)

## Where to Go Next

With the Figure 1 workflow verified on your machine, follow the natural reading order of this documentation set:

- [External Data Acquisition](3-external-data-acquisition) — a deep guide to `esm2_interp_data.py` and the committed-vs-live data trade-offs, including how to pin the exact paper datasets for reproducibility.
- [Reproducing Paper Figures](4-reproducing-paper-figures) — command sequences for Figures 3–5 (ClinVar residues, contact maps, the Rg predictor with `mlp_final.pt`).
- [Script Pipeline Architecture](5-script-pipeline-architecture) — how the fourteen scripts in `scripts/` relate and share state.
- [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction) — the internals of stage 1 you just ran: tokenization, `need_head_weights`, and chunked serialization.
- [Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm) — the math behind `discard_ratio=0.9` and `head_fusion="mean"` from stage 2.
- [Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A](10-disorder-scoring-with-iupred2a) — why the line-25 edit in Step 2 matters biologically.

# External Data Acquisition



This page explains how `plm_interp` obtains every external dataset used in the paper — where each source lives, which downloads are automated, which are manual, and how raw downloads become the curated files committed to `data/`. Because this repository studies proteins drawn from public biology databases, data acquisition is the first practical step for anyone reproducing the analyses, and it is deliberately designed around one central script: `scripts/esm2_interp_data.py`.

## The Two-Track Data Philosophy: Committed Snapshots vs. Living Databases

The repository's foundational design decision is captured in a warning at the top of `esm2_interp_data.py`: sources like PDB, ClinVar, gene2refseq, GRCh38, and DisProt are **living databases** with no version pinned in their URLs, so a file downloaded today *will* differ from the version used in the study (PDB snapshot July 16, 2025; DisProt July 28, 2025; ClinVar/NCBI files February 3, 2026). The script's docstring therefore lays out two explicit paths: use the **exact sequences committed to the repo** to reproduce results, or pull fresh data knowing downstream outputs will drift.

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L6-L17), [README.md](README.md#L42)

This duality shows up in every downstream consumer as a single switch. In `clinvar_expanded.py`, the `derived = True` flag (the default) reads the committed `data/clinvar_sequences.csv` snapshot; setting it to `False` instead loads freshly downloaded ClinVar and NCBI files and regenerates that CSV from scratch. The same pattern applies to the PDB/DisProt side, where the committed `protein_input_sets.csv` and `pdb_disprot.fasta` let you skip the filtering steps entirely.

Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L17-L19), [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L19-L27)

| Aspect | Derived track (default) | Live track |
|---|---|---|
| What you use | Committed snapshots in `data/` | Fresh downloads from external DBs |
| Reproducibility | Exact match to paper | Approximate (databases update weekly) |
| Required action | None — clone and run | Run `esm2_interp_data.py`, flip `derived = False` |
| Curation step | Skipped | Must re-run filtering/regeneration |

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L19-L35), [README.md](README.md#L36-L42)

## The Complete Source Inventory

The docstring of `esm2_interp_data.py` doubles as the canonical catalog of external data: each entry names the source, its access date, the download URL, and the exact file path where it must land in `data/`. The table below consolidates that catalog along with the acquisition method for each source — a distinction that matters because some files download automatically, some require browser interaction, and some are already committed.

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L36-L76), [README.md](README.md#L44-L63)

| Source | Snapshot accessed | Saved as | Method | Stability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RCSB PDB sequences | July 16, 2025 | `data/pdb_seqres.txt.gz` | Automatic | Living DB, updated weekly |
| NCBI ClinVar variants | Feb 3, 2026 | `data/variant_summary.txt.gz` | Automatic | Living DB, updated weekly |
| NCBI gene2refseq | Feb 3, 2026 | `data/gene2refseq` (decompressed TSV) | Automatic + gzip decompress | Updated regularly |
| NCBI GRCh38 latest protein | Feb 3, 2026 | `data/GRCh38_latest_protein_copy.faa` | Automatic + gzip decompress | Unpinned "latest" release |
| DisProt release 2025_06 | July 28, 2025 | `data/disprot.fasta` | Committed to repo | Archived snapshot |
| DescribeProt (human, 9606) | Feb 3, 2026 | `data/9606_database.json` | **Manual** browser download | Server-side resource |
| IDRome Supplementary Table 3 | Static | `data/Supplementary_Table_3.xlsx` | Automatic | Stable file |
| STARLING/SAXS comparison | Static | `data/all_comparison_data_WITH_STARTING.csv` | Automatic | Stable GitHub file |
| IDRome DB (MD-derived Rg) | — | Referenced by `rg_mlp.py` | Documented in README | GitHub-hosted CSV |

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L38-L76), [README.md](README.md#L60-L63), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L21-L30)

Within the `data/` directory, the committed snapshots and the to-be-downloaded raw files sit side by side:

```
data/
├── disprot.fasta                        # Committed DisProt snapshot (2025_06)
├── pdb_disprot.fasta                    # Derived: curated PDB + DisProt set
├── protein_input_sets.csv               # Derived: filtered ID + sequence pairs
├── clustered_input.fasta(.clstr)        # Derived: CD-HIT clustered inputs
├── clinvar_sequences.csv                # Derived: validated ClinVar variants
├── idrome.fasta / idrome_clustered.fasta(.clstr)   # IDRome sequence snapshots
├── attn_corr_norm_es.csv / esm2_perplexities.csv   # Script-generated summaries
├── jac_batch_directory.csv
├── pdb_seqres.txt.gz                    # ↓ Auto-downloaded
├── variant_summary.txt.gz               # ↓ Auto-downloaded
├── gene2refseq                          # ↓ Auto-downloaded + decompressed
├── GRCh38_latest_protein_copy.faa       # ↓ Auto-downloaded + decompressed
├── 9606_database.json                   # ↓ Manual browser download
├── Supplementary_Table_3.xlsx           # ↓ Auto-downloaded
└── all_comparison_data_WITH_STARTING.csv# ↓ Auto-downloaded
```

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L43-L76), [README.md](README.md#L44-L46)

## Inside the Acquisition Hub: `scripts/esm2_interp_data.py`

The script's architecture is a thin orchestration layer over two reusable helpers. `download_file()` performs a streaming HTTP request with a 120-second timeout, validates the response with `raise_for_status()`, and writes the body in 8192-byte chunks while a `tqdm` progress bar tracks bytes against the reported `content-length`. `decompress_gz()` then expands gzip archives (used for `gene2refseq.gz` and `GRCh38_latest_protein.faa.gz`) with a streamed `shutil.copyfileobj` copy.

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L93-L115)

On top of these helpers sit six purpose-named download functions — `download_pdb()`, `download_clinvar()`, `download_gene2refseq()`, `download_grch38()`, `download_idrome_supplementary()`, and `download_starling()` — each wrapped in print statements that restate the access date and warn when the target is a living database. The intent is that a beginner can read the console output and immediately understand the provenance of every file landing in `data/`.

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L124-L214)

> [!TIP]
> When you run `python scripts/esm2_interp_data.py`, only two downloads execute by default: `download_idrome_supplementary()` and `download_starling()`. The four NCBI/RCSB download calls in the `__main__` block are **commented out** — you must uncomment them if you intend to run the live ClinVar or PDB/DisProt pipelines rather than the committed snapshots.

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L228-L233)

The end-to-end flow when you run the script looks like this:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["python scripts/esm2_interp_data.py"] --> B{"Which downloads<br/>are uncommented?"}
    B -->|"Default state"| C["IDRome Suppl. Table 3 (.xlsx)"]
    B -->|"Default state"| D["STARLING/SAXS comparison (.csv)"]
    B -->|"Uncommented"| E["PDB pdb_seqres.txt.gz"]
    B -->|"Uncommented"| F["ClinVar variant_summary.txt.gz"]
    B -->|"Uncommented"| G["gene2refseq.gz → gene2refseq"]
    B -->|"Uncommented"| H["GRCh38_latest_protein.faa.gz → .faa"]
    C & D & E & F & G & H --> I["data/ directory populated"]
    I --> J["Console prints manual-download reminders:<br/>disprot.fasta (archived) + 9606_database.json"]
```

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L219-L249)

## Manual Downloads and the IUPred2A Tool Dependency

Two data files cannot be fetched by the script and require manual action. The first is **`data/9606_database.json`** — the DescribeProt evolutionary conservation database for *Homo sapiens*, which you download through the VCU biomine server by selecting the human (taxon 9606) row and saving the raw data; the script's closing console message repeats these instructions after the automatic downloads finish.

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L62-L67), [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L237-L247)

The second is **DisProt itself**: rather than pointing at a live DisProt URL, the script instructs you to use the archived `release_2025_06 with_ambiguous_evidences` snapshot already committed as `data/disprot.fasta`, preserving the exact disorder-annotation provenance of the study.

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L38-L44), [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L240-L242)

Beyond data, one **external tool** must be acquired before attention analyses can run: IUPred2A, the intrinsic-disorder predictor, which you install manually from `https://iupred2a.elte.hu/` and then register by updating `iupred_filepath` near the top of `scripts/attention_functions.py` (it currently points to the authors' HPC path, so it will not resolve on your machine). This is the only configuration edit the README explicitly requires post-installation.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L17-L19), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L23-L25)

## From Raw Downloads to Derived Datasets

The raw files above are not consumed directly by the analyses — two curation scripts transform them into the compact derived datasets committed to the repo. On the PDB/DisProt side, `define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py` reads the DisProt FASTA and the PDB `pdb_seqres.txt.gz`, applies symmetric quality filters (deduplicate sequences, keep lengths between 50 and 1024 residues, drop PDB sequences containing non-canonical characters `X|U|O`), and then bin-matches the ordered PDB set to the DisProt length distribution across 20 length bins (using `random_state=42` for reproducibility) before writing `data/protein_input_sets.csv`.

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L14-L50), [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L51-L56)

> [!TIP]
> The repeated length ceiling of **1024 residues** across both curation scripts is not arbitrary — it aligns with ESM-2's usable context window (the Rg training script pins `SEQ_LENGTH = 1022`). Filtering at acquisition time guarantees no sequence silently exceeds what the model can embed later.

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L17-L18), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L108-L110), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L34-L35)

On the ClinVar side, running `clinvar_expanded.py` with `derived = False` executes the full live pipeline: it filters `variant_summary.txt.gz` to pathogenic single-nucleotide variants, maps mRNA (NM) accessions to protein (NP) accessions by streaming `gene2refseq` in 100,000-row chunks and keeping only human taxon 9606, joins sequences from the GRCh38 protein FASTA via BioPython's `SeqIO`, enforces the same 50–1024 length window, drops ambiguous residues, removes genes mapping to multiple sequences, and finally validates that each parsed mutation's wild-type amino acid actually appears at the stated position before regenerating `data/clinvar_sequences.csv`.

Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L70-L119), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L120-L140)

The complete acquisition-to-analysis data flow looks like this:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph EXT["External databases"]
        DP["DisProt<br/>(archived snapshot)"]
        PDB["RCSB PDB<br/>pdb_seqres.txt.gz"]
        CV["ClinVar<br/>variant_summary.txt.gz"]
        G2R["gene2refseq"]
        GR["GRCh38 protein FASTA"]
    end
    subgraph CUR["Curation scripts"]
        S1["define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py"]
        S2["clinvar_expanded.py (derived=False)"]
    end
    subgraph OUT["Committed derived datasets (data/)"]
        O1["protein_input_sets.csv"]
        O2["pdb_disprot.fasta"]
        O3["clustered_input.fasta(.clstr)"]
        O4["clinvar_sequences.csv"]
    end
    DP --> S1
    PDB --> S1
    S1 --> O1 --> O2 --> O3
    CV --> S2
    G2R --> S2
    GR --> S2
    S2 --> O4
```

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L9-L12), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L22-L33)

If you stay on the derived track (the default), you can skip both curation scripts entirely and go straight to analysis — which is why the README's reproduction table shows `esm2_interp_data.py` as step 1 only for Figure 3 (ClinVar) and Figure 5 (Rg/SAXS), where genuinely external files are mandatory inputs.

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L19-L27), [README.md](README.md#L88-L97)

## Licensing and Redistribution Boundaries

Because this repository redistributes snapshots of third-party biological data, the README is explicit that the MIT license covers **code only**: the committed DisProt files are CC BY 4.0, PDB-derived entries are CC0 1.0, IDRome sequences are GPL-3.0, and ClinVar-derived data is public domain, each with its citation listed in a dedicated table. Critically, anything you download via `esm2_interp_data.py` is *not* redistributed here and remains under its provider's terms.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L67-L78)

A parallel note covers **third-party code**: the contact-map functions adapted from the `pLMs-interpretability` project carry no stated license and are explicitly excluded from this repo's MIT coverage — worth knowing if you plan to reuse `get_contact_maps.py` in your own work.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L82-L84)

With data acquisition understood, a natural progression is to see how these inputs feed the analyses. Continue in order with [Reproducing Paper Figures](4-reproducing-paper-figures) to run the full figure pipeline, then move into the Deep Dive with [Script Pipeline Architecture](5-script-pipeline-architecture) for the execution graph. When you want the deeper treatment of topics touched lightly here, see [Dataset Curation and CD-HIT Clustering](21-dataset-curation-and-cd-hit-clustering) for the clustering stage that produces `clustered_input.fasta`, [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility) for the snapshot strategy in depth, and the consumer analyses [Ordered Versus Disordered Comparison](12-ordered-versus-disordered-comparison) and [ClinVar Disease Residue Attention](13-clinvar-disease-residue-attention) that sit immediately downstream of the files this page helps you acquire.

# Reproducing Paper Figures



This page is your operational guide to regenerating every figure from the paper *Mechanistic Interpretability of Protein Language Models Reveals Encoded Structural and Functional Properties of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins*. The reproduction layer consists of exactly two files at the repository root: **`scripts/figures.py`** — a single script that draws all main-text figures (1–5) and appendix figures (A1–A5) — and **`publication.mplstyle`** — a matplotlib stylesheet that enforces the journal's visual language. Crucially, `figures.py` does not compute any analysis itself; it is a pure *rendering stage* that reads pre-computed summary CSVs and turns them into final SVG files. Understanding this "plots-from-CSV" design is the key to reproducing results without re-running expensive GPU analyses unnecessarily.

Sources: [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L1-L53), [publication.mplstyle](/publication.mplstyle#L1-L15), [README.md](/README.md#L88-L96)

## The Two-File Reproduction Layer

The repository separates *computation* from *presentation*. The upstream analysis scripts (attention extraction, ClinVar analysis, contact maps, MLP training) do the heavy lifting and persist their results as small summary tables. `figures.py` then acts as a single consolidated rendering pass over those tables. The full data flow looks like this:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph RAW["Stage 1 — Raw inputs (committed in data/)"]
        R1["protein_input_sets.csv"]
        R2["attn_corr_norm_es.csv"]
        R3["FASTA / ClinVar / IDRome sources"]
    end
    subgraph PIPE["Stage 2 — Analysis pipeline (scripts/)"]
        S1["get_esm2_attention_matrices.py"]
        S2["get_esm2_attention_rollout.py"]
        S3["clinvar_expanded.py"]
        S4["md_contact_maps_analysis.py"]
        S5["rg_mlp.py / es_ablation2.py"]
    end
    subgraph DERIVED["Stage 3 — Summary tables (data/figure_data/)"]
        C1["umap_df.csv"]
        C2["comb_data.csv"]
        C3["comparison.csv"]
        C4["df_eval.csv, ols_df.csv, ..."]
    end
    subgraph RENDER["Stage 4 — Rendering layer"]
        F["figures.py"]
        ST["publication.mplstyle"]
    end
    OUT["figures/final/*.svg (300 dpi)"]

    RAW --> PIPE
    PIPE --> DERIVED
    DERIVED --> F
    ST --> F
    F --> OUT
```

A few foundational facts anchor this architecture. First, `figures.py` resolves all paths relative to the repository root via `SCRIPT_DIR`/`BASE_PATH`, so it must be run from a normal clone — not a flattened copy. Second, every plot block applies the shared stylesheet (`plt.style.use(...)`) plus a colorblind-safe Okabe–Ito color cycle, and configures SVG output so that text stays as live text rather than being rasterized into paths. Third, each figure block is self-contained: it loads its own CSVs, draws, and saves, which means the blocks execute sequentially with no shared state between figures.

Sources: [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L6-L29), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](/scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L33-L41), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L17-L18)

> [!TIP]
> **The summary directory `data/figure_data/` is *not* committed to this repository.** The committed `data/` folder contains only raw inputs (e.g., `protein_input_sets.csv`, `attn_corr_norm_es.csv`). Running `python scripts/figures.py` on a fresh clone will fail at its very first `pd.read_csv` call. You must first run the upstream pipeline for the figure(s) you want — the command chains are in the README's "Reproducing Results" table — which generate the summary CSVs that `figures.py` consumes.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L25-L48), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L60-L60)

## End-to-End Reproduction Workflow

The practical workflow follows the same three phases regardless of which figure you target: prepare the environment, run the figure-specific analysis pipeline, then render. Note that the most computationally expensive steps (ESM-2 forward passes on GPU) live entirely in the pipeline stage — `figures.py` itself needs only pandas, NumPy, SciPy, and matplotlib.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["1. conda env create -f environment.yml && conda activate torch-gpu"] --> B["2. mkdir -p figures/final"]
    B --> C{"Which figure?"}
    C -->|Fig 1 & 2| D["get_esm2_attention_matrices.py → get_esm2_attention_rollout.py → attention_rollout_analysis.py"]
    C -->|Fig 3| E["esm2_interp_data.py → clinvar_expanded.py"]
    C -->|Fig 4| F["get_contact_maps.py → md_variable_cutoff.py → md_contact_maps_analysis.py"]
    C -->|Fig 5| G["esm2_interp_data.py → rg_mlp.py → es_ablation2.py"]
    D --> H["3. python scripts/figures.py"]
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H
    H --> I["SVGs land in figures/final/"]
```

The README's "Reproducing Results" table is the authoritative mapping between paper figures and pipeline commands (all commands run from inside the `scripts/` directory):

| Paper Figure | Pipeline Command Chain |
|---|---|
| Figure 1 | `get_esm2_attention_matrices.py` → `get_esm2_attention_rollout.py` → `attention_rollout_analysis.py` |
| Figure 2 | `get_esm2_attention_matrices.py` → `get_esm2_attention_rollout.py` → `attention_rollout_analysis.py` |
| Figure 3 | `esm2_interp_data.py` → `clinvar_expanded.py` |
| Figure 4 | `get_contact_maps.py` → `md_variable_cutoff.py` → `md_contact_maps_analysis.py` |
| Figure 5 | `esm2_interp_data.py` → `rg_mlp.py` → `es_ablation2.py` |

Two constraints from the README deserve emphasis for beginners: the raw attention-matrix and rollout artifacts are large and are explicitly *not* committed to GitHub, so Figures 1 and 2 always require a GPU re-run of the extraction scripts; and external databases (ClinVar, IDRome, SAXS datasets) are downloaded via `esm2_interp_data.py`, which should be run before Figures 3, 4, and 5.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L9-L16), [README.md](/README.md#L44-L48), [README.md](/README.md#L88-L96)

## The Complete Figure Inventory

`figures.py` is organized top-to-bottom as one commented block per paper figure. Each block reads its specific inputs from `data/figure_data/` and writes SVGs to `figures/final/` at 300 dpi. This table is your map for locating — and selectively editing — any panel:

| Figure | Panels Rendered | Input CSVs (`data/figure_data/`) | Output SVGs (`figures/final/`) | Code Lines |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fig 1 — Attention Analysis | UMAP (grouped + IDR-fraction colored), disorder-bin KDE, TDP-43 annotation track | `umap_df.csv`, `disorder_comp_concat.csv`, `si_examples.csv` | `umap.svg`, `attn_kde.svg`, `tdp43.svg` | L56–135 |
| Fig 2 — AA Attention Allocation | Mean attention-by-amino-acid bars; Cys/Asp head×layer heatmaps (PDB vs DisProt) | `mean_aa_attn.csv`, `attn_occur_norm.csv` | `mean_aa_attn_received.svg`, `asp_cys_heatmaps.svg` | L137–207 |
| Fig 3 — Pathogenicity | ClinVar attention-percentile histograms, boxplots by disorder bin, disease AA counts, AA-group boxplots, logistic + OLS betas | `comb_data.csv`, `log_df.csv`, `ols_df.csv` | `clinvar_expanded_*.svg`, `clinvar_log_reg.svg`, `ols_clinvar.svg` | L211–363 |
| Fig 4 — Contact Maps | Observed-vs-null Spearman distribution; ESM/MD enrichment agreement matrix | `combined_data.csv`, `comparison.csv` | `jac_md_observed_vs_null_distribution.svg`, `md_esm_top_decile_agreement.svg` | L365–413 |
| Fig 5 — Rg MLP | Parity plots (Tesei/SAXS/STARLING); head-ablation sweep with random-ablation band | `df_eval.csv`, `saxs_proteins.csv`, `es_ablation_sweep_df_idrome_random_consecutive.csv` | `rg_mlp.svg`, `head_ablation_sweep_.svg` | L415–510 |
| Fig A1 — Dataset Profiles | Sequence-length histogram, IDR-count histogram, AA frequency bars | `protein_input_sets.csv` (committed, at `data/`), `idr_df.csv`, `comb_props.csv` | `input_sets_seqlen_distribution.svg`, `input_sets_disorder.svg`, `aa_proportional_frequency.svg` | L513–570 |
| Fig A2 — SI Examples | Per-protein attention/disorder line tracks | `si_examples.csv` | `si_examples.svg` | L574–598 |
| Fig A3 — Enrichment Heatmaps | ESM-2 Jacobian and MD top-decile enrichment matrices | `comparison.csv` | `esm2_top_decile_enrichment.svg`, `md_top_decile_enrichment.svg` | L601–637 |
| Fig A4 — MLP Training | Train/validation MSE learning curves with best-epoch marker | `training_curve_long.csv` | `mlp_final_curves.svg` | L639–660 |
| Fig A5 — DEKR Heatmaps | Per-amino-acid head×layer attention grids (20 amino acids) | `attn_corr_norm_es.csv` | `DEKR_heatmaps.svg` | L662–706 |

Because the script is monolithic with no command-line arguments, it executes every block in order on each run. If you only need, say, Figure 4, the pragmatic beginner strategy is to comment out the blocks above it — each block fails independently if its CSV is missing, so partial runs are best done by selective commenting rather than expecting graceful skipping.

Sources: [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L56-L135), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L211-L363), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L415-L510), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L513-L706)

## The Publication Styling System

Every figure inherits its look from `publication.mplstyle`, a 15-line stylesheet loaded once at the top of `figures.py`. The settings encode standard journal-figure conventions: Arial at 6 pt, hairline axes (0.5 pt) with top/right spines removed, borderless legends, and thin data lines. Two entries are especially meaningful for downstream editing: `pdf.fonttype: 42` embeds TrueType glyphs so PDF text remains selectable, and the companion rcParam `svg.fonttype: 'none'` set in code keeps SVG text as editable `<text>` elements rather than converting labels to outlines.

| Style Setting | Value | Visual Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `font.family` / `font.size` | Arial / 6 | Compact journal typography |
| `axes.spines.top` / `.right` | False | Open, minimal frame |
| `axes.linewidth` | 0.5 | Hairline axis frame |
| `xtick/ytick.major.width` / `.size` | 0.5 / 2 | Fine, unobtrusive ticks |
| `legend.frameon` | False | Borderless legends |
| `lines.linewidth` | 1 | Thin data series |
| `pdf.fonttype` | 42 | Editable TrueType text in PDFs |

Beyond the stylesheet, `figures.py` implements a **modular panel grid** for multi-panel composition. The canvas is defined as 183 × 170 mm (183 mm being the standard double-column width of major scientific journals), divided into a 4 × 4 grid of 42 × 38.75 mm units separated by 5 mm gaps. The `panel_size(cols, rows)` helper converts any grid footprint into matplotlib's `figsize` in inches — so `panel_size(cols=4, rows=1)` yields exactly (7.2, 1.53), the wide strip used for Figure 1's TDP-43 track and Figure 5's parity plots, while `panel_size(cols=2, rows=2)` yields the square used for heatmap panels. A reference table at module load even prints the `figsize` call for all eight used grid shapes, as an aid when collating panels in a vector editor.

Color semantics are also centralized: PDB proteins render in orange and DisProt in steelblue via `group_color_map`, disease-relevant residues swap to orange in Figure 3, the head-ablation sweep uses a fixed red/blue/gray scale, and the base color cycle is the colorblind-safe Okabe–Ito palette.

Sources: [publication.mplstyle](/publication.mplstyle#L1-L15), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L26-L45), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L49-L53), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L29-L29)

> [!TIP]
> **SVG text stays editable by design.** The combination of `svg.fonttype: 'none'` and `pdf.fonttype: 42` means axis labels, legends, and titles survive into vector editors (Illustrator, Inkscape) as real text — this is intentional so figures can be collated and annotated for the paper. If you convert these SVGs through rasterizing tools, you will destroy that editability; keep them as vectors.

## Relationship to the Exploratory Pipeline Plots

A subtle point worth understanding: the analysis scripts already produce their own plots as they run, but these are *exploratory* drafts saved to `figures/` — for example, `attention_rollout_analysis.py` saves an intermediate sequence-length distribution to `figures/input_sets_seqlen_distribution.svg`, and `es_ablation2.py` saves an exploratory D/E/K/R heatmap to `figures/DEKR_heatmaps.svg`. The versions in `figures.py` are the *final* publication rebuilds, re-drawn from the persisted summary CSVs into `figures/final/` with refined layout, panel sizing, and legend placement. This two-tier pattern means you can iterate on final figure aesthetics cheaply (just re-run `figures.py`) without ever touching the GPU-bound analysis stage.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](/scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L51-L66), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L136-L172)

## Troubleshooting Guide

| Symptom | Root Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `FileNotFoundError` on `data/figure_data/umap_df.csv` (first block) | `figure_data/` is a derived directory, not committed | Run the upstream pipeline chain for your target figure (see README table), then re-run `figures.py` |
| `FileNotFoundError` when saving to `figures/final/` | Neither `figures.py` nor pipeline scripts create directories | Run `mkdir -p figures/final` before first execution |
| Figure A5 fails on `attn_corr_norm_es.csv` in `figure_data/` | `figures.py` reads it from `data/figure_data/`, but the committed copy lives at `data/attn_corr_norm_es.csv` (as read by `es_ablation2.py`) | Copy `data/attn_corr_norm_es.csv` into `data/figure_data/` |
| Matplotlib warning about missing Arial | Linux containers typically lack MS core fonts | Install `ttf-mscorefonts-installer` (or accept the DejaVu fallback; layout will shift slightly) |
| Script re-runs everything on every execution | `figures.py` is a sequential, argument-free script | Comment out blocks above the figure you need; each block is self-contained |
| "Do I need a GPU for figures.py?" | Confusion with the pipeline stage | No — `figures.py` only uses pandas/NumPy/SciPy/matplotlib; GPU work happens in `get_esm2_attention_matrices.py` and friends |

Sources: [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L60-L60), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L85-L85), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L136-L136), [README.md](/README.md#L88-L96)

- For the science behind individual figures, proceed to **[Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm)** (Figures 1–2), **[ClinVar Disease Residue Attention](13-clinvar-disease-residue-attention)** (Figure 3), **[Categorical Jacobian Contact Maps](14-categorical-jacobian-contact-maps)** and **[MD Trajectory Contact Validation](15-md-trajectory-contact-validation)** (Figure 4), and **[MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor)** plus **[Attention Head Ablation Study](18-attention-head-ablation-study)** (Figure 5).

# Script Pipeline Architecture



This page explains how the fourteen Python scripts in `scripts/` are organized as a research codebase: the shared foundation module, the four independently reproducible analysis pipelines that each produce one paper figure, and the cross-cutting engineering patterns (path resolution, chunked serialization, memory management) that hold the system together. This is an architecture-level explanation — algorithm internals are deferred to their dedicated pages in the Deep Dive catalog.

## Layered Architecture: Foundation, Pipelines, and Presentation

The codebase follows a three-layer architecture despite being a flat directory of scripts. At the bottom sits `attention_functions.py`, a 530-line library containing every reusable routine — FASTA parsing, disorder prediction, attention rollout, embedding extraction, and statistical comparison. Above it, ten executable analysis scripts are arranged into four independent pipelines, each corresponding to one figure of the paper. At the top, `figures.py` acts as a pure presentation layer that consumes CSV intermediates under `data/figure_data/` and renders publication-quality output using the committed `publication.mplstyle` stylesheet.

The critical insight is that **data flows through files, not function calls**: scripts communicate only through serialized artifacts (`joblib` chunks, CSV files, FASTA files), which makes every stage independently interruptible and re-runnable. This decoupling is what allows the README to express the entire study as five short command sequences in its "Reproducing Results" table, where each figure maps to a linear chain of script invocations.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph DATA["data/ — committed inputs"]
        INPUTS["protein_input_sets.csv<br/>clinvar_sequences.csv<br/>idrome.fasta ..."]
    end
    subgraph FOUNDATION["Foundation Layer"]
        AF["attention_functions.py<br/>(530 lines, shared library)"]
    end
    subgraph PIPELINES["Analysis Pipelines (scripts/)"]
        P1["get_esm2_attention_matrices<br/>→ get_esm2_attention_rollout<br/>→ attention_rollout_analysis"]
        P2["esm2_interp_data<br/>→ clinvar_expanded"]
        P3["get_contact_maps<br/>→ md_variable_cutoff<br/>→ md_contact_maps_analysis"]
        P4["esm2_interp_data → rg_mlp<br/>→ es_ablation2<br/>+ esm2_ppl_by_disorder"]
    end
    subgraph ARTIFACTS["Derived Artifacts"]
        CHUNKS["attention_matrices_chunks/<br/>(22 joblib chunks, not committed)"]
        FIGDATA["data/figure_data/*.csv"]
    end
    FIG["figures.py<br/>(706 lines) → figures/"]

    INPUTS --> P1
    INPUTS --> P2
    INPUTS --> P3
    INPUTS --> P4
    AF --> P1
    AF --> P2
    AF --> P4
    AF -->|"read_fasta"| P0["define_pdb_disprot_datasets"]
    P0 --> INPUTS
    P1 --> CHUNKS --> P1
    P1 --> FIGDATA
    P2 --> FIGDATA
    P3 --> FIGDATA
    P4 --> FIGDATA
    FIGDATA --> FIG
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L97), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L1-L25), [figures.py](scripts/figures.py#L26-L60)

## The Shared Foundation Module

`attention_functions.py` is the only module imported by other scripts, and it never imports from them — a strict one-directional dependency that prevents circular imports entirely. Six of the fourteen scripts import from it, with varying selectivity: three use wildcard imports (`from attention_functions import *`), while the others import named functions, signaling which capabilities each pipeline actually consumes.

The module's functions cluster into five cohesive concerns, each mapping to a different analytical stage:

| Function | Lines | Concern | Primary Consumer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `read_fasta` | L28–L37 | FASTA → DataFrame ingestion | `define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py` |
| `extract_IDR` / `extract_IDR_profile` | L39–L99 | IUPred2A disorder scoring (subprocess) | `clinvar_expanded.py`, `esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py` |
| `attention_rollout` / `get_attn_rollout` | L144–L249 | Attention fusion across layers/heads | `get_esm2_attention_rollout.py`, `clinvar_expanded.py` |
| `get_esm2_embeddings` | L391–L429 | Mean-pooled layer-33 embeddings | `rg_mlp.py` |
| `get_head_layer_attn` / `get_aa_attn_perc` / `run_aa_analysis_head_layer` | L256–L389 | Per-head/per-layer amino-acid statistics | `attention_rollout_analysis.py` |
| `fast_statistical_comparison` / `cohens_d` | L431–L530 | Welch t-tests + Cohen's d effect sizes | `attention_rollout_analysis.py` |

Two design details deserve attention. First, the disorder functions shell out to an external IUPred2A installation via `subprocess.Popen` against a hardcoded `iupred_filepath` (L25) — a documented external dependency that every user must reconfigure locally, as the README installation notes instruct. Second, `safe_load` (L252–L254) is a deceptively simple wrapper that calls `gc.collect()` before every `joblib.load`; because the chunk files can be gigabytes, forcing garbage collection *before* the new allocation prevents the old and new chunks from coexisting in memory. This is the module's most load-bearing function, invoked in the rollout loop for all 22 chunks.

```mermaid
graph TD
    AF["attention_functions.py"]
    ARA["attention_rollout_analysis.py<br/>import *"]
    ROLLOUT["get_esm2_attention_rollout.py<br/>import safe_load, attention_rollout"]
    CLINVAR["clinvar_expanded.py<br/>import attention_rollout,<br/>extract_IDR_profile, extract_IDR, get_attn_rollout"]
    RG["rg_mlp.py<br/>import get_esm2_embeddings"]
    PPL["esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py<br/>import extract_IDR_profile"]
    ABL["es_ablation2.py<br/>import *"]
    DEF["define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py<br/>import * (read_fasta)"]

    AF --> ARA
    AF --> ROLLOUT
    AF --> CLINVAR
    AF --> RG
    AF --> PPL
    AF --> ABL
    AF --> DEF

    STANDALONE["Standalone scripts<br/>(no foundation dependency):<br/>get_esm2_attention_matrices.py<br/>get_contact_maps.py<br/>md_variable_cutoff.py<br/>md_contact_maps_analysis.py<br/>esm2_interp_data.py<br/>figures.py"]
```

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L252-L254), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L8), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L10), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L6), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L19), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L8), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L11), [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L5)

## The Attention Pipeline: A Chunked Producer–Consumer Contract

The Figure 1/2 pipeline is the repository's architectural centerpiece, and its robustness comes from an explicit **file-format contract** between producer and consumer. `get_esm2_attention_matrices.py` (89 lines) loads ESM-2 (`esm2_t33_650M_UR50D` via the fairseq interface, L29), reads `data/protein_input_sets.csv` (L36), and runs inference with `need_head_weights=True` at `batch_size=2` (L45, L55). Each protein is stored as a dictionary with exactly three keys — `sequence`, `attention_matrix` (a NumPy array of shape 33 layers × 20 heads × L × L), and `sequence_length` (L63–L67).

The producer never holds the full dataset in memory. Every 200 proteins (`save_interval = 200`, L42), it flushes accumulated results to a compressed joblib chunk named `attention_matrices_labeled_{chunk_num}_{model_type}.joblib` with `compress=3` (L78), resets its buffer, and forces garbage collection (L82). The result is 22 chunks on disk.

The consumer, `get_esm2_attention_rollout.py` (57 lines), is deliberately thin: it iterates `range(0, 22)` (L36), loads each chunk through `safe_load`, computes rollout per protein with `discard_ratio=0.9, head_fusion="mean"` (L48), and accumulates everything into a single dictionary that it saves as one combined joblib file. The downstream `attention_rollout_analysis.py` (483 lines) then loads that single file (L40), splits it into PDB/DisProt dictionaries by ID substring matching (L44–L45), and runs the statistical suite — UMAP embedding, silhouette scoring, GroupKFold logistic regression, and false-discovery-rate control (L9–L16).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["protein_input_sets.csv"] --> B["get_esm2_attention_matrices.py<br/>ESM-2 inference, batch_size=2"]
    B --> C1["attention_matrices_labeled_0_original.joblib"]
    B --> C2["attention_matrices_labeled_1_original.joblib"]
    B --> C3["... 22 chunks total (200 proteins each)"]
    C1 & C2 & C3 --> D["get_esm2_attention_rollout.py<br/>safe_load per chunk →<br/>attention_rollout(discard_ratio=0.9)"]
    D --> E["attention_rollout_comb_original.joblib<br/>(single combined dict)"]
    E --> F["attention_rollout_analysis.py<br/>UMAP · silhouette · logistic regression · FDR"]
    F --> G["data/figure_data/*.csv"]
    G --> H["figures.py → Figure 1 & 2"]
```

This contract has a practical consequence for reproducibility: attention matrices are the only major dataset not committed to the repository (README L47), so this three-script chain is mandatory before any Figure 1/2 analysis. The algorithmic details of the rollout computation itself are covered in [Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm), and the memory-pressure reasoning behind chunk sizing in [Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management).

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L42-L88), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L36-L53), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L36-L45), [README.md](README.md#L44-L48)

## The Three Validation Pipelines

The remaining pipelines validate ESM-2's encoded knowledge against external ground truth, and each reveals a different architectural decision.

**ClinVar pipeline (Figure 3).** `clinvar_expanded.py` (448 lines) is the largest consumer of the foundation module, importing four functions spanning both concerns — rollout (`attention_rollout`, `get_attn_rollout`) and disorder (`extract_IDR`, `extract_IDR_profile`). Its most architecturally significant feature is the `derived = True` flag (L22): when set, the script reads the committed `data/clinvar_sequences.csv` snapshot instead of downloading live NCBI databases. This flag-based reproducibility switch is documented extensively in `esm2_interp_data.py` (L18–L27), which serves as both a downloader and an in-file data provenance manual — its first 60 lines are documentation about living-database version drift, embedded as code comments.

**Contact map / MD validation pipeline (Figure 4).** This branch is the only one that is *fully standalone* — `get_contact_maps.py` (276 lines) computes categorical Jacobians and contains the `do_apc`, `get_categorical_jacobian`, and `get_contacts` functions adapted from external prior work (Zhang et al., per the README's third-party code notice, L82–L84). It is followed by `md_variable_cutoff.py` (161 lines), which encodes a per-amino-acid distance threshold table (`sigma_map`, L19–L40) sourced from published geometry, and `md_contact_maps_analysis.py` (293 lines), which validates correlations via 1000-permutation null distributions with a fixed seed (L22–L36). The three-stage structure — generate, threshold-tune, statistically validate — mirrors the classic compute/calibrate/test separation.

**Rg prediction and causal ablation pipeline (Figure 5).** `rg_mlp.py` (415 lines) trains a radius-of-gyration predictor on mean-pooled ESM-2 embeddings obtained through `get_esm2_embeddings`, with a constants block at the top (L36–L47) that fully specifies the training regime: `SEED=42`, `EPOCHS=200`, `HIDDEN_DIM=512`, `REPR_LAYER=33`. The model weights are committed as `mlp_final.pt` at the repository root. Its counterpart `es_ablation2.py` (562 lines) ablates attention heads to test causality — and here the architecture shows its research-code tradeoff: the script *duplicates* the `RgMLP` class (L47–L50) and the hyperparameter constants (L35–L36) rather than importing them from `rg_mlp.py`, keeping both scripts independently runnable at the cost of literal code duplication. A supplementary fourth analysis, `esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py` (141 lines), runs perplexity-versus-disorder regression using the HuggingFace model interface and imports only `extract_IDR_profile` from the foundation.

| Pipeline | Scripts (in execution order) | Foundation Imports | Standalone? | Output Consumer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Attention (Fig 1–2) | matrices → rollout → analysis | 3 of 3 scripts | No | `figures.py` |
| ClinVar (Fig 3) | interp_data → clinvar_expanded | Yes (4 functions) | No | `figures.py` |
| Contact/MD (Fig 4) | contact_maps → cutoff → analysis | None | **Fully standalone** | `figures.py` |
| Rg/Ablation (Fig 5) | interp_data → rg_mlp → ablation | 2 of 3 scripts | No | `figures.py` |

Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L20-L34), [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L7-L34), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L16-L21), [md_variable_cutoff.py](scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py#L14-L40), [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L22-L36), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L35-L47), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L32-L50)

## Cross-Cutting Engineering Patterns

Three conventions are replicated verbatim across all fourteen scripts, forming the codebase's implicit style contract.

**Path resolution idiom.** Every script begins with the same two lines: `SCRIPT_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent` followed by `BASE_PATH = SCRIPT_DIR.parent`. All file access then flows through these anchors — inputs from `{BASE_PATH}/data/`, derived tensors to `{BASE_PATH}/attention_matrices_chunks/` — making scripts location-independent regardless of the working directory from which they are launched.

**Dual model interfaces.** The codebase deliberately uses two different ESM-2 APIs depending on the analysis type: the fairseq `esm.pretrained.esm2_t33_650M_UR50D()` interface for raw attention tensors (matrices script, L29) and Jacobian contact maps, versus HuggingFace `AutoModelForMaskedLM` for perplexity computation (`esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py`, L24–L29) and attention extraction within the ClinVar branch (`clinvar_expanded.py`, L9). Each interface exposes what the other lacks — `need_head_weights` for per-head tensors versus `output_attentions` for transformer-native lists — and the choice is dictated purely by the shape of the tensor each analysis needs.

**Explicit GPU memory hygiene.** Computationally heavy scripts follow an identical release discipline: delete tensor references (`del`), call `torch.cuda.empty_cache()`, and force `gc.collect()` inside the batch loop (matrices script, L70–L82), combined with the `safe_load` pre-collection pattern from the foundation module. For an intermediate developer, the lesson generalizes well: when per-item artifacts are large (33×20 attention matrices for proteins up to 1022 residues), *file-level checkpointing with explicit cache eviction* beats clever batching for correctness and resumability.

| Pattern | Mechanism | Benefit | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flat peer imports | Scripts run from `scripts/` dir, import `attention_functions` directly | Zero package scaffolding | Breaks if run from repo root without path setup |
| Chunked joblib contract | 22 files × 200 proteins, `compress=3`, fixed key schema | Resumable, memory-bounded | 22 disk round-trips per full pass |
| `derived` flag | Snapshot CSV vs. live download switch | Bit-exact reproducibility | Two code paths to maintain |
| Constants duplication | `es_ablation2.py` re-declares `RgMLP` + hyperparameters | Scripts remain independent | Divergence risk between trainer and ablator |

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L9-L10), [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L70-L82), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L24-L29), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L9-L22), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L35-L50)

## The Presentation Layer

`figures.py` (706 lines) is the terminal consumer of all four pipelines and is architecturally pure: it performs no model inference, reads only from `data/figure_data/*.csv`, and writes only to `figures/`. It establishes the visual identity centrally — `plt.style.use(f'{BASE_PATH}/publication.mplstyle')` (L26) plus a colorblind-safe palette (L27) — and implements a millimeter-based panel layout system (a 183 mm canvas grid with a `panel_size()` helper, L31–L53) so that multi-panel figures assemble at exact journal column widths. Its file is organized into commented sections, one per paper figure ("Figure 1 - Attention Analysis" at L56), making the script a literal table of contents for the paper's visual output. The styling system itself is examined further in [Publication Figure Styling](23-publication-figure-styling).

> [!TIP]
> The chunk contract (22 joblib files with the `{sequence, attention_matrix, sequence_length}` schema) is the load-bearing interface of the entire repository: if you regenerate attention matrices with modified code, downstream rollout and analysis scripts will silently accept any dict with those keys — verify chunk count matches the consumer's hardcoded `range(0, 22)` before running long jobs.

## Navigating the Deep Dive

With the architectural map established, the natural progression is to descend into each pipeline's internals. For the attention chain, continue with [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction) and [Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm); for disorder scoring used across multiple pipelines, see [Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A](10-disorder-scoring-with-iupred2a); for the validation branches, proceed to [ClinVar Disease Residue Attention](13-clinvar-disease-residue-attention), [Categorical Jacobian Contact Maps](14-categorical-jacobian-contact-maps), and [MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor). The engineering patterns summarized here are expanded in [Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management) and [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility).


# ESM-2 and IDP Biology Primer



This page is the conceptual gateway to the *Interpretability Foundations* section. Everything downstream — attention rollout, disorder comparisons, Rg prediction — rests on two vocabularies: how the **ESM-2 protein language model** works as it is *concretely instantiated* in this repository, and what **intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs)** are as *operationally measured* by this repository's scripts. No prior machine-learning or biophysics background is assumed; every claim below is anchored to code and committed data you can inspect yourself.

## Why One Research Question Needs Two Vocabularies

The repository exists to answer a single question, stated in its own paper title: does mechanistic interpretability of ESM-2 reveal structural and functional properties that the model has *encoded* about intrinsically disordered proteins? To follow any analysis in this repo, you must constantly translate between two kinds of quantities: **machine-learning quantities** (attention weights, embeddings, perplexity) and **biophysics quantities** (disorder probability, IDR segment length, radius of gyration). The code performs this translation on nearly every line, so building both vocabularies up front prevents confusion later.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph ML["Machine-learning vocabulary"]
        A["Amino acid sequence"] --> B["ESM-2 forward pass"]
        B --> C["Attention weights"]
        B --> D["Embeddings / perplexity"]
    end
    subgraph BIO["Biophysics vocabulary"]
        E["Disorder probability (IUPred2A)"]
        F["Radius of gyration (Rg)"]
        G["Disease residues (ClinVar)"]
    end
    C --> H["Do attention patterns track IDP properties?"]
    D --> H
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H
```

The two subgraphs above are not parallel universes — the entire repo is the arrow labeled "Do attention patterns track IDP properties?" The rest of this page defines each node precisely.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L3-L6)

## ESM-2: The Protein Language Model as Instantiated Here

For beginners, the core idea is simple: proteins are strings written in a 20-letter alphabet (`ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY`), and ESM-2 is a **transformer** trained on millions of natural protein sequences to predict letters that have been deliberately hidden.
