During that training it must learn which residues *depend* on which other residues — and the repo's bet is that this learned dependency structure is visible in the model's attention weights. The 20-letter alphabet is explicit in the code's amino acid list [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](/scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L38).

This repository uses one specific checkpoint throughout: `esm2_t33_650M_UR50D`. The name encodes the architecture — **t33** means 33 transformer layers, **650M** means ~650 million parameters, **UR50D** refers to the UniRef50 sequence database it was trained on. The table below summarizes every architecture constant as it appears in the code, so you can map each number to its definition when you read the analysis scripts.

| Property | Value in this repo | Where it is set |
|---|---|---|
| Model checkpoint | `esm2_t33_650M_UR50D` | [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](/scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L29-L32), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](/scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L24-L30) |
| Transformer layers | 33 | [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L149) |
| Attention heads per layer | 20 | [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L160) |
| Embedding dimension | 1280 | [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L47) |
| Max residues per sequence | 1022 (1024 tokens incl. special tokens) | [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L45), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](/scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L45) |
| Representation layer used for embeddings | 33 (final layer) | [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L44) |
| Loading APIs | fairseq `esm.pretrained` (attention), HuggingFace `AutoModelForMaskedLM` (perplexity) | both files above |

> [!TIP]
> The same model weights are loaded through **two different libraries** in this repo: the fairseq-style `esm.pretrained.esm2_t33_650M_UR50D()` for raw per-head attention, and HuggingFace's `AutoModelForMaskedLM` for masked-language-model perplexity. They are the identical checkpoint — do not treat the two loading paths as different models when comparing analyses.

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](/scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L29-L32), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](/scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L24-L38), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L35-L48)

### From Sequence to Attention Tensor

Before a sequence enters the model, it is **tokenized**: each residue becomes a token, and two special tokens are added — a `<cls>` token at the start and an `<eos>` token at the end. This matters enormously for interpreting attention matrices, because the raw model output includes rows and columns for these special tokens; the downstream helper `get_head_layer_attn` explicitly slices them off with `[1:actual_seq_len+1, 1:actual_seq_len+1]` before any biological interpretation [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L273-L277).

The attention output itself is what a beginner most often visualizes incorrectly. When the extraction script calls the model with `need_head_weights=True`, the returned `attentions` tensor is **4-dimensional**: `(33 layers, 20 heads, L, L)`, where L is the padded sequence length. One 2-D slice of this — layer `i`, head `j` — is an L×L matrix in which cell `(row, col)` answers: *"how much did residue `row`'s representation draw on residue `col`'s information?"* The repository's own docstring states this shape requirement verbatim [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L148-L153), and the per-head extraction confirms it by indexing `[layer_idx, head_idx]` to pull a single `(seq_len, seq_len)` slice [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L256-L277).

> [!TIP]
> The attention tensor is **(33, 20, L, L)** — not a single L×L matrix. With 33 layers × 20 heads, there are **660 distinct attention matrices per protein**. Every analysis in this repo is fundamentally a strategy for deciding *which* of those 660 slices (or which summary of them) to compare against biology.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["FASTA sequence"] --> BC["batch_converter tokenization<br/>(adds cls / eos tokens)"]
    BC --> M["esm2_t33_650M_UR50D forward pass<br/>need_head_weights=True"]
    M --> AT["attentions tensor (33, 20, L, L)"]
    AT --> RAW["Per-head matrices<br/>(cls/eos stripped)"]
    AT --> ROLL["Attention rollout<br/>(single L x L summary)"]
    M --> EMB["Layer-33 embeddings (1280-d)"]
    M --> PPL["Masked-LM perplexity"]
```

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](/scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L45-L58), [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L148-L160), [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L256-L277)

## The Three Signals the Repo Extracts from ESM-2

Every interpretability analysis in this catalog consumes one of three derived signals, and knowing their names now makes the rest of the catalog legible. First, **per-head attention matrices** are the raw 4-D tensor saved in chunks to disk — the most detailed, least summarized view [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](/scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L57-L67). Second, **attention rollout** collapses all 33 layers and 20 heads into a single L×L matrix meant to approximate *total* information flow between residue pairs; the algorithm mean-fuses heads within each layer, discards the lowest 90% of attention values, blends in the identity matrix to account for residual connections, then multiplies the per-layer matrices together [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L159-L218), with fusion and discard parameters set at the call site [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](/scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L48). Third, **embeddings and perplexity** probe what the model *knows* rather than where it *looks*: 1280-dimensional layer-33 vectors feed a compactness (Rg) predictor [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L99-L104), while perplexity measures prediction surprise under 15% random masking [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](/scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L49-L83).

| Signal | Shape / form | Intuition | Consumed by (catalog page) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-head attention | `(33, 20, L, L)` tensor | Which residue pairs each of 660 heads links | [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction), [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics) |
| Attention rollout | `L × L` matrix | Net information flow across all layers, all heads | [Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm) |
| Embeddings / perplexity | 1280-d vector / scalar per protein | What the model encodes / how predictable a sequence is | [MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor), [Perplexity-Disorder Regression](16-perplexity-disorder-regression) |

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](/scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L57-L67), [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L159-L218), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](/scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L48), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](/scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L49-L83), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L99-L104)

## IDP Biology: Proteins Without a Single Fixed Fold

The classical structure–function paradigm says a protein sequence folds into one stable 3D shape, and that shape determines function. **Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs)** — and the **intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)** within larger proteins — break this rule: they exist as a dynamic *ensemble* of interconverting conformations with no single stable fold, yet they are common and functional, especially in signaling and regulation. The repo studies both poles of this spectrum side by side, which is why its core input dataset pairs **DisProt** sequences (curated disordered proteins) with **PDB** sequences (experimentally solved, folded structures) [README.md](/README.md#L44-L46).

| Property | Ordered (folded) proteins | Intrinsically disordered proteins |
|---|---|---|
| Conformation | Single stable 3D fold | Dynamic ensemble of many conformations |
| Representative data in repo | PDB sequences | DisProt sequences, IDRome MD ensembles |
| Compactness measure | Well-defined structure | Radius of gyration (Rg) describes ensemble spread |
| Sequence character | Hydrophobic-core forming | Enriched in charged/polar residues |
| How the repo quantifies it | Serves as the "ordered" control group | IUPred2A probability scores, MD-derived Rg |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L44-L46), [README.md](/README.md#L56-L63)

### How "Disorder" Becomes a Number

Biology alone cannot be compared to attention matrices — it must be **operationalized**. This repository uses **IUPred2A** (run in `long` disorder mode), which assigns every residue a disorder probability between 0 and 1 [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L50-L57). Crucially, the code does not treat any residue scoring above 0.5 as disordered; it defines an IDR as a stretch of **more than 20 consecutive residues** each with probability **greater than 0.5** (constants `TH1 = 0.5`, `TH2 = 20`) [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L59-L77). This two-threshold rule is what turns a fuzzy biological concept into a countable quantity — the number of IDR residues — that can be regressed against attention statistics.

> [!TIP]
> When this documentation says a protein is "disordered," it means **disordered by this specific operational definition** (IUPred2A long-mode probability > 0.5 sustained over > 20 consecutive residues) — not an absolute biological verdict. The same sequence's disorder status can differ under other predictors or thresholds, which is why the exact thresholds are hardcoded at [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L59-L60).

Sources: [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L39-L77)

### Radius of Gyration: Measuring Ensemble Spread

The second operational quantity is the **radius of gyration (Rg)** — intuitively, the characteristic spatial size of the chain: a compact, collapsed ensemble has small Rg; an extended, expanded ensemble has large Rg, measured in Ångströms. The repo's Rg analyses draw on **IDRome**, a database of molecular-dynamics simulations of thousands of disordered regions that yields MD-derived Rg values, plus experimental SAXS-measured Rg for validation [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L22-L33), [README.md](/README.md#L60-L63). One subtlety worth knowing early: the prediction target is not raw Rg but the **residual** of Rg relative to a length baseline that scales with `log(N)` — because longer chains are trivially larger, the interesting signal is whether a chain is more or less compact *than its length predicts* [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L90-L96).

Sources: [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L22-L33), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L90-L96), [README.md](/README.md#L60-L63)

## Where the Two Worlds Meet

The research premise that unifies this catalog is: **if ESM-2's attention weights encode which residues "matter" to which other residues, then those weights should leave measurable fingerprints on IDP biology**. Concretely, the repo tests whether attention statistics differ between disordered and ordered proteins, whether high-attention residues overlap disease-associated variants from ClinVar, whether attention-derived summaries predict ensemble size (Rg), and whether the model finds disordered sequences intrinsically less predictable (higher perplexity).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["Central premise:<br/>attention encodes residue relationships"] --> H1["Attention rollout differs<br/>between ordered and disordered proteins?"]
    P --> H2["Attention concentrates on<br/>known IDR segments and amino acids?"]
    P --> H3["High-attention residues overlap<br/>ClinVar disease variants?"]
    P --> H4["Embeddings/attention predict<br/>ensemble compactness (Rg)?"]
    H1 --> A["Ordered Versus Disordered Comparison<br/>Perplexity-Disorder Regression"]
    H2 --> B["Amino Acid Attention Statistics<br/>Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A"]
    H3 --> C["ClinVar Disease Residue Attention"]
    H4 --> D["MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor<br/>Attention Head Ablation Study"]
```

This is not just a hypothesis — a first hint is already visible in the repository's committed data. The file `data/esm2_perplexities.csv` pairs each protein's masked-LM perplexity with its mean masked-residue disorder score, and the trend is striking: a compact, cytochrome-c-like sequence has perplexity **≈ 2.35** at mean disorder **0.37**, while highly disordered sequences reach perplexity **≈ 9–15.8** at disorder scores of **0.46–0.73**. Disordered sequences are genuinely *harder for ESM-2 to predict* — exactly the kind of signal the downstream regression analyses formalize.

Sources: [esm2_perplexities.csv](/data/esm2_perplexities.csv#L1-L5), [README.md](/README.md#L3-L6)

### The Datasets Behind the Concepts

Each biological concept above is grounded in a committed dataset with its own provenance and license. Knowing which file encodes which concept will save you significant navigation time across the catalog.

| Dataset file | Biological concept | Role in the repo |
|---|---|---|
| `data/disprot.fasta` | Curated disordered proteins | Disordered group for attention comparisons |
| PDB-derived entries (`data/protein_input_sets.csv`, `data/pdb_disprot.fasta`) | Experimentally solved (ordered) structures | Ordered control group |
| `data/idrome.fasta` / IDRome DB | MD ensembles of disordered regions | Source of MD-derived Rg targets |
| `data/clinvar_sequences.csv` | Disease-associated human variants | Tests whether attention marks pathogenic residues |
| `data/esm2_perplexities.csv` | Perplexity + disorder per protein | Derived data for the perplexity regression |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L44-L54), [protein_input_sets.csv](/data/protein_input_sets.csv#L1-L5), [esm2_perplexities.csv](/data/esm2_perplexities.csv#L1-L5)

## Key Terms at a Glance

| Term | One-line definition for this repo |
|---|---|
| **ESM-2** | 33-layer, 20-head transformer (`esm2_t33_650M_UR50D`) trained to predict masked amino acids |
| **Attention head** | One of 660 per-protein L×L matrices of residue-to-residue information flow |
| **Attention rollout** | Single L×L summary matrix collapsing all layers and heads, including residual connections |
| **`<cls>` / `<eos>` tokens** | Special start/end tokens included in raw attention output; stripped before biological interpretation |
| **Embedding** | 1280-dimensional per-residue (or mean-pooled) vector from layer 33 |
| **Perplexity** | `exp(loss)` under 15% masking — how surprised ESM-2 is by a sequence's true residues |
| **IDP / IDR** | Protein/region lacking a single stable fold; operationalized as IUPred2A p > 0.5 over > 20 residues |
| **IUPred2A** | External tool producing per-residue disorder probability (0–1), run in `long` mode |
| **Rg (radius of gyration)** | Spatial size of the chain's conformational ensemble; modeled as residual from a `log(N)` length baseline |
| **IDRome** | MD-simulation database of thousands of disordered regions providing Rg values |

Sources: [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L59-L77), [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L148-L160), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](/scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L40-L83), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L90-L104)

## Reading Path Forward

With both vocabularies in place, the natural next step is the framing of what the pipeline is actually testing. Continue in this section with **[Research Questions and Hypotheses](7-research-questions-and-hypotheses)**, then follow the attention analysis chain: **[Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction)** shows how the `(33, 20, L, L)` tensors are produced and stored, **[Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm)** dissects the collapse-to-L×L math, and **[Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A](10-disorder-scoring-with-iupred2a)** details the operational disorder definition introduced above. If you prefer to start from the quantitative surprise signal, jump directly to **[Perplexity-Disorder Regression](16-perplexity-disorder-regression)**; if the structure side interests you more, **[MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor)** builds directly on the 1280-dimensional embeddings described here.

# Research Questions and Hypotheses



This page is the conceptual bridge between the biological background ([ESM-2 and IDP Biology Primer](6-esm-2-and-idp-biology-primer)) and the implementation deep dives that follow. Rather than describing *how* the code works (that is the job of the pipeline pages), it formalizes *why* each script exists: the specific questions the `plm_interp` authors posed about ESM-2 (`esm2_t33_650M_UR50D`), the falsifiable hypotheses attached to each question, and the statistical machinery that converts raw attention tensors into defensible evidence. Every downstream page in this catalog implements exactly one link in this hypothesis chain.

## The Central Thesis: One Claim, Six Testable Questions

The repository is organized around a single central thesis, stated in the paper title: *mechanistic interpretability of protein language models reveals encoded structural and functional properties of intrinsically disordered proteins*. Rather than testing this as one monolithic claim, the codebase decomposes it into six research questions arranged along a **causal ladder** — starting with purely correlational observations and climbing toward explicit causal intervention. Each question has a dedicated script and maps onto a numbered figure in the paper's reproduction table.

| ID | Research Question | H₀ (Null Hypothesis) | H₁ (Alternative Hypothesis) | Primary Script(s) | Figure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Does attention distinguish ordered from disordered proteins? | Attention is identical between PDB and DisProt sets | Attention distributions differ systematically | `attention_rollout_analysis.py` | 1–2 |
| RQ2 | Is attention enriched at disease-relevant residues? | Pathogenic and non-pathogenic residues receive equal attention | Pathogenic residues receive more attention | `clinvar_expanded.py` | 3 |
| RQ3 | Do Jacobians recover IDP contact structure? | Jacobian contacts are unrelated to MD ensemble contacts | Jacobian contacts correlate with transient MD contacts | `get_contact_maps.py`, `md_contact_maps_analysis.py` | 4 |
| RQ4 | Do embeddings encode ensemble-level physics? | Embeddings cannot predict radius of gyration beyond length scaling | Embeddings predict length-normalized Rg | `rg_mlp.py` | 5 |
| RQ5 | Which attention heads are *causally* responsible? | No specific head contributes to Rg prediction | Charged-residue-enriched heads are causal for Rg | `es_ablation2.py` | 5 |
| RQ6 | Does predictive uncertainty track disorder? | Perplexity is independent of disorder fraction | Perplexity rises with disorder | `esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py` | Supporting |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L3-L6), [README.md](README.md#L86-L97), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L22-L25)

The dependency structure matters: RQ2–RQ4 are only interpretable if RQ1 establishes that attention carries *some* order/disorder signal, and RQ5 is the causal audit of the correlational result in RQ4.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    T["Central Thesis: ESM-2 encodes<br/>IDP structural and functional properties"]
    T --> RQ1["RQ1: Attention separates<br/>ordered vs. disordered sets"]
    T --> RQ6["RQ6: Perplexity tracks disorder<br/>(convergent evidence)"]
    RQ1 --> RQ2["RQ2: Attention enriches<br/>ClinVar disease residues"]
    RQ1 --> RQ3["RQ3: Jacobians recover<br/>MD-derived contacts"]
    RQ1 --> RQ4["RQ4: Embeddings predict<br/>length-normalized Rg"]
    RQ4 --> RQ5["RQ5: Charged-residue heads<br/>causally drive Rg (ablation)"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L86-L97)

## RQ1 — Do Attention Patterns Distinguish Ordered from Disordered Proteins?

The first hypothesis is tested on two deliberately contrasted input sets: PDB-derived sequences (labeled `pdb`) and DisProt-derived sequences (labeled `disprot`), assigned to groups purely by string matching on `ProteinID` and split into separate dictionaries holding their precomputed attention rollout matrices. The embeding-space version of the hypothesis is probed with UMAP of mean-pooled layer-33 representations colored by group and by IDR fraction, then quantified three ways: a silhouette score computed in the full 1280-dimensional ESM-2 space, a density comparison of per-sequence disordered-residue counts, and a logistic regression classifier evaluated under 5-fold `GroupKFold` cross-validation where groups are CD-HIT clusters at 40% sequence identity — a design choice that prevents near-identical homologs from leaking between train and test folds.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L27-L38), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L63-L96), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L134-L179)

The residue-level refinement asks a sharper question: *after controlling for how often each amino acid appears*, do specific residue types receive systematically different attention in disordered versus ordered contexts? The analysis normalizes attention by per-sequence amino acid occurrence (one of three available schemes: `local`, `occurrence`, `global`), then runs the full statistical battery — Welch's t-test with `equal_var=False` plus Cohen's d with pooled standard deviation — for every combination of 20 amino acids × 33 layers × 20 heads (~13,200 comparisons), correcting with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR and keeping only results below 0.05.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L294-L332), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L430-L530), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L208-L280)

A dedicated confound check plots the proportional amino-acid frequency of each set side by side, because a difference in mean attention per residue could otherwise simply reflect that disordered proteins are compositionally enriched in certain residues — the code treats composition as a rival explanation to be ruled out, not an assumption.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L295-L345)

## RQ1b — Is Attention Spatially Aligned with Disorder Within Proteins?

Between RQ1 and RQ2 sits a positional hypothesis: attention received by a residue should track that residue's *local* disorder probability, not just the protein's global class. For every protein the code computes the IUPred2A long-disorder profile (residues are called disordered when probability exceeds 0.5 within stretches longer than 20) and correlates it residue-by-residue with the attention-rollout-received vector, then visualizes the resulting attention distributions stratified by disorder-probability quartile. Five single-protein case studies — TDP-43 (with NTD/RRM1/RRM2/CTD annotated regions), p53, FUS, MDM2, and APOE — overlay the two signals to make the alignment inspectable by eye.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L26-L94), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L347-L380), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L383-L430)

## RQ2 — Does Attention Concentrate on Disease-Relevant Residues?

RQ2 upgrades "attention correlates with disorder" to "attention correlates with *function*", using pathogenicity as a functional ground truth. The cohort is built from ClinVar single-nucleotide variants only, filtered to Pathogenic / Likely pathogenic / Pathogenic-Likely pathogenic labels, then aggressively quality-controlled: sequences restricted to 50–1024 residues, sequences containing `U` removed, genes mapping to more than one RefSeq protein dropped entirely, and — most importantly — every annotated wild-type amino acid cross-validated against the residue actually retrieved from NCBI at that position, discarding mismatches.

Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L25-L38), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L69-L74), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L100-L124)

The unit of analysis is deliberately the **within-protein attention percentile** (`attn_perc`, a per-sequence `rank(pct=True)`), not raw attention — this absorbs any protein-level differences in attention magnitude. The hypothesis is then tested at three stratification levels: the overall disease-vs-non-disease percentile distribution, the same comparison within ten disorder-percentile bins (to test whether enrichment is uniform or disorder-dependent), and within amino-acid chemistry groups (Hydrophobic, Polar, Cation, Anion, Aromatic — to test whether it is merely a chemistry artifact). IUPred2A profiles are computed alongside rollout for every unique sequence so disorder is always available as a covariate.

Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L154-L181), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L199-L247)

## RQ3 — Do Model Derivatives Recover IDP Contact Structure?

This question moves from scalars to matrices. The instrument is the **categorical Jacobian** — the derivative of the 20 amino-acid logits at every position with respect to every possible 20-substitution at every other position (a `ln × 20 × ln × 20` tensor, extracted via logits slice `4:24`), followed by Average Product Correction to strip dominant eigen-component artifacts. The implementation credit is explicit: `do_apc`, `get_categorical_jacobian`, and `get_contacts` are adapted from Zhang et al.'s pLMs-interpretability work. The hypothesis is notably ambitious: IDPs lack fixed structure, so the test is whether Jacobian-derived contact scores still correspond to *transient* contacts in molecular dynamics ensembles.

Sources: [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L13-L19), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L21-L56)

Validation against MD is treated as a formal hypothesis test, not a visual comparison. For each protein, the observed statistic is the Spearman correlation between MD contact strength and Jacobian contact fraction; the null distribution is generated by 1,000 random permutations of the contact-strength vector (seeded, vectorized), yielding a z-score and a one-sided empirical p-value of `(count(null ≥ observed) + 1) / (1001)`. A companion sweep (`md_variable_cutoff.py`) re-derives the MD contact definition under variable distance cutoffs so the conclusion is not an artifact of one arbitrary σ.

Sources: [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L17-L42), [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L44-L70)

## RQ4 — Do Embeddings Encode Ensemble-Level Physics?

The physical quantity chosen is the radius of gyration (Rg), the canonical scalar summary of an IDP ensemble size. Ground truth comes from two independent sources: IDRome MD-derived Rg values (Tesei et al.) and experimental SAXS Rg. The critical design decision is that the MLP (1280 → 512 → 256 → 128 → 1, with LayerNorm/GELU/Dropout 0.3) does *not* predict raw Rg — it predicts the **residual over a polymer-scaling baseline**, then the final prediction is reconstructed as residual + `baseline_poly(log N)` and evaluated as reduced Rg, `Rg / (R0 · N^ν)` with fitted constants ν = 0.533, R₀ = 2.420.

> [!TIP]
> Predicting the residual over the length-scaling law is what makes RQ4 falsifiable: a model that only memorized sequence length would score exactly zero on this target, so any nonzero Spearman correlation is attributable to sequence-encoding content beyond trivial size scaling.

Sources: [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L14-L34), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L26-L32), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L197-L199), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L239-L253)

## RQ5 — Which Heads Are Causally Responsible? (The Electrostatics Hypothesis)

RQ5 is the repository's causal capstone, stated verbatim in the script docstring: ablate heads likely associated with electrostatics and evaluate the effect on MLP Rg prediction. Head *selection* is correlational — heads are ranked by mean occurrence-normalized attention to positively charged residues (K, R) and negatively charged residues (D, E), read from the committed `data/attn_corr_norm_es.csv` — and the circuit-level hypothesis is probed by computing pairwise correlations between the D/E and K/R head-attention heatmaps across all 660 layer-head units.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L22-L24), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L127-L137), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L183-L199)

The *intervention* is a true zero-ablation: forward pre-hooks registered on `out_proj`'s **input** zero the 64-dimensional slice of the concatenated per-head output before the output projection mixes heads, setting `Att_h(x) = 0` while every other head passes through untouched. Cumulative ablation sweeps (up to 50 heads) are run for the targeted charged-residue rankings and compared against 5 seeded random-ablation control runs, with degradation measured as ΔSpearman / ΔPearson / ΔMAE on normalized Rg for both the IDRome test split (held out by `GroupShuffleSplit` over CD-HIT clusters) and the SAXS set.

> [!TIP]
> The hook targets `out_proj`'s *input*, not its output — zeroing after the output projection would contaminate neighboring heads via the projection matrix, silently invalidating the causal claim. This placement is the difference between a clean single-head lesion and a leaked multi-head lesion.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L202-L253), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L276-L280)

## RQ6 — Does Predictive Uncertainty Track Disorder?

The final hypothesis uses a completely different lens on the same question: if IDPs sit outside the evolutionary statistics ESM-2 absorbed during training, the model's masked-LM perplexity should be elevated on them. The script computes per-protein perplexity under standard 15% random masking and runs an OLS regression of perplexity on disorder (using the same IUPred2A machinery), providing convergent, attention-independent evidence for the central thesis.

Sources: [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L13-L15), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L36-L43)

## The Shared Statistical Doctrine

The six hypotheses are disciplined by a common control vocabulary. This is the single most important table on this page: every potential confounder identified in the analysis design has a named, code-level countermeasure.

| Threat to Validity | Countermeasure | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| Homolog leakage inflating classifier/probe accuracy | CD-HIT 40%-identity clusters as CV groups | `GroupKFold` / `GroupShuffleSplit` over `.clstr` files |
| Amino-acid composition confound | Occurrence-normalized attention + explicit composition plots | `get_aa_attn_perc(normalize='occurrence')`, `comb_props` |
| Multiple comparisons (~13,200 t-tests) | Benjamini-Hochberg FDR at α = 0.05 | `false_discovery_control`, `multipletests` |
| Unequal variances between groups | Welch's t-test (`equal_var=False`) | `fast_statistical_comparison`, `cohens_d` |
| Arbitrary contact-map cutoff | Variable distance-cutoff sweep + permutation nulls | `md_variable_cutoff.py`, `compute_null_distribution_for_protein` |
| Protein-level attention scale differences | Within-protein percentile ranking | `rank(pct=True)` in `clinvar_expanded.py` |
| Length confound in Rg | Residual over fitted scaling law `R0·N^ν` | `to_rg` / `baseline_poly` in `es_ablation2.py` |
| "Any ablation hurts" artifact | 5-run seeded random-ablation control | `run_sweep` with `N_RANDOM_RUNS = 5` |

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L430-L530), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L276-L280), [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L17-L42)

## How to Read the Rest of the Catalog Through This Lens

Every remaining page is the implementation record of one row in the hypothesis table. The measurement layer comes first: [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction) and [Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm) build the attention tensors that RQ1 consumes, while [Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A](10-disorder-scoring-with-iupred2a) supplies the ground-truth labels used by RQ1, RQ1b, and RQ6. The validation pages then execute the hypotheses in causal-ladder order: [Ordered Versus Disordered Comparison](12-ordered-versus-disordered-comparison) and [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics) resolve RQ1; [ClinVar Disease Residue Attention](13-clinvar-disease-residue-attention) resolves RQ2; [Categorical Jacobian Contact Maps](14-categorical-jacobian-contact-maps) with [MD Trajectory Contact Validation](15-md-trajectory-contact-validation) resolve RQ3; [Perplexity-Disorder Regression](16-perplexity-disorder-regression) resolves RQ6; and [MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor), [Attention Head Ablation Study](18-attention-head-ablation-study), and [Electrostatics Hypothesis Testing](19-electrostatics-hypothesis-testing) resolve RQ4 and RQ5.


# Attention Matrix Extraction



This page documents the repository's foundation stone: converting raw protein sequences into persisted, per-residue attention tensors from ESM-2. The entry point is `scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py`, which runs a 33-layer, 20-head transformer over 4,241 curated protein sequences and shards the resulting ~660 attention matrices per protein into 22 compressed chunks. Everything downstream in the *Attention Analysis Pipeline* — attention rollout, amino acid statistics, disorder correlations — consumes these artifacts, so understanding the exact output contract (tensor shape, token offsets, chunk naming) is a prerequisite for any modification to the pipeline. This page focuses strictly on extraction; the mathematical post-processing lives in [Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm).

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L12-L15), [README.md](README.md#L44-L48)

## Architectural Overview

The extraction stage sits at the head of the attention analysis pipeline. It reads the curated dataset committed at `data/protein_input_sets.csv` (4,241 sequence/ID pairs, including both DisProt and PDB-derived proteins), tokenizes and pads sequences in micro-batches, performs a single forward pass per batch on the GPU, and then reshapes the batch-level attention tensor into one dictionary entry per protein. Because a single long protein's attention tensor can exceed 2 GB, the script deliberately never accumulates everything in memory: results flush to disk every 200 proteins, and GPU caches are purged after every batch.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["data/protein_input_sets.csv<br/>(Sequence, ProteinID × 4,241)"] --> B["batch_converter<br/>tokenize + pad + add BOS/EOS"]
    B --> C["GPU forward pass<br/>need_head_weights=True"]
    C --> D["results['attentions']<br/>(batch, 33, 20, L_pad, L_pad)"]
    D --> E["Per-protein record<br/>sequence · attention_matrix · sequence_length"]
    E --> F["all_results accumulator"]
    F -->|&ge; 200 proteins| G["joblib.dump<br/>compress=3"]
    G --> H["attention_matrices_chunks/<br/>..._labeled_{0..21}_original.joblib"]
    H --> I["Downstream consumers:<br/>rollout · per-head statistics"]
```

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L34-L45), [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L51-L78), [protein_input_sets.csv](data/protein_input_sets.csv#L1-L2)

## Model Configuration and Environment Probing

The script instantiates `esm.pretrained.esm2_t33_650M_UR50D()` via the `fair-esm` package (pinned at `2.0.0`), operating under `torch==2.5.1+cu121` inside the `torch-gpu` conda environment. Two details matter here for extraction semantics. First, `model.eval()` is called explicitly, disabling dropout so attention weights are deterministic per sequence. Second, the header block prints the torch version, CUDA availability, GPU name, and total GPU memory before any work begins — an intentional diagnostic that surfaces hardware constraints *before* a multi-hour extraction job fails mid-run.

| Extraction Parameter | Value | Purpose | Code Location |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model checkpoint | `esm2_t33_650M_UR50D` | 33 transformer layers, 650M parameters, 20 heads/layer | [L29](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L29) |
| Mode | `model.eval()` | Deterministic attention (no dropout) | [L32](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L32) |
| Device | CUDA if available, else CPU | Auto-selected at import time | [L23](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L23) |
| `batch_size` | 2 | Fits attention tensors in GPU memory budget | [L45](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L45) |
| `need_head_weights` | `True` | Returns per-head matrices instead of head-averaged only | [L55](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L55) |
| `save_interval` | 200 proteins | Chunk flush frequency | [L42](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L42) |
| `model_type` | `'original'` | Encoded into chunk filenames to distinguish from fine-tuned variants | [L38](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L38) |

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L19-L32), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L486), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L553)

## The Extraction Loop, Step by Step

Each iteration processes exactly two proteins through a five-stage micro-cycle: tokenize on CPU, transfer tokens to device, forward under `torch.no_grad()`, slice out per-protein tensors, and purge GPU memory. The critical call is `model(batch_tokens, need_head_weights=True)` — without this flag, fair-esm returns head-averaged attention only, collapsing the 20 heads per layer into one and forfeiting the per-head analysis that [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics) depends on. The resulting `results["attentions"]` tensor has shape `(batch, 33, 20, L_pad, L_pad)`, where `L_pad` includes the `<cls>` token, the residues, the `<eos>` token, and any padding to the longest sequence in the batch.

Alongside the attention tensor, the script records `raw_sequence_lengths` computed as `len(seq)` over the *unmodified* amino acid strings — special tokens excluded. This integer is the pipeline's coordinate system: every downstream consumer uses it to trim the padded tensor back to true residues.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S[Load ESM-2, eval mode, device probe] --> T[Read CSV into list of ID/sequence tuples]
    T --> U{More batches remain?}
    U -->|yes| V[batch_converter on 2 proteins, tokens to device]
    V --> W[Forward pass: no_grad + need_head_weights=True]
    W --> X[Per protein j: attentions j .cpu .numpy]
    X --> Y[Store sequence + attention_matrix + sequence_length]
    Y --> Z[Delete refs, torch.cuda.empty_cache]
    Z --> AA{Accumulator &ge; 200 proteins?}
    AA -->|yes| AB[Dump chunk k, reset accumulator, gc.collect]
    AA -->|no| U
    AB --> U
    U -->|no| AC[Dump final partial chunk]
    AC --> AD[End: 22 shards on disk]
```

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L47-L58), [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L61-L67), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L149-L160)

## Output Contract: The Chunk File Schema

Extraction writes `attention_matrices_chunks/attention_matrices_labeled_{chunk_num}_{model_type}.joblib` with zlib compression level 3. Each chunk is a dictionary keyed by protein ID, so consumers gain random access to any protein without loading the full corpus — but any given chunk must still be deserialized whole. With 4,241 proteins flushed at intervals of 200, the arithmetic yields ⌈4241/200⌉ = 22 chunks, indexed 0 through 21. This is not incidental: both downstream consumers hardcode `range(0, 22)` over these shards, making the chunk count a de facto coupling point between extraction and analysis code. Changing `save_interval` in the extractor silently breaks every consumer.

| Contract Aspect | Value | Verified By |
|---|---|---|
| File path pattern | `attention_matrices_chunks/attention_matrices_labeled_{0..21}_original.joblib` | [L78, L87](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L76-L87) |
| Top-level structure | `dict[ProteinID → record]` | [L63](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L61-L67) |
| Record: `sequence` | Raw amino acid string (no special tokens) | [L64](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L61-L67) |
| Record: `attention_matrix` | `float32`, shape `(33, 20, L_pad, L_pad)` | [L65](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L61-L67) |
| Record: `sequence_length` | Integer `L`, raw residue count | [L66](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L58) |
| Chunk count | 22 (indices 0–21) | [attention_functions.py L349](scripts/attention_functions.py#L349), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py L36](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L36-L39) |
| Loader utility | `safe_load(path)` — runs `gc.collect()` then `joblib.load` | [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L252-L254) |

The token layout inside the padded matrix follows ESM-2's convention: index `0` is `<cls>`, indices `1..L` are the actual residues, index `L+1` is `<eos>`, and anything beyond is batch padding. The extraction stores the *full padded* tensor per protein and preserves `sequence_length` so consumers can trim it themselves — `get_head_layer_attn` in `attention_functions.py` is the canonical example, slicing `[1:actual_seq_len+1, 1:actual_seq_len+1]` to yield a clean `(L, L)` residue-only matrix.

> [!TIP]
> All offset arithmetic in downstream code assumes residue *i* lives at matrix index *i + 1*. If you regenerate chunks with a different tokenizer or prepend sequences, `get_head_layer_attn`'s `[1:L+1]` slice and every length bookkeeping step will silently misalign. The cleanest safeguard is to always derive offsets from the stored `sequence_length` field, never from matrix dimensions.

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L76-L87), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L256-L277), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L349-L350), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L36-L39)

> [!TIP]
> Matrix orientation convention: rows are queries (positions doing the attending), columns are keys (positions being attended). This is confirmed by `get_aa_attn_perc`, which computes "attention received by each amino acid" via `attn_matrix.sum(axis=0)` — summing over columns. Any custom statistic you add should inherit this row-query/column-key orientation or your interpretations will be transposed.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L296-L301)

## Memory Strategy During Extraction

The extraction is dominated by a quadratic scaling problem: each protein's attention tensor contains 33 × 20 = 660 `(L_pad × L_pad)` float32 slices. For a 500-residue protein (padded length 502), that is 660 × 502² × 4 B ≈ 0.66 GB; at 1,000 residues it climbs to ≈ 2.65 GB per protein. This arithmetic alone justifies the design choices — `batch_size = 2`, immediate `.cpu().numpy()` transfer after the forward pass, `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` after every batch, and `gc.collect()` after each 200-protein chunk flush. The deletion block uses `del locals()[obj]`, which works at module scope because `locals()` aliases `globals()` there; inside a function scope this idiom would not actually free the names. The full rationale for these techniques — including why compression level 3 was chosen over higher levels — is expanded in [Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management).

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L45-L74), [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L82-L87)

## Reproduction Context and Input Provenance

The attention matrices themselves are **not committed to GitHub** — the README states explicitly that they must be regenerated with `python scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py`, outputting to `/attention_matrices_chunks`. This makes the extraction step the mandatory first stage of reproducing Figures 1 and 2, each of which chains extraction → rollout computation → analysis. The input dataset `data/protein_input_sets.csv` is the *derived* artifact of dataset curation (DisProt release 2025_06 and PDB sequences accessed July 16, 2025), and the repository's reproducibility policy lets you either reuse the committed sequences exactly or regenerate them from live databases via `define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py` — see [Dataset Curation and CD-HIT Clustering](21-dataset-curation-and-cd-hit-clustering) and [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility) for that upstream decision. For the biological and modeling context of why per-head attention from ESM-2 is informative for intrinsically disordered proteins, consult [ESM-2 and IDP Biology Primer](6-esm-2-and-idp-biology-primer).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L44-L48), [README.md](README.md#L88-L97), [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L20-L27), [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L38-L46)

## Summary of Key Invariants

Before moving on, anchor these four facts, since every attention analysis page builds on them: (1) stored tensors are **per-head and per-layer** — `(33, 20, L_pad, L_pad)` — because `need_head_weights=True`; (2) chunk shards are keyed by protein ID with **22 shards** derived from `save_interval = 200`; (3) `sequence_length` is the **only** authoritative length, since stored matrices are padded; and (4) data is **not distributed** — extraction must run locally on a CUDA-capable machine, typically hours of GPU time. With the extraction contract established, the natural next step is how these raw tensors are distilled into interpretable residue-level signals.

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L29-L45), [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L55-L67)

## Next Steps

- **[Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm)** — how the extracted `(33, 20, L, L)` tensors are fused across heads and layers into a single rollout matrix; this is the primary consumer of the chunks documented above.
- **[Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics)** — the per-head/per-layer statistical analyses enabled by storing head-separated matrices.
- **[Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management)** — deep dive into the batching, purging, and chunking strategy touched on above.
- **[Dataset Curation and CD-HIT Clustering](21-dataset-curation-and-cd-hit-clustering)** — how `protein_input_sets.csv`, this page's input, was constructed.

# Attention Rollout Algorithm



This page dissects the mechanism that collapses ESM-2's 33-layer × 20-head attention tensor into a single `(L, L)` residue-interaction matrix per protein — the **attention rollout**. It covers the mathematical foundation, the six-stage implementation in `attention_functions.py`, the chunked batch orchestrator, and how downstream analyses consume the resulting "attention received" signal. This page sits between upstream raw matrix extraction and downstream statistical validation; for how the `(33, 20, x, x)` tensors are produced in the first place, see [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction).

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L144-L218), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L32-L56)

## Architectural Position and Module Interaction

The rollout occupies the transformation bottleneck of the attention pipeline: it converts bulky, cached raw attention artifacts into a compact per-protein summary that every subsequent statistical analysis depends on. Three modules collaborate through a strict producer–library–consumer decomposition — the orchestrator never re-implements algorithmic logic, and the analysis script never touches raw attention tensors.

- **`attention_functions.py`** — the shared library: `attention_rollout()` (the algorithm), `get_attn_rollout()` (single-sequence live-inference wrapper), `safe_load()` (memory-conscious chunk loader), and `get_attention_distribution_df()` (matrix→table reduction).
- **`get_esm2_attention_rollout.py`** — the batch orchestrator: iterates 22 pre-computed joblib chunks, applies rollout per protein, persists one combined artifact.
- **`attention_rollout_analysis.py`** — the consumer: splits results into PDB (ordered) vs DisProt (disordered) cohorts and derives every figure-level statistic.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L102-L142), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L36-L56), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L39-L45)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Producer["Upstream: Attention Matrix Extraction"]
        A["attention_matrices_chunks/<br/>attention_matrices_labeled_{0..21}<br/>{protein: sequence, attention_matrix, sequence_length}"]
    end
    subgraph Transformer["This Page"]
        B["get_esm2_attention_rollout.py<br/>safe_load → attention_rollout → del"]
    end
    subgraph Consumer["attention_rollout_analysis.py"]
        C1["Per-AA attention distribution<br/>+ Cohen's d / FDR"]
        C2["Disorder↔attention correlation<br/>(IUPred2A profile)"]
        C3["TDP-43 / SI case studies<br/>(live inference path)"]
    end
    A -->|"22 chunked joblib loads"| B
    B -->|"attention_rollout_comb_original.joblib"| C1
    B --> C2
    C3 -.->|"bypasses cached chunks"| B
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Lib["attention_functions.py — shared API surface"]
        F1["attention_rollout()<br/>tensor-in, tensor-out"]
        F2["get_attn_rollout()<br/>seq + model → numpy vector"]
        F3["safe_load()<br/>gc.collect() + joblib.load"]
        F4["get_attention_distribution_df()<br/>rollout → tidy DataFrame"]
    end
    subgraph Orc["get_esm2_attention_rollout.py"]
        O1["chunk loop 0..21"]
        O2["joblib.dump(compress=3)"]
    end
    subgraph Ana["attention_rollout_analysis.py"]
        A1["PDB/DisProt dict split"]
        A2["AA stats + Cohen's d"]
        A3["disorder correlation"]
        A4["case-study inference"]
    end
    O1 --> F3
    O1 --> F1
    O2 --> A1
    A1 --> F4
    A1 --> A3
    A4 --> F2
```

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L10), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L206-L220), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L343-L370)

## Mathematical Foundation

Raw attention matrices describe only *direct* token-to-token information flow within a single layer. Attention rollout (Abnar & Zuidema, 2020) recovers *indirect* flow: if residue `i` attends strongly to `j` in layer 1, and `j` attends strongly to `k` in layer 2, rollout attributes signal to the `i → k` path by composing the per-layer transition matrices. The implementation formalizes this in three moves per layer:

1. **Head fusion** — collapse the 20 heads into one `(x, x)` matrix via `dim=0` aggregation.
2. **Stochasticization** — after masking special tokens and sparsifying, inject residual connections as `(A + I) / 2`, then row-normalize so each row sums to 1. Row normalization is applied *after* residual injection because `(A + I)/2` rows no longer sum to unity — the division at line 211 is what makes each layer a valid Markov transition operator.
3. **Composition** — multiply the 33 normalized matrices in sequence order: `R = Ã⁽³³⁾ · Ã⁽³²⁾ · … · Ã⁽¹⁾`, with `R[i, j]` quantifying total (direct + indirect) attention flowing from residue `i` to residue `j`.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L209-L218)

## Inside `attention_rollout()`: Stage-by-Stage Tensor Analysis

The function accepts a padded attention stack of shape `(33, 20, x, x)` — where `x` includes `<cls>`, the protein residues, `<eos>`, and any batch padding — plus the raw length `L`. It returns a rollout matrix of shape `(L, L)` (or `(L+1, L+1)` if `include_cls=True`): all special-token structure is eliminated before return. The stages below trace exact shapes through the code.

| Stage | Code Region | Input Shape | Output Shape | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Head fusion | L162–177 | per-layer `(20, x, x)` | list of 33 × `(x, x)` | collapse heads into layer consensus |
| 2. Special-token mask | L184–200 | `(x, x)` | `(x, x)`, zeroed outside `[start:end]²` | confine signal to real residues |
| 3. Quantile discard | L201–208 | `(L', L')` | sparsified `(L', L')` | keep top 10% of attention mass |
| 4. Residual injection | L209–210 | `(L', L')` | `(A + I)/2`, shape `(L', L')` | preserve identity/self-attention path |
| 5. Row normalization | L211–212 | `(L', L')` | row-stochastic `(L', L')` | Markov transition validity |
| 6. Composition | L214–218 | 33 × `(L', L')` | `(L', L')` | cross-layer information flow |

Here `L' = L` normally, or `L + 1` when `include_cls=True` (line 192).

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L144-L218)

### Stage 1 — Head Fusion and the `dim=0` Contract

Each layer's `(20, x, x)` tensor is reduced over heads with `attention.mean(dim=0)` (or `max`/`min`). The code comments are unusually explicit about the dimensional contract: `dim=0` is mandatory because head count lives on axis 0; using `dim=1` or `dim=2` would silently produce a malformed `(20, x)` result instead of the intended `(x, x)`. An invalid `head_fusion` string raises `ValueError` immediately rather than defaulting silently (lines 175–176).

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L159-L179)

> [!TIP]
> Fusion via `mean`/`max`/`min` allocates a **fresh tensor**, so the subsequent in-place mutation `layer_attn *= mask` (line 199) never touches the caller's cached `attentions` stack. This is what makes chunk reuse safe — the orchestrator can drop references (`del`) after processing without corrupting anything.

### Stage 2 — Special-Token Masking

Masking operates on a boolean region of ones: `mask[start_idx:end_idx, start_idx:end_idx] = 1`, where `start_idx = 1` skips `<cls>` and `end_idx = start_idx + L` spans exactly the protein residues (tokenized ESM-2 sequences place residues at indices `1..L`, with `<eos>` and padding beyond). Multiplying element-wise zeroes every row and column associated with `<cls>`, `<eos>`, and padding, guaranteeing they can neither emit nor receive rollout signal.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L183-L200)

### Stage 3 — Quantile Discard

For each layer, the valid `(L', L')` submatrix is flattened and `torch.quantile(flat_att, discard_ratio)` computes a cutoff; entries strictly below it are zeroed via a boolean mask multiplication (line 206). With the production value `discard_ratio=0.9`, only the top ~10% of attention mass per layer survives into composition — a sparsification step that suppresses diffuse, low-signal edges and concentrates rollout on high-confidence pathways.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L201-L208)

> [!TIP]
> The quantile is computed **after** masking, so the flattened distribution includes the zeros introduced by Stage 2 — the 90th-percentile threshold therefore reflects the masked distribution, not the raw one. Combined with the `>=` comparison (which retains threshold ties), the retained mass is the top decile *of the cleaned distribution*, slightly more aggressive than a naive top-10% over raw values.

### Stages 4–6 — Residual, Normalization, Composition

`I = torch.eye(actual_len)` is built on the target device, `(protein_attn + I) / 2` injects the residual path at exactly half weight, and row-wise normalization (`sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)` division) yields a row-stochastic matrix. Composition then left-multiplies each successive layer onto an accumulator seeded with layer 1's matrix — `torch.matmul(joint_attention, rollout)` — so the final tensor is `Ã⁽³³⁾ · … · Ã⁽¹⁾` and `R[i, j]` reads as flow *from* `i` *to* `j`.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L209-L218)

## Head Fusion Strategy Comparison

Only `"mean"` is used in production (both orchestrator and wrapper hard-code it), but the function exposes three fusion semantics with distinct interpretive consequences:

| Strategy | Reduction (`dim=0`) | Saliency Character | Risk Profile |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mean` (production) | `attention.mean(dim=0)` | Consensus flow; robust to individual-head noise | Dampens strongly specialized heads |
| `max` | `attention.max(dim=0)[0]` | Strongest path per position; sharp, high-contrast rollout | Overweights single-head outliers |
| `min` | `attention.min(dim=0)[0]` | Weakest-path estimate; conservative lower bound | Can erase genuine signal |

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L169-L177), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L48)

## Parameter Reference

| Parameter | Type | Default | Verified Usage | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `attentions` | tensor | — | `(33, 20, x, x)` padded stack | raw input to be rolled out |
| `raw_sequence_lengths` | int | — | per-protein `sequence_length` field | defines the retained residue window |
| `discard_ratio` | float | 0.9 | 0.9 in orchestrator (L48) and wrapper (L246) | quantile cutoff for Stage 3 sparsification |
| `head_fusion` | str | `"mean"` | `"mean"` everywhere | Stage 1 reduction rule |
| `include_cls` | bool | `False` | never set `True` in production | widens window to include `<cls>` row/col |
| `device` | str | `'cpu'` | CUDA when available | hosts `eye`, matmuls, quantile |

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L144-L158), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L20), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L48)

## Batch Orchestration: Chunked, Memory-Bounded Execution

The orchestrator processes the corpus in 22 sequential joblib chunks, applying the pipeline `safe_load → per-protein rollout → del → del chunk`. Each protein's dict is unpacked into `sequence`, `attention_matrix` (moved to GPU exactly once, line 45), and `sequence_length`; the rollout call is issued with production defaults (`discard_ratio=0.9`, `head_fusion="mean"`). Explicit `del` statements after every protein and every chunk, combined with `safe_load`'s `gc.collect()` before each load, keep peak memory bounded to roughly one chunk plus one protein. The final accumulator — a flat dict mapping protein ID to `{'sequence', 'rollout'}` — is persisted with `joblib.dump(..., compress=3)` as the canonical downstream artifact `attention_rollout_comb_original.joblib`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["for i in range(0, 22)"] --> L["attn_i = safe_load(chunk_i)<br/>gc.collect() → joblib.load"]
    L --> P["for protein in attn_i"]
    P --> T["attentions = tensor(..., device='cuda')<br/>single H2D transfer"]
    T --> R["rollout = attention_rollout(<br/>discard_ratio=0.9, head_fusion='mean')"]
    R --> ST["attn_rollout[protein] = {sequence, rollout}"]
    ST --> D1["del rollout, protein_attn, attentions"]
    D1 --> P
    P -->|chunk exhausted| DC["del attn_i"]
    DC -->|more chunks| S
    DC -->|chunk 21 done| OUT["joblib.dump(attn_rollout,<br/>compress=3)"]
```

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L33-L56), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L252-L254)

## From Matrix to Signal: The "Attention Received" Reduction

Every downstream statistic operates on a single derived quantity: the **attention received** vector, computed as the column sum of the rollout matrix — `rollout.sum(dim=0)` — so entry `j` measures total incoming attention at residue `j` after cross-layer composition. This reduction appears in three independent places, all consistent:

- `get_attn_rollout()` (lines 247–248) performs the same column-sum inside the live-inference wrapper, which encodes a raw sequence via the tokenizer, runs the model under `torch.no_grad()` with `output_attentions=True`, stacks the 33 layer tensors at batch index 0, and returns a NumPy vector of length `L`.
- `get_attention_distribution_df()` (line 123) applies `attn_matrix.sum(axis=0)` per protein, emitting tidy records of `(protein_id, amino_acid, attention)` with optional min-max normalization or z-standardization.
- The disorder-correlation block (line 350) calls `data['rollout'].sum(dim=0).cpu().numpy()` directly on loaded artifacts before pairing with IUPred2A per-residue probabilities.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L220-L249), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L115-L142), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L343-L363)

## Downstream Consumption Patterns

The rollout artifact feeds three distinct analysis patterns, each isolating a different facet of the signal:

| Pattern | Input | Statistical Treatment | Output Artifact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-AA distribution | `get_attention_distribution_df` over PDB/DisProt dicts | group means ± SE, Cohen's d, FDR correction | `mean_aa_attn.csv` + bar figure |
| Disorder correlation | per-residue `attn_received` paired with IUPred2A profile | per-protein Pearson correlation; KDE by disorder-probability bin | `disorder_comp_concat.csv` + KDE figure |
| Case studies | `get_attn_rollout` live on 5 named proteins (TDP-43, P53, FUS, MDM2, APOE) | qualitative overlay of attention vs disorder per region | `si_examples.csv` + TDP-43 region figure |

Notably, the case-study path deliberately **bypasses the cached chunks** and re-runs model inference live — demonstrating that `get_attn_rollout` provides a self-contained end-to-end path (sequence → tokens → forward pass → rollout → received vector) without any dependence on pre-computed artifacts. The disorder side of these comparisons is detailed in [Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A](10-disorder-scoring-with-iupred2a), and the statistical treatment of per-residue attention in [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics).

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L206-L220), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L343-L387), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L393-L453)

## Next Steps

To continue through the pipeline in dependency order:

- See how the `(33, 20, x, x)` inputs are produced and cached: [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction)
- Understand the disorder scores that rollout vectors are correlated against: [Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A](10-disorder-scoring-with-iupred2a)
