# Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A



This page explains how the plm_interp repository integrates **IUPred2A** — the external intrinsic disorder predictor — as the quantitative "ground truth" layer that turns raw protein sequences into per-residue disorder probabilities and IDR (Intrinsically Disordered Region) residue counts. Every downstream claim in the attention analysis pipeline (which residues receive attention, whether DisProt proteins differ from PDB proteins, whether perplexity tracks disorder) is conditioned on these scores. Here you will find the dependency configuration, the two scoring functions, their subprocess-based invocation mechanics, the IDR segmentation rule, and a map of every consumer in the codebase.

## Why Disorder Scores Anchor the Attention Pipeline

Attention rollout matrices (produced by the upstream stage described in [Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm)) are unlabeled per-residue quantities — the repository needs an independent, biologically grounded signal to interpret them. IUPred2A provides that signal in three distinct roles: **set validation** (confirming the DisProt set is genuinely more disordered than the PDB set), **protein-level stratification** (IDR fraction as a coloring variable in embedding space), and **residue-level correlation** (aligning per-residue disorder probability against per-residue attention received). This division of labor is visible in the concept map below, where the two scoring functions fan out into three separate analysis branches.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    SEQ["Protein sequence"] --> P1["extract_IDR_profile<br/>per-residue probability 0..1"]
    SEQ --> P2["extract_IDR<br/>count of residues in long IDRs"]
    P1 --> A["attention_rollout_analysis.py<br/>residue-level corr + quartile bins"]
    P2 --> B["attention_rollout_analysis.py<br/>IDR fraction for UMAP coloring"]
    P2 --> C["attention_rollout_analysis.py<br/>DisProt vs PDB validation KDE"]
    P1 --> D["esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py<br/>mean masked-residue disorder"]
    A --> E["figures/attention_disorder_kde.svg"]
    B --> F["figures/umap.svg"]
    C --> G["figures/input_sets_disorder.svg"]
    D --> H["data/esm2_perplexities.csv"]
```

The repository deliberately treats IUPred2A as an **external system dependency**, not a pip-installable package: the tool must be obtained separately and wired in by editing one path constant. This keeps the analysis code decoupled from the predictor's lifecycle, but it also makes the integration fragile in specific, knowable ways — covered in the sections below.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L21-L25), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L339-L370), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L85-L109)

## External Dependency and One-Line Configuration

The README states the requirement explicitly: *"You will need to install Iupred2a https://iupred2a.elte.hu/ to run and update iupred_filepath (line 25) of scripts/attention_functions.py to redirect to your local copy."* In the code, this manifests as a single hardcoded module-level constant pointing to the original author's cluster path — which means any fresh clone fails on first IUPred2A call until you edit it.

| Configuration Item | Location | Default Value | Required Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| `iupred_filepath` | `scripts/attention_functions.py` L25 | `/rds/user/ln399/hpc-work/llps/DeePhase_LN/__PREDICT_LN/tools/iupred2a.py` | Replace with path to your local `iupred2a.py` downloaded from iupred2a.elte.hu |
| Python interpreter | `subprocess.Popen` call sites | `python` | Must resolve to an environment where IUPred2A's dependencies (e.g., BioPython-era stdlib deps) are importable |
| Prediction mode | Hardcoded in both functions | `'long'` | None — long-disorder mode is appropriate for IDP analysis |

Because both scoring functions shell out to `python <iupred2a.py>`, the tool runs in whatever `python` is first on `PATH` at call time — not necessarily the `torch-gpu` conda environment you activated. If IUPred2A fails inside its own interpreter, the error surfaces through `stderr=subprocess.STDOUT` and typically crashes downstream float parsing rather than failing silently.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L18-L18), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L21-L25), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L50-L51)

## The Two Scoring Functions: Profile Versus Count

`attention_functions.py` contains two IUPred2A wrappers credited to an external contributor (`https://github.com/kadiliissaar`), each answering a different question about the same sequence. `extract_IDR_profile` answers *"how disordered is each residue?"* and returns a list of float probabilities — one per residue, in sequence order. `extract_IDR` answers *"how much of this protein is in a long disordered region?"* and returns a single integer count of residues qualifying under the segmentation rule described in the next section.

| Dimension | `extract_IDR_profile` | `extract_IDR` |
|---|---|---|
| Return type | `list[float]`, length = seq length | `int` (residue count) |
| Per-residue resolution | Yes — raw IUPred2A scores | No — binary region membership |
| Threshold logic | None (raw passthrough) | TH1 = 0.5, TH2 = 20 |
| Primary consumers | PPL regression, residue-level attention correlation | IDR fraction, DisProt/PDB validation |
| Output artifacts | `disorder_comp_concat.csv`, `esm2_perplexities.csv` | `umap_df.csv`, `idr_df.csv` |

Both functions share an identical invocation skeleton, shown in the interaction diagram: write the sequence into a temporary single-record FASTA, spawn IUPred2A as a subprocess in `long` disorder mode, capture stdout, discard the 40-token header, then parse `(position, amino acid, score)` triplets. The parsing loop extracts every third whitespace-separated token starting at offset 2 — the score column — and casts to `float`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller as Analysis script
    participant Fn as extract_IDR_profile / extract_IDR
    participant Tmp as tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile
    participant IUP as iupred2a.py (subprocess)
    Caller->>Fn: seq (str)
    Fn->>Tmp: write ">1\n" + seq
    Fn->>IUP: python iupred2a.py <tmp> long
    IUP-->>Fn: stdout (header + triplets)
    Fn->>Fn: stdout.split()[40:]
    Fn->>Fn: score = token[3*i + 2] per residue
    alt extract_IDR_profile
        Fn-->>Caller: list of per-residue floats
    else extract_IDR
        Fn->>Fn: region scan (0.5 / 20 rule)
        Fn-->>Caller: int IDR residue count
    end
```

> [!TIP]
> The `[40:]` header offset is the system's most fragile coupling point: it assumes IUPred2A's stdout preamble is exactly 40 whitespace tokens long for every invocation. If you upgrade to a different IUPred2A release whose header length changes, the triplet alignment breaks and you will get float-cast crashes at best — or silently misaligned scores at worst. Pin your IUPred2A version and verify one output against known residues before trusting bulk runs.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L79-L99), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L39-L77), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L41-L43)

## From Scores to IDR Regions: The 0.5/20 Segmentation Rule

`extract_IDR` does not simply count residues with score > 0.5. It implements the canonical definition of a *long* disordered region: scan the probability array left to right, accumulate a run counter while scores exceed `TH1 = 0.5`, and only commit residues to the IDR set when a run exceeds `TH2 = 20` residues. The scan handles the sequence-boundary edge case (a run still active at the final residue is committed with a clamped start index), and resets the counter whenever a run terminates without qualifying. The return value is `len(IDR_residues)` — the total number of residues belonging to *qualifying regions*, not the number of above-threshold residues.

The practical consequence is asymmetry worth internalizing: a 15-residue run of scores at 0.9 contributes **zero** to the IDR count, while a single 21-residue run at 0.51 contributes **21**. This means `extract_IDR` measures *region-scale* disorder (the kind relevant to IDP biology and phase-separation behavior), whereas `extract_IDR_profile` preserves *local-scale* fluctuation. When you see "number of disordered residues" in figures, it is the region-based quantity; when you see a disorder probability axis, it is the raw score.

> [!TIP]
> Downstream percent calculations divide the region-based count by sequence length — e.g., `idr_frac = idr / Sequence_length * 100` and `disorder_frac = tot_idr / seq_len * 100`. Because short disordered stretches are excluded by design, these fractions systematically *underestimate* total above-threshold disorder in proteins with fragmented disorder. If you extend this codebase, decide explicitly whether your new metric wants region-scale or residue-scale semantics and pick the corresponding function.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L59-L77), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L90-L99), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L367-L367)

## Downstream Consumers and Data Flow

Two analysis scripts call these functions, and both operate on the PDB (ordered-proxy) versus DisProt (disordered) input sets constructed in `define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py` — whose DisProt/PDB provenance and filtering are documented in [Dataset Curation and CD-HIT Clustering](21-dataset-curation-and-cd-hit-clustering). The consumer table below maps every call site to its derived quantity and committed output artifact, all of which flow into final publication rendering via `figures.py`.

| Consumer Script | Function Called | Derived Quantity | Output Artifact |
|---|---|---|---|
| `attention_rollout_analysis.py` (UMAP stage) | `extract_IDR` | `idr`, `idr_frac` per protein | `data/figure_data/umap_df.csv` (`IDR Frac` column) → `figures/umap.svg` |
| `attention_rollout_analysis.py` (set validation) | `extract_IDR` | Per-group IDR count distributions | `data/figure_data/idr_df.csv` → `figures/input_sets_disorder.svg` |
| `attention_rollout_analysis.py` (correlation stage) | `extract_IDR_profile` + `extract_IDR` | Residue-level `idr` + `attn_received`, per-protein Pearson `corr`, quartile `idr_bin` | `data/figure_data/disorder_comp_concat.csv` → `figures/attention_disorder_kde.svg` |
| `esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py` | `extract_IDR_profile` | `mean_masked_residue_disorder` aligned to masked tokens | `data/esm2_perplexities.csv` → OLS regression input |

Notably, `rg_mlp.py` imports from `attention_functions` but pulls only `get_esm2_embeddings` — the Rg predictor pipeline is disorder-score-free, consuming IDRome sequences rather than IUPred2A labels. And `figures.py` re-reads the precomputed CSVs rather than calling IUPred2A directly, which is why re-rendering final figures does not require the tool to be installed — a deliberate separation that supports the workflow described in [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    DS["data/protein_input_sets.csv"] --> ARA["attention_rollout_analysis.py"]
    DS --> PPL["esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py"]
    IUP["IUPred2A subprocess"] --> ARA
    IUP --> PPL
    ROLL["attention_rollout_comb_original.joblib"] --> ARA
    ARA --> U["umap_df.csv"]
    ARA --> I["idr_df.csv"]
    ARA --> D["disorder_comp_concat.csv"]
    PPL --> E["esm2_perplexities.csv"]
    U --> F1["figures.py"]
    D --> F1
```

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L90-L99), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L183-L199), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L90-L109), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L19-L19), [figures.py](scripts/figures.py#L60-L100)

## Residue-Level Disorder–Attention Coupling

The most analytically significant consumer is the **Cor(Disorder, Attn Rollout Received)** section of `attention_rollout_analysis.py`. For every protein in both sets, it computes the per-residue disorder profile and the per-residue attention received (column sum of the rollout matrix), builds a paired residue-level dataframe, and records the Pearson correlation between the two vectors *per protein* as the `corr` column. It also quantizes raw scores into four bins via `pd.cut(bins=4)` — a quartile binning over each protein's own score distribution — and persists the full table to `data/figure_data/disorder_comp_concat.csv`.

```python
idr_profile = extract_IDR_profile(sequence)
tot_idr = extract_IDR(sequence)
attention_received = data['rollout'].sum(dim=0).cpu().numpy()
...
disorder_df['corr'] = np.corrcoef(disorder_df['idr'], disorder_df['attn_received'])[0, 1]
...
disorder_comp_concat['idr_bin'] = pd.cut(disorder_comp_concat['idr'], bins=4)
```

The binned table then feeds a log-scale KDE plot: attention-received distributions rendered separately for each disorder-probability bin (lightest blue = lowest quartile, darkest = highest), producing `figures/attention_disorder_kde.svg` — the direct visual test of whether ESM-2 allocates attention as a function of predicted disorder. This residue-level framing is what connects disorder scoring to the amino-acid-level statistics covered next in [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statsics) and to the group-level comparisons in [Ordered Versus Disordered Comparison](12-ordered-versus-disordered-comparison).

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L343-L370), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L372-L387), [figures.py](scripts/figures.py#L89-L100)

## Disorder Scores in the Perplexity Regression

In `esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py`, the raw profile gets a sequence-aware transformation: each protein's masked-LM perplexity run produces a per-token mask dataframe, special tokens (`<cls>`, `<eos>`) are stripped, the disorder profile is attached as a `Disorder` column, and the analysis keeps only *masked* positions — collapsing each protein to `mean_masked_residue_disorder`, the average disorder of exactly the residues the language model had to predict. A length guard skips (and logs) any protein where the IUPred2A output length fails to match the tokenized sequence length, preventing silent misalignment between the two per-residue vectors.

This guarded join is the entire feature-construction step for the regression: perplexity (response) versus mean masked-residue disorder (predictor), later fit with OLS under HC1 robust covariance and reported with standardized betas. The statistical machinery itself is the subject of [Perplexity-Disorder Regression](16-perplexity-disorder-regression); the IUPred2A-relevant design point here is that **disorder enters the model as an averaged masked-position quantity**, not as a whole-sequence mean — masking is the only reason the pairing is well-defined.

Sources: [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L90-L101), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L111-L141)

## Practical Considerations for Reproducibility

Three operational realities follow from this architecture. **First, throughput:** every sequence triggers a fresh `python` subprocess and a full IUPred2A prediction — there is no batching or caching, so scripts over hundreds of proteins pay process-spawn cost per sequence, and re-running correlation stages re-predicts everything. **Second, alignment by construction:** the parser derives residue count from stdout length rather than validating against the input sequence; the only explicit check exists in the PPL script, so treat profile length as unverified everywhere else. **Third, environment duality:** the analysis code runs in your conda environment while IUPred2A runs in whatever `python` resolves on `PATH`, so dependency problems in the predictor do not manifest as import errors in your session.

The committed `data/figure_data/*.csv` artifacts mitigate the worst of this: `umap_df.csv`, `idr_df.csv`, and `disorder_comp_concat.csv` all persist IUPred2A-derived quantities, so figure regeneration paths avoid the tool entirely. Only stages that recompute disorder (or that you modify) require the configured local installation — consistent with the repo's overall derived-versus-live data strategy referenced in [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility).

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L45-L57), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L93-L95), [figures.py](scripts/figures.py#L60-L89)

## Where to Go Next

With the disorder scoring layer understood, the natural progression follows the pipeline order: proceed to [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics) to see how per-residue quantities aggregate to amino-acid-level comparisons, then [Ordered Versus Disordered Comparison](12-ordered-versus-disordered-comparison) for the group-level analyses that consume the `idr` and `idr_frac` columns, and finally [Perplexity-Disorder Regression](16-perplexity-disorder-regression) for the full statistical treatment of the `esm2_perplexities.csv` feature table. If you need to rebuild the input sets these scores are computed on first, start from [Dataset Curation and CD-HIT Clustering](21-dataset-curation-and-cd-hit-clustering).


# Amino Acid Attention Statistics



This page explains how the pipeline transforms raw ESM-2 attention tensors into **amino-acid-resolved statistics** — answering the question: *does the model allocate its attention differently depending on residue identity?* The analysis operates at two granularities: a whole-network rollout-level summary and a per-head/per-layer sweep, each with its own aggregation function, normalization strategy, and statistical validation. The implementation is distributed across three files: `attention_functions.py` provides the reusable aggregation primitives, `attention_rollout_analysis.py` orchestrates the three analysis blocks, and `figures.py` renders the publication-grade Figure 2.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L18-L23), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L26-L30), [figures.py](scripts/figures.py#L137-L139)

## The Core Abstraction: "Attention Received"

Every statistic on this page derives from a single reduction: the **column sum** of an attention matrix. In a matrix of shape `(seq_len, seq_len)`, entry `[i][j]` quantifies how much token `i` attends to token `j`; summing over the row axis (`axis=0`) collapses the "attending side" and yields a vector of length `seq_len` where each element is the total attention *received* by that residue. The row dimension (who attends) is deliberately marginalized out — the analysis only asks who is attended to. In `get_attention_distribution_df`, each residue is labeled as `f"{aa}_{i}"` (identity plus position), the rollout matrix is converted to NumPy, reduced to this received-attention vector, and then exploded into tidy `(protein_id, amino_acid, attention)` records — one row per residue instance, which makes amino-acid identity a first-class grouping key for downstream `groupby` operations.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Rollout matrix\n(seq_len × seq_len)"] -->|"sum(axis=0)"| B["Received-attention vector\n(seq_len)"]
    B -->|"zip with labels\naa_1, aa_2, …"| C["Tidy records\n(protein_id, amino_acid, attention)"]
    C -->|"groupby amino_acid"| D["Per-AA distribution\n→ mean, SE, Cohen's d"]
```

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L102-L142)

The function exposes two per-protein rescaling options — `standardize` (z-score: subtract mean, divide by std, with a zero-σ fallback) and `normalize` (min-max scaling) — both applied to the received-attention vector *before* the tidy explosion, so scaling happens within a single protein's context. In the production run both flags are `False`, meaning raw summed rollout values feed the statistics unmodified.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L115-L133), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L206-L207)

## Two Measurement Granularities

The analysis deliberately computes amino-acid statistics at two scales, because they answer different questions. The **rollout-level** view uses one precomputed rollout matrix per protein (loaded from `attention_rollout_comb_original.joblib`, then split into PDB/DisProt dictionaries by filename substring) — it captures network-wide attention flow as propagated through all 33 layers. The **head/layer-resolved** view re-enters the raw per-layer attention tensors and asks where, specifically in the 33×20 grid of (layer, head) positions, each amino acid attracts attention.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Inputs["Precomputed artifacts"]
        R["attention_rollout_comb_original.joblib\n(one rollout per protein)"]
        M["attention_matrices_labeled_0..21_original.joblib\n(22 chunks, full 33×20×L×L tensors)"]
    end
    R -->|"get_attention_distribution_df"| A["Block 1:\nRollout distribution per AA"]
    M -->|"run_aa_analysis_head_layer\n→ get_head_layer_attn\n→ get_aa_attn_perc"| B["Block 2:\nPer head/layer AA attention"]
    A --> S1["mean_aa_attn.csv\n+ Welch t-test / Cohen's d"]
    B --> S2["attn_occur_norm.csv\n+ FDR-corrected tests"]
    M2["Residue labels only"] -->|"occurrence counting"| C["Block 3:\nAA composition control"]
    C --> S3["comb_props.csv"]
    S1 --> F["figures.py — Figure 2"]
    S2 --> F
```

| Dimension | Rollout-level | Head/layer-resolved |
|---|---|---|
| Input artifact | One rollout matrix per protein | 22 joblib chunks of raw attention tensors |
| Aggregation function | `get_attention_distribution_df` | `run_aa_analysis_head_layer` → `get_aa_attn_perc` |
| Token filtering | Handled upstream in rollout computation | Explicit `cls`/`eos` strip in `get_head_layer_attn` |
| Output granularity | One value per residue instance | One value per (AA, layer, head, protein) |
| Statistical scope | ~20 tests (one per AA) | up to 20 × 33 × 20 = 13,200 tests |
| Figure output | Grouped bar chart | Cys/Asp head×layer heatmaps |

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L39-L45), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L256-L277)

## Normalization Strategies: Three Modes, One Question

The single most consequential design decision in this pipeline is how per-amino-acid sums are normalized, because raw attention sums are confounded by residue frequency. `get_aa_attn_perc` implements three modes selected by the `normalize` argument, each producing a distinct output column:

| Mode | Computation | Answers | Output column | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `local` | AA's attention ÷ protein's total attention × 100 | What *share* of a protein's attention budget does each AA type capture? | `attn_percent` | High-frequency AAs dominate by construction |
| `occurrence` | AA's total attention ÷ count of that AA in the sequence | On average, how much attention does a *single instance* of each AA receive? | `attn_occur_norm` | Removes frequency bias; per-protein values noisy for rare AAs |
| `global` | Raw summed attention (optionally rescaled by the full-matrix sum across all heads/layers) | Where is absolute attention mass concentrated? | `sum_attn` / rescaled `attn_percent` | Not comparable across proteins of different length |

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L280-L333)

The production run invokes `run_aa_analysis_head_layer(normalize='occurrence', model='original')` — the occurrence mode is the headline choice for the head/layer analysis precisely because it decouples residue identity from residue abundance. The `global` mode's rescaling variant is handled at the caller level: `run_aa_analysis_head_layer` computes each protein's total attention mass once (flattening the full 33×20 matrix after stripping special tokens) and then divides each per-head result by it, rather than recomputing per slice.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L250-L254), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L356-L374)

> [!TIP]
> The three normalization modes share a single bottleneck: the column-sum reduction happens once, *before* the mode branch. This means the same received-attention vector feeds all three strategies — switching modes is a pure post-processing choice, so you can re-run all modes from one pass over the attention chunks without recomputing reductions.

## Inside the Head/Layer Sweep: Chunked Iteration with Memory Discipline

`run_aa_analysis_head_layer` must process the full attention tensor stack for every protein — 33 layers × 20 heads × seq_len² per protein, across the entire corpus. It does this by streaming through 22 pre-sharded joblib chunks, using `safe_load` (which forces `gc.collect()` before each `joblib.load`) to reclaim memory between chunks. For each protein it reads `sequence_length` and `sequence` from the chunk metadata, then enters a nested loop over all 33 layers and 20 heads. `get_head_layer_attn` slices out one `(seq_len, seq_len)` matrix while trimming the `<cls>` prefix and `<eos>`/padding suffix (offset 1 through `actual_seq_len + 1`), guaranteeing that special tokens never contaminate amino-acid statistics. Each per-slice result is immediately stamped with `protein`, `layer`, and `head` columns, appended to a list, and explicitly deleted alongside the sliced tensor — the `del head_layer_attn, aa_attn_df` statement inside the innermost loop is load-bearing, not decorative.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L336-L389), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L252-L254)

## Statistical Validation: From Bar Charts to Effect Sizes

Every amino-acid comparison is backed by parametric statistics rather than visual inspection alone. At the rollout level, the script first builds descriptive summaries — `groupby(['amino_acid', 'Group'])` aggregating mean, std, and count, then deriving standard error as `std / √count` — which become the error bars in the grouped bar chart. Effect sizes come from `cohens_d`, which computes pooled standard deviation as `√(((n₁−1)s₁² + (n₂−1)s₂²)/(n₁+n₂−2))` and pairs it with a Welch's t-test (`equal_var=False`), correctly avoiding the homoscedasticity assumption for two biological groups of unequal size.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L202-L220), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L488-L530)

The head/layer sweep multiplies the testing burden by 660, which motivates `fast_statistical_comparison`'s performance engineering: instead of filtering the DataFrame per combination, it builds a sorted multi-index on `['aa', 'layer', 'head', 'Group']` for O(log n) lookups, then iterates the cartesian product of AAs × 33 layers × 20 heads. A minimum-sample guard (`n < 3` in either group skips the test) prevents degenerate statistics on rare residues in short proteins.

| Statistical component | Scope | Implementation detail | Threshold / correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standard error bars | Rollout level, per (AA, group) | `std / √count` after groupby | Descriptive only |
| Welch's t-test | Both levels | `scipy.stats.ttest_ind(..., equal_var=False)` | Raw p-value |
| Cohen's d | Both levels | Pooled-SD formula, guarded against `pooled_std = 0` | Effect-size magnitude |
| FDR correction | Head/layer level only | `scipy.stats.false_discovery_control` | Significant if `p_fdr < 0.05` |

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L431-L485)

After `false_discovery_control` reshapes the ~13,000 raw p-values, significant results are filtered and Cohen's d values are summarized via `groupby('amino_acid').describe()` — reporting how effect size *varies* across head/layer positions per amino acid, not just an aggregate verdict. The oversized intermediate `attn` DataFrame is then explicitly deleted to free memory before plotting begins.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L255-L265)

## The Composition Confounder — and Its Explicit Control

There is a subtle trap in any per-amino-acid comparison between protein sets: PDB (ordered) and DisProt (disordered) proteins have genuinely different amino-acid compositions — disordered regions are enriched in polar and charged residues and depleted in hydrophobic ones. Any raw attention sum per AA type therefore confounds *differential attention* with *differential abundance*. The pipeline defends on two fronts. First, the occurrence normalization itself: dividing by per-sequence AA counts converts totals into per-instance means, so a residue type only scores high if its individual instances receive above-average attention. Second, an explicit composition audit (Block 3) computes each AA's proportional frequency within each group — occurrences summed per amino acid, divided by total occurrences per group, expressed as percentages — and saves it as `comb_props.csv` alongside its own grouped bar chart. This lets any observed attention asymmetry be checked against the null hypothesis "it's just composition."

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Observed: AA X receives\nmore attention in DisProt"] --> B{Composition check}
    B -->|"comb_props shows X\nequally frequent in both groups"| C["Interpretation:\nattention preference is real"]
    B -->|"comb_props shows X\nenriched in DisProt"| D["Interpretation:\nconfounded by abundance\n→ rely on occurrence normalization"]
```

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L299-L337)

> [!TIP]
> The occurrence computation on line 303–304 uses `transform('count')` — broadcasting per-(AA, protein) counts back onto every residue row — rather than an aggregation. This keeps the tidy frame row-aligned per residue, which is what allows the same DataFrame to serve both the per-instance statistics and the per-type composition sums without a join.

## From figure_data CSVs to Publication Figure 2

The analysis script writes intermediate artifacts to `data/figure_data/`, and `figures.py` treats them as a frozen contract for final rendering — a deliberate producer/consumer split that separates heavy computation from styling (see [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility)). Figure 2, titled "AA Attention Allocation," consumes two of these artifacts:

| Artifact | Producer section | Final figure | Visual encoding |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mean_aa_attn.csv` | "Rollout Distr for Each AA" | `mean_aa_attn_received.svg` | Grouped bars per AA (PDB orange / DisProt steelblue), ± SE caps |
| `attn_occur_norm.csv` (filtered to C, D) | "AA Attn Received @ Each Head/Layer" | `asp_cys_heatmaps.svg` | 2×2 grid of head×layer heatmaps, shared color scale |
| `comb_props.csv` | "AA Composition Distributions" | Analysis-stage only (`aa_proportional_frequency.svg`) | Composition bars per group |

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L222-L243), [figures.py](scripts/figures.py#L142-L159)

A detail worth noting in the heatmap rendering: all four panels (Cys×PDB, Cys×DisProt, Asp×PDB, Asp×DisProt) are computed with a **shared** `vmin`/`vmax` derived from the entire `attn_occur_norm` column, and the panel layout drops tick labels on interior edges for a compact 7.2×3.25-inch canvas. Shared scaling is what makes the cross-panel comparison valid — per-panel scaling would visually exaggerate differences within low-attention panels.

Sources: [figures.py](scripts/figures.py#L161-L207)

Note also that `figures.py` and `attention_rollout_analysis.py` produce *parallel versions* of the same figures: the analysis script emits draft exploratory plots (e.g., `figures/mean_aa_attn_received.svg` with a title and per-panel styling), while `figures.py` regenerates publication variants under `figures/final/` using `publication.mplstyle` constraints (see [Publication Figure Styling](23-publication-figure-styling)). To regenerate everything end-to-end, follow [Reproducing Paper Figures](4-reproducing-paper-figures).

Sources: [figures.py](scripts/figures.py#L26-L29), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L227-L243)

## Relation to the Broader Pipeline

The amino-acid statistics layer sits downstream of raw tensor extraction and upstream of every functional-validation analysis. Its inputs presuppose the rollout algorithm ([Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm)) and the chunked attention matrix extraction ([Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction)); its per-residue received-attention vectors are the same quantities later joined with IUPred2A disorder profiles ([Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A](10-disorder-scoring-with-iupred2a)) and with ClinVar variant positions ([ClinVar Disease Residue Attention](13-clinvar-disease-residue-attention)). Where this page asks *which residues* attract attention, the set-level contrast — whether disordered proteins as a class receive different attention than ordered ones — is developed in [Ordered Versus Disordered Comparison](12-ordered-versus-disordered-comparison). For the memory-management rationale behind the chunked sweep design, see [Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management).


# Ordered Versus Disordered Comparison



This page explains how the repository operationalizes its central validation question — **does ESM-2 allocate attention differently to ordered versus intrinsically disordered protein regions?** — by constructing length-matched protein cohorts and comparing them across embedding geometry, amino-acid-level attention allocation, head/layer resolution, and residue-level attention–disorder coupling. Rather than a single script, the comparison is a *framework*: one script builds fair cohorts, another computes per-protein signals, a third runs every statistical comparison, and a fourth assembles publication figures. If you have followed [Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm) and [Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A](10-disorder-scoring-with-iupred2a), this page shows how those two ingredients are brought together as paired evidence.

The design rests on a deliberate duality: cohorts give **binary ground truth** (PDB = structurally resolved/ordered, DisProt = experimentally characterized disorder), while IUPred2A gives a **continuous per-residue disorder profile**. Comparing both lets the analysis triangulate — if attention tracks disorder, the signal should appear both between cohorts and within each protein along its sequence.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L26-L45), [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L8-L13)

## Concept Map: How the Comparison Is Organized

The notation below: rounded boxes are data artifacts, sharp boxes are computational steps, arrows show the flow from raw sequences to statistical conclusions. Everything on this page sits inside the "Comparisons" cluster.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Inputs["Raw Inputs"]
        DP["data/disprot.fasta<br/>(DisProt release 2025_06)"]
        PDB["pdb_seqres.txt.gz<br/>(PDB sequences)"]
    end
    subgraph Build["Cohort Construction"]
        F["Filters: length 50–1024,<br/>dedup, drop X/U/O"]
        LM["Length-bin matching:<br/>subsample PDB to mirror<br/>DisProt length histogram"]
        OUT["data/protein_input_sets.csv"]
    end
    subgraph Signals["Per-Protein Signals"]
        ROL["attention_rollout_comb_original.joblib"]
        EMB["1280-D mean ESM-2<br/>embeddings (layer 33)"]
        IDR["IUPred2A disorder profiles"]
    end
    subgraph Compare["Comparative Analyses"]
        G["Embedding geometry:<br/>UMAP, silhouette, GroupKFold LR"]
        AA["Per-AA attention received:<br/>Cohen's d + Welch t"]
        HL["Per-head/layer stats:<br/>FDR-corrected"]
        COR["Per-protein corr(disorder, attention)<br/>+ KDE by disorder quartile"]
    end
    DP --> F --> LM --> OUT
    PDB --> F
    OUT --> ROL
    OUT --> EMB
    OUT --> IDR
    ROL --> AA
    ROL --> HL
    ROL --> COR
    EMB --> G
    IDR --> COR
    IDR --> G
```

The pipeline is strictly ordered: cohort construction must precede everything else because `protein_input_sets.csv` is the single source of protein identity for all downstream analyses; the rollout artifact must exist before `attention_rollout_analysis.py` can split proteins into groups by their ID prefix.

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L15-L64), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L36-L45)

## Constructing Matched Cohorts

The comparison begins in `define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py`, which loads DisProt sequences via `read_fasta` and PDB sequences from a gzipped `pdb_seqres.txt.gz`. Both cohorts pass through the same length window (50–1024 residues) and deduplication, but the PDB cohort additionally excludes sequences containing ambiguous residues (`X`, `U`, `O`) to keep the amino-acid alphabet standard for tokenization.

| Filter | DisProt (disordered) | PDB (ordered) | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source file | `data/disprot.fasta` | `pdb_seqres.txt.gz` | Curated disorder evidence vs. structurally resolved chains |
| Sequence length | 50 < len < 1024 | 50 < len < 1024 | Fit ESM-2 context window and avoid trivially short chains |
| Duplicates | Dropped by sequence | Dropped by sequence | Prevent double-counting identical chains |
| Ambiguous residues | — | Drop `X`/`U`/`O` | Keep canonical 20-AA alphabet |
| Length distribution | Reference histogram | **Subsampled to match** | Eliminate length as a confound |

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L15-L34)

The length-matching step is the most important methodological decision in the whole page. Without it, any attention difference between groups could simply reflect sequence length (rollout matrices for longer proteins distribute attention differently). The script bins DisProt lengths into 20 bins with `np.digitize`, counts proteins per bin, then samples PDB proteins from the corresponding bins with a fixed `random_state=42` — taking all candidates when a bin has fewer PDB proteins than needed. The result is a PDB cohort whose length histogram mirrors DisProt's, verified visually later by the shared-bin histogram in the analysis script.

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L39-L58), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L47-L66)

Finally, every protein receives a deterministic ID (`pdb_protein_N`, `disprot_protein_N`) and the union is written to `data/protein_input_sets.csv`. This naming convention is load-bearing: every downstream script infers group membership by substring matching on the ID (`'pdb' in k.lower()`), so the cohort label travels with the protein through every artifact without requiring a separate metadata join.

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L60-L64), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L36-L45)

## Module Interaction: Who Consumes What

The comparison spans four files with a clean dependency direction — shared utilities at the bottom, orchestration in the middle, publication styling at the top. This diagram shows each script's imports from `attention_functions.py` and the artifact hand-off to `figures.py`:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph AF["attention_functions.py (shared utilities)"]
        RD["read_fasta"]
        EI["extract_IDR /<br/>extract_IDR_profile"]
        GAD["get_attention_distribution_df"]
        AR["attention_rollout"]
        GAR["get_attn_rollout"]
        GE["get_esm2_embeddings"]
        FSC["fast_statistical_comparison"]
        CD["cohens_d"]
    end
    subgraph Scripts["Pipeline scripts"]
        DEF["define_pdb_disprot_<br/>datasets.py"]
        GET["get_esm2_attention_<br/>rollout.py"]
        ANA["attention_rollout_<br/>analysis.py"]
    end
    FIG["figures.py<br/>(publication layer)"]
    DEF --> RD
    GET --> AR
    ANA --> GAD
    ANA --> CD
    ANA --> FSC
    ANA --> GE
    ANA --> EI
    ANA --> GAR
    ANA -->|"data/figure_data/*.csv"| FIG
```

Note the hand-off pattern: `attention_rollout_analysis.py` performs all statistics and dumps intermediate tidy CSVs into `data/figure_data/`, while `figures.py` re-reads those files to assemble final multi-panel layouts (reloading `umap_df.csv`, `disorder_comp_concat.csv`, `mean_aa_attn.csv`, `attn_occur_norm.csv`, and `si_examples.csv`). This separation means the expensive model inference never re-runs just to restyle a figure.

Sources: [figures.py](scripts/figures.py#L47-L152), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L36-L56)

The rollout artifact itself is produced by `get_esm2_attention_rollout.py`, which loads the 22 precomputed attention-matrix chunks, computes one rollout per protein (discard ratio 0.9, mean head fusion), and persists everything into a single joblib dictionary keyed by protein ID. This is a pure batch-compute step with no group awareness — the ordered/disordered framing only enters when `attention_rollout_analysis.py` splits the dictionary into `pdb_dict` and `disprot_dict` by key substring.

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L26-L56), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L36-L45)

## Four Axes of Comparison

The analysis script compares the cohorts along four independent axes, each answering a slightly different version of the core question. The table below is the map for the rest of this section; the unit of observation column is worth studying — it ranges from whole proteins down to single residues, and this determines how the statistics must be interpreted.

| Axis | Question answered | Unit of observation | Signal | Key statistic | Artifact |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Embedding geometry | Are the cohorts separable in representation space? | Protein | 1280-D mean layer-33 embedding | Silhouette score + GroupKFold logistic regression accuracy | `umap_df.csv` |
| Per-AA attention allocation | Does ESM-2 route more attention to certain amino acids in disorder? | Residue | Rollout column-sum ("attention received") | Cohen's d + Welch's t-test per amino acid | `mean_aa_attn.csv` |
| Head/layer resolution | Where in the 33×20 grid does the difference live? | Residue × head × layer | Occurrence-normalized head attention | Welch's t + FDR across 13,200 tests | `attn_occur_norm.csv` |
| Attention–disorder coupling | Does attention track disorder *within* each protein? | Residue | IUPred2A probability vs. rollout received | Per-protein Pearson correlation + KDE by disorder quartile | `disorder_comp_concat.csv` |

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L68-L387)

### Axis 1: Embedding Geometry (UMAP, Silhouette, and Leakage-Aware Classification)

Before touching attention at all, the script checks whether the cohorts differ in ESM-2's *representations*. It computes mean-pooled layer-33 embeddings for every protein (1280 dimensions), standardizes them, and projects to 2-D with UMAP, coloring points first by cohort and then by each protein's IDR fraction (percentage of residues in long disordered segments, computed by `extract_IDR` — ≥20 consecutive residues above IUPred2A probability 0.5). The dual-coloring is deliberate: if the second panel's viridis gradient aligns with the first panel's cohort split, disorder content — not cohort identity per se — is the latent structure organizing the space.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L68-L132), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L39-L77)

Two quantitative separations complement the visual: a silhouette score computed in the original 1280-D space (avoiding UMAP's distortion of distances), and a logistic regression trained to predict cohort labels with **5-fold GroupKFold cross-validation where the groups are CD-HIT clusters at 40% sequence identity**. Homologous proteins share clusters, so no cluster's members can straddle the train/test split — the reported accuracy reflects generalization to *unseen sequence families*, not memorization.

> [!TIP]
> The GroupKFold-over-CD-HIT-clusters design is the difference between a real result and an artifact. A naive k-fold split would let near-identical homologs appear on both sides, letting the classifier succeed by recognizing families rather than disorder. If you adapt this pipeline, preserve the cluster-grouped CV or your accuracy numbers will be silently inflated.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L134-L177), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L394-L429)

As a sanity check on the cohorts themselves, the script also plots the kernel density of disordered-residue counts per protein for each group — this validates that the labels carry the expected biological signal (DisProt proteins should be far richer in disordered residues than PDB ones) before any attention claims are made.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L179-L200)

### Axis 2: Amino-Acid-Level Attention Allocation

Here the comparison moves from proteins to residues. For every protein in both cohorts, `get_attention_distribution_df` sums each column of the rollout matrix — producing a per-residue "attention received" vector — and melts it into a tidy long table of `(protein_id, amino_acid, attention)` rows. Group-wise summary statistics (mean, std, count, standard error) are then computed per amino acid and plotted as paired bar charts, PDB in orange, DisProt in steel blue.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L101-L141), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L202-L243)

Differences between groups are quantified with the `cohens_d` helper, which for each of the 20 amino acids computes the DisProt-minus-PDB mean difference, a pooled-standard-deviation Cohen's d effect size, and a Welch's t-test (unequal variances assumed). Sorting the output by Cohen's d surfaces which amino acids carry the largest attention-allocation differences — this feeds directly into the amino-acid comparisons detailed in [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics).

> [!TIP]
> Note that `cohens_d` counts every *residue* as an observation, not every protein — residues from the same protein are not independent, so the uncorrected p-values are optimistic. This is why the pipeline pairs them with effect sizes and, in the head/layer axis, FDR correction, and why the visual emphasis falls on Cohen's d magnitude rather than raw significance counts.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L488-L530), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L216-L243)

### Axis 3: Head/Layer Resolution with Multiple-Testing Control

The aggregate amino-acid comparison collapses 33 layers × 20 heads into one rollout number. To localize *where* in the transformer the disorder sensitivity lives, `run_aa_analysis_head_layer(normalize='occurrence')` recomputes per-amino-acid attention at every one of the 660 head/layer positions, normalizing by how many times that amino acid occurs in each sequence (so abundant residues like Leu aren't inflated simply by being common).

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L284-L390), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L246-L254)

This generates up to 20 amino acids × 660 positions = 13,200 group comparisons, handled by `fast_statistical_comparison`. The function's performance design matters at this scale: it builds a sorted multi-index on `(aa, layer, head, Group)` for O(1) lookups, iterates all combinations, guards against cells with fewer than 3 samples per group, and uses Welch's t-test rather than Mann-Whitney (the code comments note this as an explicit speed choice). The script then applies `false_discovery_control` to the full uncorrected p-value vector and flags `p_fdr < 0.05`, and summarizes the significant Cohen's d values per amino acid.

| Statistic | Purpose | Computed in |
|---|---|---|
| Welch's t-test (`equal_var=False`) | Significance of group difference without variance homogeneity assumption | `fast_statistical_comparison`, `cohens_d` |
| Cohen's d (pooled SD) | Effect-size magnitude, comparable across amino acids and head/layer cells | Both |
| Minimum group size n ≥ 3 | Prevents degenerate cells from producing spurious tests | `fast_statistical_comparison` |
| FDR correction | Controls expected false discoveries across 13,200 simultaneous tests | `attention_rollout_analysis.py` |

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L432-L486), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L255-L265)

The surviving results are visualized as head-by-layer heatmaps (batched three amino acids at a time, PDB left, DisProt right), with a separate figure-level heatmap pair for cysteine and aspartate preserved in `attn_occur_norm.csv` — the two residues singled out for the publication figure because their patterns differ most sharply between cohorts.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L267-L296), [figures.py](scripts/figures.py#L155-L215)

### Axis 4: Residue-Level Attention–Disorder Coupling

The fourth axis switches from between-cohort to within-protein comparison. For every protein in both dictionaries, the script fetches its IUPred2A per-residue disorder profile (`extract_IDR_profile`), its count of long disordered segments (`extract_IDR`), and its rollout attention-received vector, then computes a Pearson correlation between the two per-residue series with `np.corrcoef`. This yields one correlation coefficient per protein — a direct, sequence-position-resolved measure of whether attention follows disorder inside a single sequence.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L339-L363), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L79-L99)

The residues from all proteins are pooled and binned by their IUPred2A probability into four quartile bins; a kernel density estimate of attention-received per bin (log-scaled y-axis, since attention values are heavily right-skewed) shows whether higher-disorder residues systematically receive less attention *regardless of which cohort they belong to*. Because the bins pool both cohorts, this analysis tests the continuous disorder signal independent of the binary PDB/DisProt label — the strongest form of the paper's hypothesis.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L365-L387)

### The Composition Control

One confound deserves its own subsection: if DisProt proteins simply contain different amino acids than PDB proteins, per-amino-acid attention differences could be composition artifacts rather than attention-allocation differences. The script therefore computes each group's amino-acid usage as proportional frequencies (per-amino-acid counts divided by group totals, expressed as percent) and plots them side by side. Reading this figure alongside the attention-allocation bars lets you disentangle "DisProt has more of residue X" from "residue X receives more attention in DisProt."

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L299-L337)

## Case-Study Validation: TDP-43 and Friends

Aggregate statistics can hide biology, so the script closes with five single-protein dissections: TDP-43, P53, FUS, MDM2, and APOE. Sequences are hardcoded, ESM-2 is re-loaded with `output_attentions=True`, and each protein gets an on-the-fly rollout via `get_attn_rollout` paired with its IUPred2A profile — producing position-aligned overlay plots of "Attention Received" versus "Disorder" along the sequence.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L389-L425), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L218-L246)

TDP-43 receives the dedicated treatment because its domain architecture is a textbook mixed-order protein: the script annotates the N-terminal domain (residues 1–103, disordered), both RNA-recognition motifs (104–200 and 191–262, folded), and the low-complexity C-terminal domain (274–413, disordered) as shaded spans. If the aggregate finding is real, attention received should dip over the folded RRM regions and rise over the flanking disordered segments — a single-image falsification test of the whole comparison. The other four proteins are rendered as a stacked multi-panel supplementary figure and exported to `si_examples.csv` for the final layout.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L427-L483), [figures.py](scripts/figures.py#L109-L152)

## Design Rationale: What Makes This Comparison Trustworthy

Every confound that could masquerade as a disorder-attention relationship has a specific countermeasure baked into the pipeline. The table below summarizes the threat-to-control mapping — useful as a checklist if you extend the analysis to new cohorts.

| Threat to validity | Countermeasure | Where implemented |
|---|---|---|
| Sequence length differs between cohorts | 20-bin length matching, PDB subsampled to DisProt's histogram | `define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py` |
| Amino-acid composition differs | Proportional-frequency composition comparison shown beside attention results | `attention_rollout_analysis.py` (AA Composition) |
| Homology inflates classification accuracy | CD-HIT 40% identity clusters + GroupKFold CV | `attention_rollout_analysis.py` |
| Abundant residues look attention-rich | Occurrence normalization at head/layer level | `attention_functions.py` (`get_aa_attn_perc`) |
| Thousands of tests inflate false positives | FDR correction across all AA × layer × head comparisons | `attention_rollout_analysis.py` |
| Effect sizes misread from significance alone | Cohen's d reported and sorted alongside every Welch's t | `attention_functions.py` |
| Aggregate statistics hide per-protein behavior | TDP-43 + 4 SI case studies with domain annotations | `attention_rollout_analysis.py` |

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L39-L58), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L139-L177), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L432-L530)

The trade-offs are worth stating plainly. Binary cohort labels are unambiguous and easy to classify, but they conflate disorder with everything else that distinguishes DisProt entries from PDB entries (function, length regime, family composition — partially mitigated by matching). The continuous IUPred2A profile avoids cohort artifacts but imports its own model biases. Running both comparison modes and checking that they agree is the repository's answer: a conclusion is treated as credible only when the binary split, the continuous coupling, and the case studies tell the same story.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L179-L200), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L339-L387)

## Where to Go Next

This page established the comparative *scaffolding*. To go deeper along its edges: [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics) dissects the per-residue attention distributions introduced in Axis 2; [ClinVar Disease Residue Attention](13-clinvar-disease-residue-attention) replaces cohort labels with disease annotations for a finer-grained validation; [Perplexity-Disorder Regression](16-perplexity-disorder-regression) repeats the comparison using masked-LM perplexity instead of attention; and [MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor) builds on the observation that disorder correlates with global compaction. For the engineering details of the cohort inputs themselves, see [Dataset Curation and CD-HIT Clustering](21-dataset-curation-and-cd-hit-clustering).


# ClinVar Disease Residue Attention


This page explains how `scripts/clinvar_expanded.py` uses ClinVar pathogenic missense variants as a functional ground truth to test whether ESM-2 attention rollout is enriched at disease-relevant residues — and whether that enrichment persists after controlling for evolutionary conservation, stratified by disorder level. This analysis produces Figure 3 of the paper and is the first entry in the *Functional Validation Analyses* group. It builds directly on the rollout machinery from [Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm) and the disorder scoring from [Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A](10-disorder-scoring-with-iupred2a).
Sources: [README.md](README.md#L97-L105), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L24-L34)

## The Hypothesis: Attention as a Functional Probe
The core question is behavioral, not mechanistic: if ESM-2's attention budget is meaningfully allocated, residues harboring known pathogenic mutations should receive disproportionately high attention compared with the other residues of the same proteins. ClinVar is used as the probe because it provides clinically curated, position-resolved labels — the script extracts the wild-type amino acid, the mutated position, and the mutant amino acid from each variant annotation, converting them into a binary per-residue `path_mut` flag. The design is deliberately confounded-aware: disease sites are typically evolutionarily conserved, so the analysis jointly models attention alongside DescribeProt conservation scores to ask whether attention carries signal *beyond* conservation rather than merely re-encoding it.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Signals["Per-Residue Signals"]
        ATT["Attention received<br/>(rollout column-sum)"]
        CON["Conservation<br/>(DescribeProt MMseqs2 score)"]
        IDR["Disorder probability<br/>(IUPred2A long)"]
        DIS["path_mut<br/>(ClinVar site membership)"]
    end
    DIS --> DESC["Descriptive layer:<br/>distributions by disorder decile,<br/>AA group, and disease relevance"]
    ATT --> DESC
    IDR --> DESC
    ATT --> OLS["OLS per IDR bin:<br/>rollout ~ path_mut + conservation"]
    CON --> OLS
    DIS --> OLS
    ATT --> LOG["Logit per IDR bin:<br/>path_mut ~ rollout_z + conservation_z<br/>(+ LR test vs conservation-only)"]
    CON --> LOG
    DIS --> LOG
```
Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L44-L57), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L294-L297), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L357-L375)

## Pipeline Architecture
The script is a single end-to-end pipeline with two major stages: corpus construction and attention-based statistical validation. The first stage either loads the committed ClinVar corpus or rebuilds it from raw NCBI downloads; the second stage forwards every unique protein sequence through ESM-2 once, computes per-residue attention received and IUPred2A disorder profiles, then runs descriptive visualizations and per-bin regressions.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph EXT["External Data (scripts/esm2_interp_data.py)"]
        CV["variant_summary.txt.gz<br/>(ClinVar)"]
        G2R["gene2refseq<br/>(NM → NP accession map)"]
        FA["GRCh38_latest_protein.faa<br/>(NP → sequence)"]
        DP["9606_database.json<br/>(DescribeProt conservation)"]
    end
    subgraph CUR["Variant Curation (derived = False branch)"]
        F["Filter: SNVs, Pathogenic/Likely pathogenic,<br/>50 &lt; len &lt; 1024, no U, one seq per gene"]
        V["Validate WT residue<br/>at annotated position"]
    end
    CSV[("data/clinvar_sequences.csv<br/>(committed derived corpus)")]
    subgraph INF["Per-Protein Inference"]
        ESM["ESM-2 t33_650M forward pass<br/>(33 layers × 20 heads)"]
        RO["Attention rollout →<br/>attention received per residue"]
        IUP["IUPred2A long →<br/>disorder probability profile"]
    end
    FE["comb_data: per-residue table<br/>rollout, idr, path_mut, AA group,<br/>within-sequence percentiles"]
    subgraph STAT["Statistical Validation"]
        DESC["Descriptive plots"]
        OLS["Cluster-robust OLS per IDR bin"]
        LOG["Logit + LR test per IDR bin"]
    end
    OUT["figures/*.png +<br/>data/figure_data/*.csv"]
    CV --> F
    G2R --> F
    FA --> F
    F --> V --> CSV
    CSV -.->|derived = True| FE
    CSV --> ESM
    ESM --> RO --> FE
    CSV --> IUP --> FE
    DP --> OLS
    DP --> LOG
    FE --> DESC --> OUT
    FE --> OLS --> OUT
    FE --> LOG --> OUT
```
Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L20-L22), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L150-L178), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L299-L391), [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L47-L66)

## Curating the Disease Variant Corpus
When `derived = False`, the script rebuilds `data/clinvar_sequences.csv` from three NCBI resources fetched by [External Data Acquisition](3-external-data-acquisition): the ClinVar `variant_summary.txt.gz`, `gene2refseq` (read in 100k-row chunks, filtered to human tax_id 9606, to map mRNA `NM_` accessions to protein `NP_` accessions), and the GRCh38 protein FASTA (parsed with Biopython's `SeqIO` to map `NP_` accessions to sequences). Variants are then reduced to a clean missense corpus through a chain of deterministic filters, summarized below.

| Filter | Implementation | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Variant type | `Type == 'single nucleotide variant'` | Restricts to point mutations (clinvar_expanded.py#L68) |
| Clinical significance | `{Pathogenic, Likely pathogenic, Pathogenic/Likely pathogenic}` | High-confidence disease labels only (clinvar_expanded.py#L69-L70) |
| Sequence length | `50 < len < 1024` | Fits ESM-2's token budget; drops trivially short proteins (clinvar_expanded.py#L102-L104) |
| Noncanonical residues | Drop sequences containing `U` | Avoids selenocysteine ambiguity in the model vocabulary (clinvar_expanded.py#L105) |
| Gene-level uniqueness | Drop genes mapped to >1 unique sequence | Guarantees unambiguous sequence↔gene correspondence (clinvar_expanded.py#L108-L111) |
| Mutation parsing | Regex `\(p\.([A-Za-z]{3})(\d+)([A-Za-z]{3})\)` on the `Name` column, 3-letter→1-letter mapping | Extracts WT AA, position, mutant AA; unparseable codes (e.g., `Ter`) dropped (clinvar_expanded.py#L44-L49, L116-L125) |
| WT validation | `get_seq_wt` compares `seq[pos-1]` to the annotated WT AA | QA gate: mismatches trigger an `ISSUE: Some sequences do not align` warning (clinvar_expanded.py#L51-L57, L127-L132) |

One subtlety worth noting for auditors: the WT-validation step flags mismatches via a console warning rather than dropping the offending rows — the enforced exclusions are the earlier filters plus the drop of rows whose annotation codes failed to map. The validated corpus is persisted with `to_csv`, which is exactly the artifact committed as `data/clinvar_sequences.csv` (clinvar_expanded.py#L131-L133).
Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L63-L133), [README.md](README.md#L56-L60)

## From Sequence to Per-Residue Attention Signal
The inference stage loads `facebook/esm2_t33_650M_UR50D` with `output_attentions=True` and iterates over **unique sequences** rather than variant rows — a protein with multiple pathogenic variants is forwarded through the model only once (clinvar_expanded.py#L143-L156). For each sequence, two per-residue signals are computed: `get_attn_rollout` returns the column-sum of the rollout matrix (attention received), and `extract_IDR_profile` shells out to IUPred2A in `long` mode for per-residue disorder probabilities (attention_functions.py#L220-L249, L79-L99). Residues are labeled `f"{aa}_{i}"` with 1-based indexing so that variant positions align directly with sequence positions, and `path_mut` is set via membership of each position in that protein's variant-position set (clinvar_expanded.py#L157-L162).

> [!TIP]
> Interpret the attention vector directionally: `get_attn_rollout` computes `rollout.sum(dim=0)`, summing over the *source* dimension so each entry quantifies total attention flowing **into** a residue — the "attention received" convention used throughout this repo (attention_functions.py#L246-L248). This matters when comparing with per-head analyses in [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics), which use the same column-sum semantics.

The assembled per-residue table `comb_data` adds feature engineering layers that make cross-protein comparison statistically sound: each residue receives a **within-sequence percentile rank** for both attention (`attn_perc`) and disorder (`idr_perc`) via `groupby("seq").rank(pct=True)`, which neutralizes protein-level differences in overall attention magnitude and disorder content (clinvar_expanded.py#L165-L175). Residues are also grouped into biochemical classes — Hydrophobic, Polar, Cation, Anion, Aromatic — where phenylalanine's duplicate membership in both Hydrophobic and Aromatic resolves to **Aromatic** because later dict entries overwrite earlier ones (clinvar_expanded.py#L166-L173). The final table, including ten within-protein disorder-percentile deciles (`idr_perc_bin`) and human-readable `Disease-Relevant` / `Non-Disease-Relevant` labels, is written to `data/figure_data/comb_data.csv` (clinvar_expanded.py#L176-L178).

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L144-L218), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L220-L249), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L143-L178)

## Descriptive Analyses
Before any regression, the script quantifies and visualizes the raw enrichment. It prints the median and interquartile range of attention percentile separately for disease-relevant and non-disease-relevant residues — the headline enrichment numbers — and renders four figures. The two-panel histogram contrasts the attention-percentile distributions of the two groups; the decile boxplot conditions the comparison on disorder level by plotting attention percentile across the ten within-protein disorder deciles with paired orange/steelblue boxes per class; the amino-acid panel produces one subplot per biochemical group with subplot widths proportional to group sizes and amino acids ordered by median attention, so within-class confounds (e.g., charged residues attracting attention regardless of disease status) become visible; and a bar chart shows the amino-acid composition of disease-relevant wild-type residues as a composition sanity check (clinvar_expanded.py#L184-L292).

This descriptive layer is where the two binning philosophies of the script diverge: the descriptive analysis uses **within-protein percentile deciles** of disorder, enabling apples-to-apples comparison across proteins with wildly different disorder content, whereas the regression stage switches to **absolute IUPred2A probability bins** so that results can be interpreted as disorder regimes rather than relative positions (clinvar_expanded.py#L177 vs L344-L346).
Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L184-L210), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L213-L292)

## Attention Versus Evolutionary Conservation
The regression stage is the causal-style core of the analysis and proceeds in three steps. First, conservation is attached per residue: the script streams `data/9606_database.json` line by line (stripping JSON array punctuation), matches full sequence strings against the ClinVar corpus, parses the comma-separated `MMseq2_conservation_score` field with `NULL` → `NaN`, and merges on `(seq, pos, AA)` (clinvar_expanded.py#L299-L338). Second, data are split into three absolute disorder bins — `[0, 0.25)`, `[0.25, 0.75)`, `[0.75, 1.0]` — so every model answers the question separately for ordered, intermediate, and disordered regions (clinvar_expanded.py#L344-L346). Third, two complementary model families are fit per bin, both with **cluster-robust standard errors clustered by sequence**, which correctly accounts for the strong within-protein correlation of the ~20 residues-per-protein observations (clinvar_expanded.py#L355).

| Model family | Formula per IDR bin | Question answered | Key statistics |
|---|---|---|---|
| OLS | `rollout ~ path_mut + conservation` (plus single-predictor models) | Does disease relevance explain attention *beyond* conservation? | Partial R² for `path_mut` = (R²full − R²cons) / (1 − R²cons); unadjusted vs conservation-adjusted betas (clinvar_expanded.py#L357-L365) |
| Logistic | `path_mut_int ~ rollout_z + conservation_z` (plus single-predictor models) | Does attention predict disease status *beyond* conservation? | Adjusted rollout/conservation coefficients; likelihood-ratio test `−2(llf_cons − llf_both)` against χ²(1) for whether rollout adds predictive power (clinvar_expanded.py#L369-L375) |

Note the deliberate reversal of the response variable between the two families — attention as outcome in OLS, disease status as outcome in logit — which lets the paper claim the enrichment from both explanatory and predictive directions. Predictors enter the logit z-scored within each bin, making the adjusted coefficients directly comparable on a standard-deviation scale. Results are persisted to `data/figure_data/ols_df.csv` and `log_df.csv`, and visualized as per-bin bar charts: adjusted logit betas with the LR test alongside (`figures/clinvar_log_reg.png`) and OLS betas before/after conservation adjustment (`figures/ols_clinvar.png`) (clinvar_expanded.py#L388-L448).
Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L294-L391), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L393-L448)

## Reproducibility Modes and Runtime Requirements
The script's dual-mode design is governed by the `derived` flag at the top of the file and mirrors the repo-wide philosophy documented in [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility).

| Aspect | `derived = True` (default) | `derived = False` |
|---|---|---|
| Variant corpus input | Committed `data/clinvar_sequences.csv` (Feb 3, 2026 snapshot) | Raw `variant_summary.txt.gz` + `gene2refseq` + `GRCh38_latest_protein_copy.faa` |
| External downloads needed for variants | None | `python esm2_interp_data.py` (ClinVar, gene2refseq, GRCh38 sections) |
| Manual download required | `data/9606_database.json` (DescribeProt, for the regression stage) | Same |
| Use case | Exact paper reproduction | Fresh ClinVar state |

> [!TIP]
> The DescribeProt conservation file is opened **unconditionally** at the regression stage — even in `derived = True` mode, a missing `data/9606_database.json` will crash the script after all plots up to the amino-acid count have completed. Download it manually per the instructions in `esm2_interp_data.py` before running (esm2_interp_data.py#L62-L66, clinvar_expanded.py#L299-L301).

Runtime requirements follow from the dependencies: IUPred2A must be installed locally with the hardcoded `iupred_filepath` at line 25 of `attention_functions.py` updated to your copy, as noted in the README installation section (attention_functions.py#L25, README.md#L18). The ESM-2 checkpoint is loaded with `local_files_only=True`, so the `facebook/esm2_t33_650M_UR50D` weights must already be present in your HuggingFace cache — typically populated by a prior run of [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction); a cold cache will raise a lookup error rather than silently downloading. To reproduce the paper's Figure 3 end-to-end: run `python esm2_interp_data.py` for external data, then `python clinvar_expanded.py`.
Sources: [README.md](README.md#L56-L60), [README.md](README.md#L97-L105), [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L20-L27), [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L142-L190), [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L143-L147)

## Output Artifacts Reference
All artifacts are generated at runtime into `data/figure_data/` and `figures/`; none are committed to the repository.

| Artifact | Producer lines | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `data/figure_data/comb_data.csv` | clinvar_expanded.py#L178 | Per-residue table: rollout, idr, position, AA/AA-group, `path_mut`, within-sequence percentiles, decile bins |
