Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L178-L447)

## Position in the Validation Sequence and Next Steps
This analysis answers "does attention concentrate at known functional sites?" using a labeled external benchmark — the first of the four *Functional Validation Analyses*. It shares the rollout primitive with [Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm) and the IUPred2A integration with [Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A](10-disorder-scoring-with-iupred2a), but unlike the PDB/DisProt comparisons in [Ordered Versus Disordered Comparison](12-ordered-versus-disordered-comparison), it operates on single human proteins with residue-level ground truth. To continue through the functional validation track, proceed to [Categorical Jacobian Contact Maps](14-categorical-jacobian-contact-maps), which shifts from *where attention lands* to *what attention implies about inter-residue structure*; the regression methodology here (cluster-robust fitting, conservation adjustment) also sets up the statistical conventions reused in [Electrostatics Hypothesis Testing](19-electrostatics-hypothesis-testing).

# Categorical Jacobian Contact Maps



This page explains how `plm_interp` derives inter-residue **contact maps** from the **categorical Jacobian** of ESM-2 — a first-order measure of how the model's per-residue amino-acid logits respond when every input residue is systematically substituted — and how those model-intrinsic maps are quantitatively validated against physics-based molecular-dynamics (MD) contacts from the IDRome dataset. The scope covers the mathematical definition, the two implementations (notebook-reference and memory-optimized), the Jacobian→contact-map reduction pipeline, MD ground-truth construction, per-protein correlation scoring, and the batched output artifacts. The entire analysis lives in a single script, `scripts/get_contact_maps.py`, which generates the contact evidence underlying Figure 4 of the paper.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L96), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L16-L21)

## Conceptual Role: A Derivative-Based Probe of Latent Structure

The attention-based analyses in this repository interrogate where the model *looks*; the categorical Jacobian asks a complementary question: *if residue `i` were replaced by any other amino acid, how would the predicted residue distribution at position `j` change?* A strong response between positions `i` and `j` implies that ESM-2's output representation treats those two residues as functionally coupled — an intrinsic structural signal that requires no external predictor. For intrinsically disordered proteins, which lack a stable native fold and therefore lack ground-truth structural annotations, this derivative-based probe provides independently derived contact evidence that can be benchmarked against simulated ensembles rather than static crystal structures.

The overall validation architecture routes two independent views of each protein — model-derived Jacobian contacts and MD-derived physical contacts — into a per-protein correlation score:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    LOG["ESM-2 per-residue logits<br/>z ∈ R^(L×V)"]
    ATT["Attention matrices<br/>(see Attention Matrix Extraction)"]
    JAC["Categorical Jacobian<br/>J ∈ R^(L×20×L×20)"]
    ROLL["Attention rollout → residue-level scores"]
    CMAP["Center → Frobenius norm → APC<br/>→ L×L contact map"]
    MD["IDRome MD trajectories<br/>traj.xtc + top.pdb"]
    MDMAP["Cα contact map<br/>avg distance / contact fraction"]
    CORR["Per-protein Pearson & Spearman"]
    OUT["Figure 4 evidence:<br/>Jacobian contacts ≈ physical contacts"]
    LOG --> ATT
    LOG --> JAC
    ATT --> ROLL
    JAC --> CMAP
    MD --> MDMAP
    CMAP --> CORR
    MDMAP --> CORR
    CORR --> OUT
```

Sources: [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L16-L21), [README.md](README.md#L56-L58)

## Defining the Categorical Jacobian

The implementation realizes the Jacobian via **in-silico saturation mutagenesis**: for a sequence of length `L`, the tensor `J[i, a, j, b]` stores the finite-difference change in logit `b` at position `j` when residue `i` is mutated to amino-acid token `a`. Concretely, the model is evaluated once on the wild-type sequence to obtain `fx`, then every position is mutated to all 20 residue tokens, producing a four-dimensional response tensor of shape `(L, 20, L, 20)`:

```python
f = lambda x: model(x)["logits"][..., 1:(ln+1), 4:24].cpu().numpy()
fx = f(x.to(device))[0]
x = torch.tile(x, [20, 1])
for n in range(ln):
    x_h = torch.clone(x)
    x_h[:, n+1] = torch.arange(4, 24)   # mutate to all 20 aa
    fx_h[n] = f(x_h)
return fx_h - fx
```

Two indexing conventions from the ESM-2 tokenizer govern every slice in this function and must be understood to read the code correctly:

| Quantity | Code expression | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Tokenized input | `alphabet.get_batch_converter()([("seq", seq)])[-1]` | token sequence with `<cls>` occupying index 0 |
| Logit position slice | `1:(ln+1)` | the `L` real residues (skipping the `<cls>` row) |
| Amino-acid logit columns | `4:24` | the 20 residue token IDs |
| Mutated token index | `n+1` | position offset compensating for `<cls>` |
| Substitution values | `torch.arange(4, 24)` | all 20 residue tokens |

Sources: [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L42-L54)

## Reference vs. Memory-Optimized Implementation

The repository ships two implementations with identical mathematics but very different execution profiles. `get_categorical_jacobian` is the notebook-faithful version: it runs **one forward pass per position** (batch of 20 tiled copies each), yielding `L` passes total. The production path, `get_categorical_jacobian_ln`, processes positions in **chunks of 150**: it repeats the tokenized input `chunk_len × 20` times, computes all mutation coordinates with vectorized tensor indexing, and issues only `⌈L/150⌉` forward passes with batches of up to 3,000 sequences. Both return the same `(L, 20, L, 20)` array via broadcast subtraction of the wild-type logits, and both run under `torch.no_grad()`; the main loop invokes the optimized variant with the default chunk size.

| Property | `get_categorical_jacobian` | `get_categorical_jacobian_ln` |
|---|---|---|
| Forward passes per protein | `L` (one per position) | `⌈L/150⌉` |
| Batch size per pass | 20 | `chunk_len × 20` (3,000 at a full chunk) |
| Mutation application | per-position loop, `x_h[:, n+1] = arange(4,24)` | vectorized `x_chunk[arange, positions] = mutations` |
| Mutant row layout | implicit (loop-major) | row `r = k·20 + m` → position `start+k`, token `4+m` |
| Result shape | `(L, 20, L, 20)` | `(L, 20, L, 20)` — identical |
| Chunk size | — | 150 (default parameter) |

> [!TIP]
> The mutation layout is the load-bearing detail of the optimized variant: `positions = arange(start, end).repeat_interleave(20) + 1` paired with `mutations = arange(4, 24).repeat(chunk_len)` guarantees that row `r = k·20 + m` corresponds to *position `start+k` mutated to residue token `4+m`* — exactly the axis semantics that `reshape(chunk_len, 20, ln, 20)` assumes. The `+ 1` offset exists because `<cls>` occupies token index 0.

Sources: [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L42-L54), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L56-L74), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L202)

## Reducing the 4D Jacobian to a 2D Contact Map

The raw Jacobian is a response tensor, not a contact map; `get_contacts` performs the reduction. Each of the four axes is **mean-centered** (removing per-axis average structure), then the two amino-acid axes are collapsed with a **Frobenius norm**, `j_fn[i, j] = sqrt(Σₐ Σᵦ J[i,a,j,b]²)`, described in the code as the "overall strength of functional coupling between residue i and residue j". The diagonal is zeroed (no self-interactions), the result passes through the **Average Product Correction (APC)**, and the final map is symmetrized. APC itself, implemented in `do_apc`, subtracts the rank-one outer product of row and column sums, `y = x − (a1·a2)/x.sum()` — a standard suppression of large global components shared across rows and columns that would otherwise dominate the map. `do_apc` also exposes two alternative modes: `rm=0` bypasses correction entirely, and `rm ≥ 2` instead removes the top `rm` eigenvectors via SVD (`s[rm:] * u[:,rm:] @ v[rm:,:]`).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    J["Jacobian tensor<br/>(L, 20, L, 20)"] --> C["Center:<br/>subtract mean along each of 4 axes"]
    C --> S["Symmetrize 4D:<br/>(jac + jac.transpose(2,3,0,1)) / 2"]
    S --> N["Frobenius norm over AA axes<br/>→ (L, L)"]
    N --> Z["Zero diagonal"]
    Z --> P["APC correction<br/>do_apc, rm=1"]
    P --> SY["Symmetrize final map"]
    SY --> M["L×L contact map"]
```

A subtle but deliberate ordering exists in the production loop: after `get_categorical_jacobian_ln` returns, the loop *first* centers each of the four axes and *then* symmetrizes the 4D tensor via `(jac + jac.transpose(2,3,0,1))/2` — only afterwards calling `get_contacts`, which centers the four axes once more and re-symmetrizes the resulting 2D map. The effective sequence is therefore: center 4D → symmetrize 4D → center 4D again → Frobenius → zero diagonal → APC → symmetrize 2D.

> [!TIP]
> Centering *before* symmetrization is not redundant bookkeeping: symmetrizing an already-centered tensor enforces exchange symmetry `i ↔ j` on the coupling structure itself, so the Frobenius-norm map inherits symmetry by construction rather than by the final averaging step. The second centering inside `get_contacts` is inherited from the original notebook and is intentionally left in place.

Sources: [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L76-L86), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L23-L40), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L202-L213)

## MD Ground Truth: IDRome Contact Maps

Validation requires physical contact maps, which the script obtains per protein from the IDRome database. Sequences come from `data/Supplementary_Table_3.xlsx`, filtered to **≤ 160 residues** to bound compute time; the workload is enumerated by `data/jac_batch_directory.csv`, which assigns roughly 20,000 IDRome residue-range entries (`{UniProtID}_{res_start}_{res_end}`) to numbered batches that the main loop iterates independently. For each entry the script reconstructs IDRome's three-level sharded directory path from the UniProt ID, downloads `traj.xtc` and `top.pdb` from the SID archive into temporary files, loads them with MDTraj, and computes Cα–Cα distances via `md.compute_contacts(traj, scheme='ca')` followed by `md.geometry.squareform`.

The trajectory is aggregated into a single map under one of two modes controlled by `md_method` (the active configuration is `'frac'`, with threshold `0.65`; MDTraj reports distances in nanometers, so this corresponds to 6.5 Å):

| Mode | Aggregation | Uncomputed pairs | Output column |
|---|---|---|---|
| `avg` | mean Cα distance across all frames | retained as-is | `Distance` |
| `frac` (active) | fraction of frames with distance < 0.65 | masked `NaN` via `computed_mask` | `Frac` |

The `frac` branch is the more careful of the two: MDTraj only computes distances for a subset of residue pairs, so a `computed_mask` is built from the `contacts` array, pairs are binarized against the threshold, uncomputed pairs are set to `NaN` *before* aggregation, and `np.nanmean` across frames yields a true per-pair contact probability without contaminating statistics from missing pairs. The `Supplementary_Table_3.xlsx` input itself is fetched by the repository's data-acquisition script, which pins the static IDRome supplementary download.

Sources: [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L101-L110), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L117-L156), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L158-L181), [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L193-L200), [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L232), [jac_batch_directory.csv](data/jac_batch_directory.csv#L1-L3), [README.md](README.md#L56-L58)

## Correlation Scoring and Output Artifacts

Each protein produces two long-format tables that are joined on the residue-pair key: the Jacobian map is melted into `Residue_i / Residue_j / ContactStrength` rows, while the MD map contributes either `Distance` or `Frac`. The merged frame is restricted to the **upper triangle** (`Residue_i < Residue_j`) and `dropna()` removes pairs the MD computation never evaluated, after which two rank-sensitive and one linear statistic are computed per protein: **Pearson** and **Spearman** correlation between Jacobian contact strength and MD contact evidence. Each protein contributes a results row of `seq_name, sequence, pearson_corr, spearman_corr`, and its full upper-triangle pair table is retained for downstream figure generation.

Persistence is engineered for long-running, resumable execution. The base output path is `data/jacobian/jacobian_md_frac.csv`, but results are written per batch with a `_batch{batch}.csv` suffix, flushed to disk **every 500 proteins** (`save_every`), using append mode with conditional headers; upper-triangle tables are flushed separately to `_batch{batch}_upper.csv`. Within each iteration, all large intermediates — trajectory objects, distance arrays, the Jacobian tensor, merged frames — are explicitly `del`-eted and `gc.collect()` is invoked, so peak memory is governed by a single protein rather than the batch.

| Artifact | Direction | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `data/jac_batch_directory.csv` | input | ~20K `seq_name → batch_num` assignments driving the loop |
| `data/Supplementary_Table_3.xlsx` | input | IDRome sequences + metadata (downloaded, ≤160-residue filter applied) |
| `data/jacobian/jacobian_md_frac_batch{N}.csv` | output | per-protein `pearson_corr`, `spearman_corr` |
| `data/jacobian/jacobian_md_frac_batch{N}_upper.csv` | output | upper-triangle pairs: `Residue_i`, `Residue_j`, `ContactStrength`, `Frac`, `seq_name` |

Sources: [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L200-L223), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L229-L236), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L239-L264)

## Provenance and Licensing

Three of the four mathematical building blocks — `do_apc`, `get_categorical_jacobian`, and `get_contacts` — are explicitly credited in the script's docstring to the `zzhangzzhang/pLMs-interpretability` notebook (Zhang et al., *PNAS* 2024). The README's third-party code section states that these adapted functions carry no upstream license and are therefore **excluded from this repository's MIT license**; the chunked `get_categorical_jacobian_ln` variant is this repo's own memory optimization. Any reuse of this pipeline should respect that provenance boundary.

Sources: [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L16-L21), [README.md](README.md#L82-L84)

## Running the Analysis

The analysis is step two of the Figure 4 reproduction chain. The only prerequisite input that is not committed to the repository is the IDRome supplementary table, which the data-acquisition script downloads automatically; model weights for `esm2_t33_650M_UR50D` are fetched on first load, and MD trajectories are pulled per protein from the SID archive at runtime. GPU execution is selected automatically when CUDA is available.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S1["python scripts/esm2_interp_data.py<br/>→ data/Supplementary_Table_3.xlsx"] --> S2["python scripts/get_contact_maps.py<br/>Jacobian + MD contacts + correlations"]
    S2 --> S3["data/jacobian/jacobian_md_frac_batch*.csv<br/>+ *_upper.csv"]
    S3 --> S4["python scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py"]
    S4 --> S5["python scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py<br/>→ Figure 4"]
```

Runtime is dominated by two per-protein costs: the Jacobian forward passes (bounded to `⌈L/150⌉ ≤ 2` heavy batched passes for the 160-residue cap) and the trajectory downloads. Note that the `(L, 20, L, 20)` Jacobian array is allocated via `np.zeros` in float64, so a single protein at the 160-residue cap already occupies ≈82 MB before the Frobenius reduction collapses it to `L × L` — one of several reasons the per-iteration `del`/`gc` discipline and the batched flush design matter. If a long run is interrupted, completed batches remain on disk and the loop structure over `directory.batch_num.unique()` allows re-entry at a chosen batch.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L96), [esm2_interp_data.py](scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L217-L233), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L92-L99), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L103-L110), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L112)

## Key Takeaways and Next Steps

The categorical Jacobian pipeline establishes, quantitatively, that ESM-2's *input-sensitivity structure* — not just its attention routing — encodes inter-residue contact information for disordered proteins, benchmarked residue-pair-by-residue-pair against IDRome simulation ground truth. The three ideas to retain are: (1) the Jacobian is built by exhaustive saturation mutagenesis over `(position × amino acid)`, yielding an `(L, 20, L, 20)` response tensor; (2) the contact map is a *constructed* reduction — centering, Frobenius aggregation, APC — not a raw model output; and (3) validation is correlation-based against `frac`-mode MD contact probabilities, persisted per batch for resumability.

Where to go next in the catalog:

- [MD Trajectory Contact Validation](15-md-trajectory-contact-validation) — the downstream cutoff-sweep and population-level analysis that turns these per-protein correlations into Figure 4
- [Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management) — deeper treatment of the memory patterns (`chunked forwards`, `del`/`gc`, periodic flush) used here
- [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility) — how the IDRome/SID dependencies interact with the repo's reproducibility strategy
- [External Data Acquisition](3-external-data-acquisition) — full walkthrough of `esm2_interp_data.py`, including the Supplementary Table 3 download
- [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction) — the attention-based counterpart probe, for contrast with the Jacobian approach
- [Reproducing Paper Figures](4-reproducing-paper-figures) — the complete Figure 4 command chain in context


# MD Trajectory Contact Validation



This page explains how the repository validates ESM-2 Jacobian-derived contact predictions against an independent physical ground truth: molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories from the IDRome dataset. The validation lives in two dedicated scripts — `md_variable_cutoff.py`, which converts XTC trajectories into per-pair contact frequencies using amino-acid-specific distance thresholds, and `md_contact_maps_analysis.py`, which statistically tests whether Jacobian contact strength correlates with MD contact occupancy beyond a permuted null. Whereas [Categorical Jacobian Contact Maps](14-categorical-jacobian-contact-maps) covers how the model-side contact signal is *produced*, this page covers how that signal is *audited* against simulation data.

Sources: [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L17-L19), [md_variable_cutoff.py](/scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py#L14-L17)

## Role in the Validation Architecture

The validation chain is deliberately staged so that expensive computation (GPU Jacobians, trajectory downloads) is separated from statistical analysis (CPU-only, parallelized). `get_contact_maps.py` is the shared upstream producer: for every protein it computes both the ESM-2 categorical Jacobian contact map and a fixed-cutoff MD contact map, persisting the merged upper-triangle data in seven batch files. `md_variable_cutoff.py` then recomputes *only* the MD side under a refined, per-residue-pair cutoff model. Finally, `md_contact_maps_analysis.py` joins all three artifacts and runs two complementary validations: a per-protein permutation test on the Spearman correlation, and a top-decile residue-pair enrichment comparison.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph EXT["IDRome Public Dataset — sid.erda.dk"]
        XTC["traj.xtc"]
        TOP["top.pdb"]
    end

    subgraph UP["Upstream: get_contact_maps.py"]
        JAC["ESM-2 categorical Jacobian"] --> APC["APC-corrected Frobenius norm<br/>= ContactStrength"]
        FIXMD["Fixed-cutoff MD Frac<br/>(0.65 nm threshold)"]
    end

    subgraph VC["md_variable_cutoff.py"]
        SIG["Per-pair LJ-derived cutoff<br/>2^(1/6) · σ_ij / 10"]
        VARMD["Variable-cutoff MD Frac<br/>md_variable_sigma_batch*.csv"]
    end

    subgraph AN["md_contact_maps_analysis.py"]
        MERGE["Concatenate 7 batches<br/>swap fixed Frac → variable Frac"]
        NULL["Per-protein permutation null<br/>(Spearman r)"]
        DEC["Top-decile residue-pair<br/>enrichment agreement"]
    end

    XTC & TOP --> JAC
    XTC & TOP --> FIXMD
    XTC & TOP --> SIG
    APC --> MERGE
    FIXMD --> MERGE
    VARMD --> MERGE
    MERGE --> NULL
    MERGE --> DEC
    NULL --> FIG1["jac_md_observed_vs_null_distribution.svg"]
    DEC --> FIG2["md_esm_top_decile_agreement.svg<br/>+ enrichment heatmaps"]
```

The data contracts between modules are pure CSV files with a shared join key of `(seq_name, Residue_i, Residue_j)`. The protein universe is defined once in `data/jac_batch_directory.csv` — 19,961 IDRome entries partitioned into 7 batches — and both producer scripts iterate this directory identically, guaranteeing key compatibility at merge time.

Sources: [get_contact_maps.py](/scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L92-L110), [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L67-L77), [md_variable_cutoff.py](/scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py#L50-L55), [jac_batch_directory.csv](/data/jac_batch_directory.csv#L1-L10)

## The IDRome Data Interface

Both MD-consuming scripts resolve trajectories through the same convention: each `seq_name` (e.g., `A0A024RBG1_145_181`) encodes a UniProt accession plus a residue range, and the accession is split into a three-level path prefix (`p1/p2/p3/`) following standard UniProt directory sharding, with any overflow characters folded into the third level. The scripts then construct direct-download URLs against the IDRome ERDA share (`https://sid.erda.dk/share_redirect/AVZAJvJnCO/IDRome/`), fetch `traj.xtc` and `top.pdb` via `requests`, and stage them in `tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile` objects that are deleted immediately after `mdtraj.load()` succeeds.

Sources: [md_variable_cutoff.py](/scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py#L63-L94), [get_contact_maps.py](/scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L121-L151)

Two defensive patterns matter for reproduction. First, the sequence universe is restricted to `seqlen <= 160` from the IDRome supplementary table — an explicit compute-time bound, since Jacobian computation scales as O(L·20) forward passes and contact matrices scale as O(L²). Second, trajectory loads are wrapped in a bare `try/except` with `continue`, so a corrupted or missing remote file silently skips a protein rather than aborting a multi-hour batch run; the merge-time `drop_duplicates()` call downstream acts as the deduplication safety net if a protein were ever reprocessed.

Sources: [md_variable_cutoff.py](/scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py#L44-L47), [md_variable_cutoff.py](/scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py#L87-L90), [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L76-L77)

## Variable Cutoff Contact Detection

The methodological core of `md_variable_cutoff.py` is a rejection of the uniform 0.65 nm distance threshold used upstream in favor of a pairwise, chemistry-aware cutoff borrowed from a published PLOS Computational Biology protocol. Each of the 20 amino acids carries a `sigma` parameter (in Å), and the cutoff for pair *(i, j)* is computed as the Lennard-Jones contact minimum scaled and converted to nm:

```
sigma_ij    = (σ_i + σ_j) / 2          # arithmetic mean of residue sigmas
cutoff_ij   = 2^(1/6) · sigma_ij / 10  # LJ r_min, Å → nm
```

| AA | σ (Å) | AA | σ (Å) | AA | σ (Å) | AA | σ (Å) |
|----|-------|----|-------|----|-------|----|-------|
| A | 5.04 | E | 5.92 | L | 6.18 | S | 5.18 |
| R | 6.56 | G | 4.50 | K | 6.36 | T | 5.62 |
| N | 5.68 | H | 6.08 | M | 6.18 | W | 6.78 |
| D | 5.58 | I | 6.18 | F | 6.36 | Y | 6.46 |
| C | 5.48 | P | 5.56 | V | 5.86 | Q | 6.02 |

The σ range spans 4.50 Å (Glycine) to 6.78 Å (Tryptophan), meaning a Gly–Trp pair and a Trp–Trp pair are judged against cutoffs differing by over 1 Å — a significant correction when contact occupancy is the measured quantity. `sigma_ij` is built as a broadcast outer-mean (`sigmas[:, None] + sigmas[None, :]) / 2.0`), yielding an L×L cutoff matrix aligned with the contact map axes.

> [!TIP]
> The factor `2^(1/6)` is not arbitrary: it is the location of the potential-energy minimum of a Lennard-Jones 12-6 potential, *r*<sub>min</sub> = 2<sup>1/6</sup>σ. The `/10.0` converts Ångströms to nanometers, matching `mdtraj`'s native distance units — omitting either factor would shift every cutoff by a constant or unit-dependent amount.

Sources: [md_variable_cutoff.py](/scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py#L15-L40), [md_variable_cutoff.py](/scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py#L96-L98), [get_contact_maps.py](/scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L92-L94)

Contact extraction uses Cα atoms exclusively (`md.compute_contacts(traj, scheme='ca')`), which returns a frame-wise distance array for the pairs MDTraj deemed geometrically computable. The script then converts this into a per-pair **contact occupancy fraction**: binary indicators (`distance < cutoff_ij`) are averaged across all trajectory frames, producing a `Frac` value in [0, 1] per residue pair.

| Aspect | Fixed cutoff (upstream) | Variable cutoff (this pipeline) |
|---|---|---|
| Threshold | Uniform 0.65 nm | Pair-specific 2<sup>1/6</sup>·σ<sub>ij</sub>/10 |
| Source of σ | — | PLOS CBiol protocol (per-AA table) |
| Output metric | `Frac` (frames in contact) | `Frac` (frames in contact) |
| Storage | `jacobian_md_frac_batch*_upper.csv` | `md_variable_sigma_batch*.csv` |
| Rationale | Simplicity | Chemistry-aware geometry |

Sources: [md_variable_cutoff.py](/scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py#L100-L118), [get_contact_maps.py](/scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L155-L180)

A subtle correctness detail: `md.compute_contacts` only reports pairs within a hard internal cutoff, so residues separated by sequence proximity or geometry may be *absent* from the pairs list entirely. The script constructs a boolean `computed_mask` from the returned `contacts` array, sets uncomputed cells to `NaN`, and averages with `np.nanmean` — this cleanly distinguishes "never in contact" (Frac = 0.0) from "never evaluated" (Frac = NaN). The upper-triangle export then drops NaN rows, so the statistical merge downstream only ever sees physically evaluated pairs.

Sources: [md_variable_cutoff.py](/scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py#L102-L117), [md_variable_cutoff.py](/scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py#L134-L136)

## Ground-Truth Correlation Under a Permutation Null

The statistical question `md_contact_maps_analysis.py` answers is: *for each protein, does the rank ordering of Jacobian contact strengths predict the rank ordering of MD contact occupancies better than chance?* The script loads all seven `jacobian_md_frac_batch*_upper.csv` files, concatenates and deduplicates them, then — under the `variable_sigma = True` flag — drops the fixed-cutoff `Frac` column and inner-merges the variable-cutoff replacement on `(Residue_i, Residue_j, seq_name)`. A built-in integrity check compares row counts before and after the merge, printing `No loss` or an explicit `Original : N | Merged : M` diagnostic if any Jacobian contacts lacked an MD counterpart.

Sources: [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L64-L93)

The per-protein test itself is a Monte Carlo permutation test on Spearman's ρ. Because the traditional parametric significance test for a correlation requires distributional assumptions that contact data violate, the script instead shuffles the `ContactStrength` vector *within each protein* — destroying any genuine coupling with MD `Frac` while preserving each vector's marginal structure — and recomputes ρ. The implementation is vectorized where it matters: a single seeded `np.random.default_rng(seed)` generates all permutation index matrices at once (`contact_strengths[perm_indices]`), and the per-protein jobs are dispatched across 8 workers via `joblib.Parallel`. Proteins with fewer than 10 contact pairs are excluded as statistically untestable.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Per-protein pair table<br/>ContactStrength, Frac"] --> B["Observed ρ<br/>(Spearman)"]
    A --> C["Generate 100 permutations<br/>(seed = 42 + protein index)"]
    C --> D["Vectorized shuffle of<br/>ContactStrength"]
    D --> E["Null distribution of ρ<br/>(100 values)"]
    E --> F["z-score<br/>(ρ_obs − μ_null)/σ_null"]
    E --> G["Empirical p<br/>(#null ≥ ρ_obs + 1)/(N+1)"]
    B --> F
    B --> G
```

Sources: [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L22-L58), [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L90-L100)

> [!TIP]
> Note the `+ 1` in the p-value formula `(np.sum(null_corrs >= observed_corr) + 1) / (n_permutations + 1)` — this standard rank-fix guarantees the empirical p-value can never be exactly zero under finite permutation sampling, which would otherwise overstate significance at the extreme tail. Also note the effective permutation count is **100 per protein** (set at the call site, line 98), not the function's 1000 default — a deliberate runtime compromise echoed in the figure title.

The aggregate summary reports a layered statistical profile across the protein cohort: the observed correlation distribution (median, IQR, mean ± σ), the null expectation, the fraction of proteins reaching p < 0.05 with a median z-score, and an effect size expressed both as a raw ρ difference from null and as an R² (squared mean correlation, interpreted as variance explained). Observed and null distributions are exported to `data/figure_data/combined_data.csv` and visualized as overlapping histograms against a zero-reference line in `figures/jac_md_observed_vs_null_distribution.svg`.

| Statistic | Definition | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| `observed_r` | Spearman ρ(ContactStrength, Frac), per protein | Model–physics rank agreement |
| `null_mean` / `null_std` | Mean/σ of permuted ρ | Chance-level baseline per protein |
| `z_score` | (ρ_obs − μ_null) / σ_null | Standardized departure from chance |
| `p_value` | Empirical permutation tail, (k+1)/(N+1) | Conservative significance |
| `effect_size` | mean(ρ_obs) − mean(ρ_null) | Cohort-level signal above chance |
| `R²` | mean(ρ_obs)² | Approximate shared variance |

Sources: [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L105-L140), [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L142-L167)

## Top-Decile Residue-Pair Enrichment and Agreement

The correlation test establishes that the two contact maps agree *within* proteins; the second analysis asks *which physical residue-pair chemistries* drive that agreement. Every upper-triangle row is annotated with actual amino-acid identities (resolved by indexing each protein's sequence from `Supplementary_Table_3.xlsx`), and the pair label is canonicalized — `"K-E"` and `"E-K"` collapse to a single sorted token — so that aggregation counts are direction-invariant.

Sources: [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L169-L179)

Within this canonicalized space, the script independently selects the strongest contacts from each method at the 90th percentile of its own score distribution (`ContactStrength` quantile for ESM-2 Jacobian, `Frac` quantile for MD). Because the two quantile cuts naturally yield different subset sizes, both lists are truncated to the minimum length before comparison — an equal-power design that prevents the MD side from dominating the count statistics purely by subset size. For each of the 210 unordered residue-pair types, the analysis computes a **delta enrichment**: the percentage of that pair type within a method's top decile, minus its percentage in the full contact population.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Top-decile Δ enrichment<br/>per method per pair type"] --> B{"delta_md > 0<br/>AND<br/>delta_esm > 0?"}
    B -- "Yes" --> C["Both Enriched<br/>(blue)"]
    B -- "No" --> D{"Both < 0?"}
    D -- "Yes" --> E["Both Depleted<br/>(red)"]
    D -- "No" --> F["Disagree<br/>(gray)"]
    C --> G["20×20 categorical heatmap<br/>md_esm_top_decile_agreement.svg"]
    E --> G
    F --> G
```

The classification is implemented compactly with `np.select` over the sign conditions, and the resulting 20×20 agreement grid is rendered as a categorical heatmap using a `ListedColormap` (blue = both enriched, red = both depleted, gray = disagreement). Two companion magnitude heatmaps — one per method, on an `RdBu` diverging scale — expose the signed Δ values so a reader can distinguish "weak mutual enrichment" from strong concordant signal. All comparison rows persist to `data/figure_data/comparison.csv`, and the signed heatmaps to `figures/esm2_top_decile_enrichment.svg` and `figures/md_top_decile_enrichment.svg`.

Sources: [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L181-L199), [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L203-L224), [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L227-L293)

The scientific payoff of this design is interpretability at the chemistry level: if ESM-2's Jacobian genuinely recovers physical contacts, its top-decile residue-pair types (e.g., charge-pair enrichments) should overlap the MD-derived ones, and the categorical heatmap should show dominant blue regions with disagreement confined to pairs whose MD occupancy is dominated by solvent effects the model cannot see.

## Engineering Considerations for Reproduction

Running the full validation requires `mdtraj` (pinned at 1.11.1) alongside the scientific stack, and the batch conventions are strict: `md_variable_cutoff.py` flushes accumulated DataFrames to `md_variable_sigma_batch{N}.csv` every 500 proteins with append-mode headers handled manually, mirroring the identical flush protocol in `get_contact_maps.py`. Both MD-producing loops aggressively release per-protein memory (`del` on trajectory and distance arrays plus `gc.collect()`), since a 160-residue contact map expanded to long-form rows is materialized per protein and any accumulation would exhaust RAM across ~20,000 proteins. Explicit per-protein RNG seeding (`seed = 42 + i`) makes the null distributions bit-reproducible even under parallel dispatch.

| Artifact | Producer | Consumer | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `jacobian_md_frac_batch*_upper.csv` | `get_contact_maps.py` | `md_contact_maps_analysis.py` | Jacobian strengths + fixed-cutoff Frac |
| `md_variable_sigma_batch*.csv` | `md_variable_cutoff.py` | `md_contact_maps_analysis.py` | Variable-cutoff Frac replacement |
| `data/figure_data/combined_data.csv` | `md_contact_maps_analysis.py` | Figure tooling | Observed vs null histogram data |
| `data/figure_data/comparison.csv` | `md_contact_maps_analysis.py` | Figure tooling | Per-pair delta enrichment + agreement |
| `figures/*.svg` | `md_contact_maps_analysis.py` | Publication pipeline | Final validation figures |

Note that the external IDRome supplementary table (`data/Supplementary_Table_3.xlsx`) and the ERDA-hosted trajectories are *live* remote dependencies, not versioned artifacts — a provenance consideration discussed in [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility). The memory-management patterns shared with the Jacobian producer are documented in [Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management), and figure-level styling conventions in [Publication Figure Styling](23-publication-figure-styling).

Sources: [environment.yml](/environment.yml#L290), [md_variable_cutoff.py](/scripts/md_variable_cutoff.py#L139-L158), [md_contact_maps_analysis.py](/scripts/md_contact_maps_analysis.py#L96-L100), [get_contact_maps.py](/scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L239-L264)

## Where This Fits

The MD validation closes the loop on the interpretability claim established in [Categorical Jacobian Contact Maps](14-categorical-jacobian-contact-maps): a pLM-derived contact signal is shown to carry residue-level physical information that survives a permutation null and reproduces chemistry-aware enrichment patterns from explicit-solvent simulation. To see this validated signal used in a causal (rather than correlational) role, continue to [Attention Head Ablation Study](18-attention-head-ablation-study); to regenerate the figures end-to-end, follow [Reproducing Paper Figures](4-reproducing-paper-figures).


# Perplexity-Disorder Regression



This page explains how the repository tests a single, focused hypothesis: **does ESM-2 find intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) sequences harder to predict than ordered ones?** The entire experiment lives in one script, `scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py`, which computes a masked-language-model perplexity per protein, aligns each protein with its per-residue disorder probability from IUPred2A, and fits a heteroskedasticity-robust linear regression of perplexity on disorder. It is the quantitatively simplest analysis in the repository — no attention matrices, no rollout — which makes it an ideal entry point into the "Functional Validation Analyses" chapter.

Sources: [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L14-L18)

## Research Question: Does ESM-2 "Struggle" More with Disorder?

Perplexity measures a language model's surprise: the lower the perplexity, the better the model anticipates each token given context. The working hypothesis here is that residues inside intrinsically disordered regions — which lack the local structural regularities of folded domains — should be less predictable to ESM-2, yielding higher perplexity. The script operationalizes this by regressing each protein's perplexity against the **mean IUPred2A disorder probability of exactly the residues that were masked** during the perplexity measurement. This coupling of measurement and covariate is the central design decision: the disorder score is computed over the same residue subset that the model was asked to reconstruct, not over the whole sequence.

Sources: [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L85-L101)

## End-to-End Pipeline Architecture

The analysis is a four-stage pipeline executed top-to-bottom in a single script run:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["data/protein_input_sets.csv<br/>4,241 sequences"] --> B["Tokenize<br/>max_length = 1024"]
    B --> C["Random 15% masking<br/>DataCollatorForLanguageModeling<br/>seed = 42 + protein index"]
    C --> D["ESM-2 t33_650M forward pass<br/>single pass, torch.no_grad"]
    D --> E["Perplexity = exp(MLM loss)"]
    A --> F["IUPred2A 'long' mode<br/>extract_IDR_profile<br/>one disorder p per residue"]
    E --> G["Alignment guard<br/>strip &lt;cls&gt;/&lt;eos&gt; tokens,<br/>verify lengths match"]
    F --> G
    G -->|match| H["One row per protein:<br/>ppl + mean masked-residue disorder<br/>+ per-amino-acid masked counts"]
    G -->|mismatch| X["Skip protein"]
    H --> I["data/esm2_perplexities.csv"]
    I --> J["OLS: ppl ~ disorder<br/>HC1 robust covariance"]
    J --> K["β, p-value, R², t-stat,<br/>95% CI, standardized β"]
```

Stages 1–3 build the per-protein dataset; stage 4 is pure statistics. The pipeline is deterministic end-to-end: the masking randomness is seeded per protein, and the committed output file `data/esm2_perplexities.csv` (4,240 protein rows) allows the regression to be re-inspected without re-running the model.

Sources: [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L24-L30), [protein_input_sets.csv](data/protein_input_sets.csv#L1), [esm2_perplexities.csv](data/esm2_perplexities.csv#L1)

## Stage 1 — Deterministic Masked Perplexity

The script loads `facebook/esm2_t33_650M_UR50D` as a `MaskedLM` model with `local_files_only=True` and moves it to GPU when available. For each unique protein, `get_individual_ppl` tokenizes the sequence with `truncation=True, max_length=1024`, then applies Hugging Face's `DataCollatorForLanguageModeling` at `mlm_probability=0.15` — the same masking regime used in ESM-2 pretraining. Critically, the function seeds both `torch` and `numpy` with `42 + protein_index` *before* masking, so the random 15% mask is fully reproducible per protein. One forward pass under `torch.no_grad()` yields the mean masked cross-entropy loss, and perplexity is simply `math.exp(loss)`.

It is worth being precise about what this measures. Classical MLM *pseudo*-perplexity masks and predicts every residue exhaustively; this implementation instead takes **one random 15% masking pass per protein** — a single-pass approximation that trades exhaustive coverage for a 1/L reduction in forward passes.

| Aspect | This implementation | Classical pseudo-perplexity |
|---|---|---|
| Masking scheme | One random 15% pass (HF collator) | Each residue masked exhaustively |
| Forward passes per protein | 1 | L (sequence length) |
| Determinism | Seeded, `seed = 42 + idx` | Deterministic by construction |
| Cost for the full dataset | O(N) | O(N·L) |
| Loss basis | Mean CE over randomly masked residues | Mean CE over all residues |

Sources: [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L24-L30), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L40-L83)

## Stage 2 — Aligning Disorder Scores with Masked Residues

The disorder covariate comes from `extract_IDR_profile` in the shared `attention_functions.py` module — the same IUPred2A wrapper used across the attention analyses (covered in detail on the [Disorder Scoring with IUPred2A](10-disorder-scoring-with-iupred2a) page). The function writes the sequence to a temp FASTA, invokes the IUPred2A executable via `subprocess` in **`long` disorder mode**, parses the output, and returns one disorder probability per residue. IUPred2A requires a local installation; the path is hardcoded and must be edited per environment.

The alignment step is where the two measurement streams are joined, and it has two guards worth understanding:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Tokens["Tokenized sequence"]
        T1["&lt;cls&gt;"] --- T2["M"] --- T3["D"] --- T4["..."] --- T5["&lt;eos&gt;"]
    end
    subgraph Join["Join frame"]
        A1["mask == True positions"]
        A2["IUPred2A profile<br/>one p per residue"]
    end
    T1 -. "stripped from analysis" .-> Join
    T5 -. "stripped from analysis" .-> Join
    T2 & T3 & T4 --> A2
    A1 --> A3["mean(disorder over masked residues)"]
    A2 --> A3
```

First, special tokens (`<cls>`, `<eos>`) are dropped from the mask dataframe so token positions map 1:1 onto residues. Second, if the stripped dataframe length does not equal the IUPred2A profile length, the protein is skipped with a printed diagnostic. Because tokenization truncates at 1024 tokens, any protein whose disorder profile exceeds the token frame fails this check and is excluded — which is why the committed output holds 4,240 rows against the 4,241 input sequences.

> [!TIP]
> Reproduction of the exact n = 4,240 depends on this length guard: `truncation=True, max_length=1024` at tokenization silently shortens long proteins, and the mismatch check then drops them. If you raise `max_length` or change the tokenizer, expect the row count — and therefore every regression statistic — to shift.

Sources: [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L89-L98), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L79-L99), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L21-L25), [README.md](README.md#L18)

## Stage 3 — The Per-Protein Feature Table

Each surviving protein contributes one row to `data/esm2_perplexities.csv`. Beyond the two variables used in the regression, the script also records per-amino-acid counts restricted to the masked residue set:

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `seq` | string | Full amino-acid sequence |
| `ProteinID` | string | Identifier from `data/protein_input_sets.csv` (e.g., `disprot_protein1`) |
| `ppl` | float | `exp(MLM loss)` — the protein's single-pass masked perplexity |
| `mean_masked_residue_disorder` | float | Mean IUPred2A disorder probability across the 15% masked residues |
| `seq_len` | int | Sequence length |
| `A` … `Y` (20 columns) | int | Count of each amino acid among the masked residues |

The amino-acid counts make the CSV a reusable feature table: they are the raw material for controlled regressions (e.g., does perplexity track disorder *after* adjusting for composition such as proline or charged-residue fraction?), even though the committed script currently uses only `mean_masked_residue_disorder` as the sole regressor.

Sources: [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L101-L109), [esm2_perplexities.csv](data/esm2_perplexities.csv#L1)

## Stage 4 — Robust OLS Regression

The final block refits the regression in memory from the freshly built dataframe. The model is ordinary least squares with an intercept via `sm.add_constant`, but the fit is called with `cov_type="HC1"` — White's heteroskedasticity-robust covariance. This matters because per-protein perplexity variance plausibly scales with sequence length and masked-set composition; HC1 keeps the standard errors valid under that heteroskedasticity rather than assuming constant error variance.

| Statistic | Source in code | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| `beta` | `model.params` | Change in perplexity per unit increase in mean masked-residue disorder |
| `CI_lower` / `CI_upper` | `conf_int(alpha=0.05)` | 95% confidence interval under HC1 covariance |
| `p_value` | `model.pvalues` | Formatted in scientific notation (`{p:.1e}`) |
| `r2` | `model.rsquared` | Fraction of perplexity variance explained by disorder |
| `t_stat` | `model.tvalues` | Significance of the disorder coefficient |
| `beta_std` | manual formula (line 138) | β × (σ_X / σ_y) — scale-free effect size |

The script rounds β and CI bounds to two decimals, prints the full coefficient table plus the standardized β, and stops — the regression results are **printed to console only**; the persisted artifact is the perplexity CSV. Rerunning the statistics on the committed CSV is a one-liner pandas/statsmodels job, which is the intended workflow when only the analysis (not the GPU pass) needs to change.

> [!TIP]
> The `beta_std` formula standardizes with raw standard deviations (σ_X/σ_y), not the pooled correlation-based convention — it is a standardized regression coefficient, equivalent to what you would get by z-scoring both variables and refitting without HC1. Use it to state the effect size in "SDs of perplexity per SD of disorder" language, and quote the HC1-based β/CI/p for inference.

Sources: [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L112-L141)

## Practical Notes for Reproduction

Running the full pipeline requires the `torch-gpu` conda environment plus a local IUPred2A installation whose path is set in `attention_functions.py`. The GPU cost is modest relative to the attention-extraction scripts — 4,241 single forward passes — but the IUPred2A subprocess calls dominate wall time, as one OS process is spawned per protein. The input protein set is the curated DisProt/PDB collection produced by the repository's clustering pipeline, so this analysis inherits its dataset hygiene decisions; those are documented on [Dataset Curation and CD-HIT Clustering](21-dataset-curation-and-cd-hit-clustering). Because the output CSV is committed, you can also treat this page's artifact as an example of the [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility) pattern: derived statistics shipped, live computation optional.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L18), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L79-L99), [protein_input_sets.csv](data/protein_input_sets.csv#L1-L4)

## Where This Fits and Where to Go Next

Within the catalog's narrative, this analysis answers a coarse-grained question — *does the model encode disorder as unpredictability?* — before the repository zooms into *which* attention heads and residues carry that signal. The disorder scoring machinery is shared with the attention analyses described in [Ordered Versus Disordered Comparison](12-ordered-versus-disordered-comparison), and the biological framing is set out in [ESM-2 and IDP Biology Primer](6-esm-2-and-idp-biology-primer). To continue the Functional Validation chapter, proceed to [MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor), which upgrades the target variable from a sequence-level scalar (perplexity) to a physically grounded one (radius of gyration).


# MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor



This page dissects `scripts/rg_mlp.py`, the component that converts ESM-2 sequence embeddings into a quantitative predictor of the **radius of gyration (Rg)** for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). Rg measures a chain's spatial extent, making it the canonical scalar readout of IDP conformational state — compact versus expanded. The script trains an MLP regressor on IDRome molecular-dynamics-derived Rg values, validates it against experimental SAXS measurements, and emits the pretrained checkpoint `mlp_final.pt` that sits at the repository root and feeds the causal ablation studies downstream.

Sources: [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L22-L32), [README.md](README.md#L21-L31)

## Position in the Analysis Pipeline

Within the paper's Figure 5 workflow, `rg_mlp.py` is the middle stage of a strict three-step sequence. It consumes external data staged by `esm2_interp_data.py` (IDRome database CSV, IDRome Supplementary Table 3, SAXS comparison data), trains and evaluates the Rg regressor, and produces both the model checkpoint and the Flory-normalized evaluation artifacts that `es_ablation2.py` then reuses to measure how ablating electrostatics-associated attention heads perturbs Rg predictions.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["esm2_interp_data.py<br/>(stage external data)"] --> B["rg_mlp.py<br/>(train + validate Rg MLP)"]
    B --> C["es_ablation2.py<br/>(head ablation via Rg delta)"]
    B --> D["mlp_final.pt<br/>(root-level checkpoint)"]
    B --> E["data/figure_data/*.csv<br/>(evaluation artifacts)"]
    D --> C
```

The coupling is bidirectional in a subtle way: `rg_mlp.py` writes artifacts *forward*, but `es_ablation2.py` cannot independently re-derive the length-baseline coefficients — it must trust values exported from this stage (detailed in the contract section below).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L86-L93), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L22-L26)

## Why Rg Residuals Instead of Raw Rg

The core modeling decision is that the MLP never predicts Rg directly. Raw Rg scales strongly with chain length N (the Flory relation Rg ≈ R₀·N^ν), which would let the model "cheat" by learning length rather than sequence chemistry. Instead, the script fits a quadratic baseline `polyfit(log N, Rg, deg=2)` **on the training split only** and defines the learning target as the residual: `Rg − baseline(log N)`. Two inverse helpers enforce this convention everywhere — `to_target` converts raw Rg into residuals for training, and `to_rg` reconstructs physical Rg (in Ångströms) from a prediction given chain length.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    N["Sequence length N"] --> B["baseline = poly1d(polyfit(log N_train, Rg_train, deg=2))<br/>(fit on train split only)"]
    R["IDRome Rg (nm → Å)"] --> T["to_target: y = Rg − baseline(log N)"]
    B --> T
    T --> M["RgMLP learns chemistry-driven deviations<br/>from the length expectation"]
    M --> I["to_rg: Rg = ŷ + baseline(log N)"]
```

A second, related scaling appears at evaluation time: **Flory normalization**, where every Rg (true, predicted, SAXS-measured, or STARLING-predicted) is divided by `R0_fit · N^ν_fit` with the Flory exponent ν and amplitude R₀ obtained from a log-log linear regression (`linregress`) fitted on training data only. This collapses the length dependence entirely, enabling fair cross-length and cross-source comparison.

> [!TIP]
> The baseline quadratic and the Flory pair (ν, R₀) are three fitted constants that downstream code consumes verbatim. Re-running `rg_mlp.py` with different data can change them silently and desynchronize `es_ablation2.py`, which hard-codes `nu_fit=0.533, R0_fit=2.420, coeffs=[5.18129864, -31.57633081, 63.38468187]`. Any retraining must be followed by propagating these values.

Sources: [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L205-L221), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L88-L95), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L32-L40)

## Model Architecture and Configuration

`RgMLP` is a four-layer fully connected network mapping the 1280-dimensional mean-pooled ESM-2 embedding to a single scalar residual. Every hidden block follows the same modern pattern — **Linear → LayerNorm → GELU → Dropout** — with width halving at each stage, and the final projection squeezes to shape `[batch]` for direct MSE comparison.

| Block | Input → Output dim | Components |
|---|---|---|
| Block 1 | 1280 → 512 | Linear, LayerNorm, GELU, Dropout(0.3) |
| Block 2 | 512 → 256 | Linear, LayerNorm, GELU, Dropout(0.3) |
| Block 3 | 256 → 128 | Linear, LayerNorm, GELU, Dropout(0.3) |
| Head | 128 → 1 | Linear, `squeeze(-1)` |

The training configuration is deliberately conservative and fully deterministic — global seeds (Python, NumPy, CUDA), `cudnn.deterministic=True`, and `benchmark=False` guarantee bitwise-reproducible runs on identical hardware.

| Constant | Value | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `SEED` | 42 | All RNG seeding |
| `BATCH_SIZE` | 256 | MLP minibatch (over precomputed embeddings) |
| `TOKENS_PER_BATCH` | 4096 | ESM-2 token-budget batching during embedding extraction |
| `EPOCHS` / `PATIENCE` | 200 / 20 | Max epochs / early-stopping patience |
| `LR` / `WEIGHT_DECAY` | 1e-3 / 1e-4 | AdamW settings |
| `HIDDEN_DIM` / `DROPOUT` | 512 / 0.3 | Architecture width / regularization |
| `REPR_LAYER` / `SEQ_LENGTH` / `EMB_DIM` | 33 / 1022 / 1280 | ESM-2 layer, token cap, embedding width |

Sources: [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L97-L125), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L35-L56)

## Data Provenance and Leakage-Safe Splitting

Training targets come from the IDRome database (Tesei et al., MD-derived Rg in nm, converted to Å by ×10), joined with sequences from IDRome Supplementary Table 3 by `seq_name`, with duplicates and NaNs dropped. The merged sequences are written back out as `data/idrome.fasta`, then clustered **externally** with CD-HIT at 40% identity (`cd-hit -i idrome.fasta -o idrome_clustered.fasta -c 0.4 -n 2`); the script parses the resulting `.clstr` file to recover a cluster label per sequence and flags unmapped entries. This grouping is what makes the split leakage-safe.

Splitting proceeds in two `GroupShuffleSplit` rounds — 80/20 into train+val versus test, then 90/10 within train+val — with `groups=` always set to cluster labels. No two sequences sharing ≥40% identity can straddle the train/test boundary, preventing near-homolog inflation of performance metrics. CD-HIT 4.8.1 is pinned in the conda environment, and the clustering workflow is covered in depth on [Dataset Curation and CD-HIT Clustering](21-dataset-curation-and-cd-hit-clustering).

| Input | Origin | Role in training |
|---|---|---|
| `IDRome_DB.csv` | KULL-Centre `_2023_Tesei_IDRome` GitHub | MD-derived Rg targets (Rg/nm × 10 → Å), chain lengths N |
| `data/Supplementary_Table_3.xlsx` | IDRome Nature supplementary (via `esm2_interp_data.py`) | Sequence strings joined by `seq_name` |
| `data/idrome.fasta` | Regenerated locally by this script | Input for external CD-HIT clustering |
| `data/idrome_clustered.fasta.clstr` | Committed CD-HIT output (c=0.4, n=2) | Cluster labels for grouped splitting |
| `data/all_comparison_data_WITH_STARTING.csv` | Holehouse-lab STARLING 2026 supporting data | SAXS ground truth + STARLING baselines for external validation |

Sources: [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L147-L181), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L183-L203), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L56), [README.md](README.md#L72-L76)

## The Embedding Extraction Interface

Rather than reimplementing inference, `rg_mlp.py` imports `get_esm2_embeddings` from `attention_functions.py` — the shared embedding utility used across the interpretability analyses. The function materializes the DataFrame's sequences into a temporary FASTA file with numeric IDs, then uses the official `FastaBatchedDataset` machinery to batch by **token budget** (`tokens_per_batch=4096`), which keeps GPU memory bounded for heterogeneous sequence lengths (see [Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management)).

Inference runs `esm2_t33_650M_UR50D` with `repr_layers=[33]` and `return_contacts=False`, then mean-pools the final-layer representations per protein. Two slicing details matter for correctness: pooling spans indices `1 : truncate_len+1`, which **excludes the `<cls>` token** at position 0, and `truncate_len = min(1022, len(seq))` silently **caps proteins at the 1022-residue ESM-2 context window** — longer chains contribute embeddings from their first 1022 residues only. Results are re-aligned to the original DataFrame row order and returned as the input DataFrame concatenated with 1280 integer-named embedding columns, which `rg_mlp.py` selects via `isinstance(c, int)` column filtering.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    DF["df_tesei DataFrame<br/>(seq_name, sequence, Rg_A, N, cluster)"] --> TMP["temp FASTA<br/>(numeric labels: 0, 1, 2 ...)"]
    TMP --> FB["FastaBatchedDataset<br/>+ get_batch_indices(4096 tokens)"]
    FB --> DL["DataLoader with<br/>alphabet.get_batch_converter(1022)"]
    DL --> ESM["esm2_t33_650M on device<br/>repr_layers=[33], no contacts"]
    ESM --> POOL["mean over representations[i, 1:trunc+1]<br/>(skip CLS, cap at 1022 residues)"]
    POOL --> OUT["1280 integer-named columns<br/>aligned to original row order"]
```

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L391-L429), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L223-L238)

> [!TIP]
> The `1:` start index and the 1022-residue cap are easy to miss and have asymmetric consequences: skipping `<cls>` keeps the pooled vector purely residue-derived, while the cap means predictions for chains >1022 residues are extrapolations from partial-sequence embeddings — relevant when interpreting SAXS validation, which includes long sequences.

## Training Procedure

Training follows a standard-but-hardened PyTorch loop: `EmbeddingDataset` tensors are loaded with `batch_size=256`, `num_workers=4`, and worker-level re-seeding (`seed_worker`) so DataLoader shuffling is deterministic too. Optimization uses AdamW with cosine annealing over 200 epochs, MSE loss, mixed-precision (`torch.cuda.amp`) with a `GradScaler`, gradient-norm clipping at 1.0, and early stopping after 20 epochs without validation improvement. Crucially, the checkpoint is saved **on best validation loss** to `mlp_final.pt` at the repository root — the exact file committed for reuse.

Note the two distinct batching regimes coexisting in this script: the ESM-2 forward passes batch by token count (4096), while the MLP consumes fixed-size embedding rows (256 per batch). After training, loss curves are melted into long format, exported to `data/figure_data/training_curve_long.csv`, and plotted with the best-epoch marker to `figures/mlp_final_curves.svg`, following the shared styling conventions of [Publication Figure Styling](23-publication-figure-styling).

| Mechanism | Implementation | Guard it provides |
|---|---|---|
| Determinism | Global seeds + `cudnn.deterministic` + `PYTHONHASHSEED` | Bitwise-reproducible runs |
| Checkpointing | `torch.save` on validation improvement → `mlp_final.pt` | Best model, not last model, persists |
| AMP | `autocast` + `GradScaler` with `unscale_` before clipping | Speed without breaking grad clipping |
| Early stopping | Patience counter vs. best val loss | Protection against late overfitting |

Sources: [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L247-L293), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L48-L56), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L296-L314)

## Evaluation and External SAXS Validation

Evaluation reloads the best checkpoint and predicts residuals on the held-out test split, reconstructing physical Rg via `to_rg`. A deliberate integrity check — `assert np.allclose(true_raw, true_raw_check)` against the original `rg_lookup` — verifies the residual round-trip introduced no bookkeeping error before any metric is reported. Predictions and ground truth are then Flory-normalized and persisted to `data/figure_data/df_eval.csv`.

The second half of the script tests **out-of-distribution generalization**: SAXS experimental Rg values from the Holehouse-lab STARLING 2026 dataset, grouped by unique sequence with per-assay averages, are embedded, predicted, Flory-normalized, and benchmarked against two STARLING predictor variants (`starling_mps`, `starling_cuda`). The final figure is a three-panel comparison — IDRome-MLP, SAXS-MLP, and SAXS-STARLING — each annotated with Pearson and Spearman correlations, saved to `figures/rg_mlp.svg`. This framing positions the ESM-2 MLP as a lightweight sequence-only alternative to a dedicated IDP ensemble predictor.

| Panel | X axis | Y axis | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| IDRome-MLP | Tesei MD Rg (Flory-norm) | MLP Rg (Flory-norm) | In-distribution held-out accuracy |
| SAXS-MLP | Experimental SAXS Rg (Flory-norm) | MLP Rg (Flory-norm) | Experimental transfer |
| SAXS-STARLING | Experimental SAXS Rg (Flory-norm) | STARLING CUDA Rg (Flory-norm) | Dedicated-model baseline |

| Output artifact | Path | Consumer |
|---|---|---|
| Model checkpoint | `mlp_final.pt` (repo root) | `es_ablation2.py`, future inference |
| Per-protein test predictions | `data/figure_data/df_eval.csv` | Figure generation / inspection |
| SAXS predictions + baselines | `data/figure_data/saxs_proteins.csv` | Figure generation |
| Loss curves | `data/figure_data/training_curve_long.csv`, `figures/mlp_final_curves.svg` | Paper figure assembly |
| Final 3-panel benchmark | `figures/rg_mlp.svg` | Paper Figure 5 |

Sources: [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L316-L342), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L344-L380), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L382-L415)

## The mlp_final.pt Contract for Causal Ablation

`mlp_final.pt` is not a standalone deliverable — it is the **measurement instrument** for the causal ablation studies. `es_ablation2.py` re-declares an architecture-identical `RgMLP` class, loads the checkpoint's state dict, and measures how perturbing ESM-2 attention heads shifts predicted Rg. Because the baseline and Flory constants cannot be serialized inside the checkpoint (they live as module-level NumPy state in `rg_mlp.py`), the ablation script hard-codes them: identical coefficients, `nu_fit=0.533`, `R0_fit=2.420`. The only sanctioned divergence between the two scripts is `TOKENS_PER_BATCH` (8192 in the ablation versus 4096 here), a pure memory-throughput knob that does not alter semantics.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph rg["rg_mlp.py (producer)"]
        M1["RgMLP weights"] --> CKPT["mlp_final.pt"]
        C1["coeffs / nu_fit / R0_fit<br/>(fitted values)"] --> EXPORT["print + hard-code into es_ablation2.py"]
    end
    subgraph ab["es_ablation2.py (consumer)"]
        CKPT --> LOAD["RgMLP.load_state_dict"]
        EXPORT --> B2["baseline_poly = np.poly1d(coeffs)"]
        LOAD --> PRED["Δ Rg under head ablation"]
        B2 --> PRED
    end
    shared["attention_functions.get_esm2_embeddings"] --> rg
    shared --> ab
```

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L22-L40), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L47-L60), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L287)

## Reproducibility Notes and Data Boundaries

A precise reading of this script reveals the repository's derived-versus-live data strategy in miniature (elaborated on [Derived Versus Live Data Reproduibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility)). The IDRome FASTA files and cluster files are committed, but the SAXS CSV and Supplementary Table 3 are fetched by `esm2_interp_data.py` per instructions in [External Data Acquisition](3-external-data-acquisition). One documentation drift is visible in-source: the header docstring cites `all_comparison_data.csv`, while the code reads `all_comparison_data_WITH_STARTING.csv` — the "WITH_STARTING" variant is the reproducibility-pinned file, and the docstring points at the live upstream URL.

| Data class | Handling | Implication for re-runs |
|---|---|---|
| Committed inputs (`idrome.fasta`, `.clstr`) | In-repo | Deterministic split recovery via `SEED=42` |
| Downloaded inputs (Supp Table 3, SAXS CSV) | Via `esm2_interp_data.py` | Upstream DB drift possible; pin files for exact reproduction |
| Derived outputs (`figure_data/*.csv`, SVGs) | Regenerated by `rg_mlp.py` | Not committed; regenerate for [Reproducing Paper Figures](4-reproducing-paper-figures) |
| Baseline/Flory constants | Fitted, then hard-coded in `es_ablation2.py` | Manual propagation required after retraining |

Sources: [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L31-L32), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L356), [README.md](README.md#L72-L76)

The immediate downstream consumer is covered in [Attention Head Ablation Study](18-attention-head-ablation-study), with the hypothesis it tests in [Electrostatics Hypothesis Testing](19-electrostatics-hypothesis-testing). # Attention Head Ablation Study



This page documents the causal arm of the repository's interpretability program: `scripts/es_ablation2.py`, the experiment that converts the *correlational* findings of [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics) into a *causal* test. The script identifies ESM-2 attention heads most strongly associated with charged residues (D, E, K, R), surgically silences them during inference via forward hooks, and measures whether the frozen Rg predictor (from [MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor)) degrades more than under matched random ablation. The study spans two benchmarks (IDRome and experimental SAXS), a cumulative 50-head sweep, snapshot evaluations, and a composition-residualization protocol that separates head-specific signal from trivial amino acid composition effects.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L30-L33), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L10-L17)

## From Correlation to Causation

Upstream analyses in this repository established that certain layer/head positions receive disproportionate attention from charged amino acids, but correlation alone cannot tell you whether those heads *carry* the electrostatic compaction signal or merely co-occur with it. The ablation study closes this gap with an intervention: the script's own docstring states its purpose — "Ablate Heads of ESM-2 likely to be associated with electrostatics and evaluate ablation effect on MLP Rg prediction" ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L30-L33)). The causal logic is asymmetric-degradation: if electrostatic heads are load-bearing, ablating them should hurt Rg prediction accuracy significantly more than ablating the same number of random heads, because random ablation controls for raw capacity loss while targeted ablation removes hypothesized *specific* information. The full experiment is a chain of five stages, each isolated in the script: ranking, hooking, embedding regeneration, prediction, and statistics.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Correlational evidence<br/>data/attn_corr_norm_es.csv"] --> B["Electrostatic head ranking<br/>D/E heads (neg) · K/R heads (pos)"]
    B --> C["Zero-ablation hooks<br/>forward pre-hook on out_proj input"]
    C --> D["ESM-2 t33 650M<br/>embeddings regenerated live"]
    D --> E["RgMLP · mlp_final.pt<br/>frozen residual prediction"]
    E --> F["Flory normalization<br/>Rg / (R0 · N^nu)"]
    F --> G["Statistics<br/>Δ Spearman/Pearson · t-test · paired bootstrap"]
    H["Random control<br/>5 pre-shuffled head sequences"] -.-> C
```

The two-headed hypothesis distinguishes **negative** residues (D/E, negatively charged) from **positive** residues (K/R, positively charged), ablating each family's top-ranked heads independently. This matters because IDRome proteins show distinct compaction behavior under net-negative versus net-positive charge regimes; if only one polarity's heads degrade prediction, the electrostatic encoding is polarity-specific rather than generic charge sensitivity.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L30-L33), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L131-L143)

## Experimental Design at a Glance

The design is a three-condition comparison evaluated across two independent benchmarks. Each condition ablates heads cumulatively or at a fixed snapshot, always against an unablated baseline prediction computed on the same frozen model pair (ESM-2 → MLP). The five random control runs pre-shuffle candidate head sequences *once*, excluding all targeted heads from the candidate pool, so random runs never dilute the targeted conditions with electrostatic heads — a subtle but important exclusion that keeps conditions statistically independent.

| Condition | Head pool | Pool size | Runs | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Negative (D/E) | Top-50 `heads_neg_ranked` by mean D/E attention | 50 | 1 cumulative sweep | Test negative-charge head causality |
| Positive (K/R) | Top-50 `heads_pos_ranked` by mean K/R attention | 50 | 1 cumulative sweep | Test positive-charge head causality |
| Random | 5 seeded permutations of all non-targeted heads | 900 candidates | 5 cumulative sweeps | Capacity-loss null distribution |
| Baseline | None (unmodified model) | 0 | 1 per benchmark | Reference for all Δ metrics |

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L263-L291)

## Electrostatic Head Ranking

The ranking input is a *derived* artifact, `data/attn_corr_norm_es.csv`, containing occurrence-normalized attention statistics for exactly four amino acids (D, E, K, R) at every layer/head pair (2,640 rows = 33 layers × 20 heads × 4 residues). Its provenance is recorded in a commented block at the top of the head-selection section: it was produced by `run_aa_analysis_head_layer(normalize='occurrence', model='original')` from [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction) chunks, meaning the ranking reflects the *original pretrained* ESM-2, not a finetuned variant ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L131-L135)). The `occurrence` normalization is defined in `attention_functions.py` as per-residue attention summed across the sequence, then divided by that amino acid's count in the sequence — so a head scores high only if it attends strongly to charged residues *per occurrence*, not merely because the protein is compositionally rich ([attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L313-L323)).

From this table the script computes two rankings: `mean_pos` averages `attn_occur_norm` over K/R rows per (head, layer), and `mean_neg` does the same over D/E rows; each is sorted descending to yield `heads_pos_ranked` and `heads_neg_ranked` ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L136-L143)). Before ablation, the script emits diagnostic visualizations: a 2×2 grid of layer-by-head heatmaps (one per residue) saved to `figures/DEKR_heatmaps.svg`, and pairwise Pearson correlations between the D/E/K/R heatmap surfaces, which quantify whether charge-polarity attention patterns are redundant (D~E, K~R high) or complementary ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L145-L186)). These diagnostics justify treating D/E and K/R as coherent head families rather than independent residue-level signals.

| Ranking artifact | Rows | Selection rule | Consumed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `attn_corr_norm_es.csv` | 2,640 | D/E/K/R only, occurrence-normalized, original model | Ranking computation |
| `heads_neg_ranked` | Top-50 used | Mean D/E attention, descending | Negative ablation |
| `heads_pos_ranked` | Top-50 used | Mean K/R attention, descending | Positive ablation |

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L131-L143), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L336-L389)

## True Zero-Ablation Hook Mechanism

The core engineering contribution is `register_esm_ablation_hooks`, which implements what the docstring calls "true zero-ablation": setting the head's output function `Att_h(x) → 0` without re-implementing attention internals ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L194-L207)). The function exploits PyTorch's `nn.MultiheadAttention` structure: each head's 64-dimensional output exists as a *contiguous slice* of the tensor fed into `out_proj`, but only at that exact point — after `out_proj`'s linear mixing, individual head contributions are algebraically entangled and cannot be cleanly separated. The hook is therefore a `register_forward_pre_hook` on `out_proj` itself, intercepting the concatenated per-head vector `[Att_0(x), …, Att_19(x)]`, zeroing the `h*64 : (h+1)*64` slice for each ablated head, and returning the modified tuple so `out_proj` runs normally on the censored input.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    X["Layer input x"] --> QKV["Q · K · V projections<br/>(per-head 64-d outputs)"]
    QKV --> A0["Att_0(x)"]
    QKV --> AH["Att_h(x)"]
    QKV --> A19["Att_19(x)"]
    A0 --> CAT["Concatenation [Att_0 … Att_19]<br/>(tgt_len, bsz, 1280)"]
    AH -- "zeroed by pre-hook" --> CAT
    A19 --> CAT
    CAT --> OP["out_proj Linear<br/>(runs unmodified)"]
    OP --> Y["Residual stream continues<br/>to layers h+1 … 33"]
```

Three implementation details make this robust for a 33-layer sweep. First, hooks are grouped per layer — one hook handles all heads ablated in that layer — avoiding redundant registrations ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L208-L226)). Second, the hook clones its input (`args[0].clone()`) before mutation, preventing in-place corruption of tensors that autograd or downstream consumers may reference. Third, every ablation call site wraps registration in `try/finally` with `remove_hooks(handles)`, guaranteeing the next condition (positive, random, or baseline) always runs on a clean model ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L296-L318)).

> [!TIP]
> The surgical precision of this hook placement is what separates true ablation from approximate ablation: zeroing *post*-out_proj activations would also zero the contributions of surviving heads wherever the projection matrix has cross-head mixing terms, contaminating the control conditions. The pre-hook on `out_proj` input is the unique point where head identity is still exactly recoverable from tensor geometry (fixed 64-dim slices), so ablated heads are silenced without perturbing anyone else.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L194-L226), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L296-L318)

## Datasets, Flory Normalization, and Metrics

Evaluation runs on two benchmarks with different ground-truth provenance. `load_idrome()` reconstructs the *held-out test split* used to train the MLP: it merges the IDRome database (downloaded live from the KULL-Centre GitHub) with `data/Supplementary_Table_3.xlsx`, converts Rg from nm to Å, attaches CD-HIT cluster labels parsed from `data/idrome_clustered.fasta.clstr`, and applies `GroupShuffleSplit(test_size=0.2, random_state=42)` — the identical seeded, cluster-grouped split from [MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor), ensuring ablation is scored on proteins the MLP never saw and that cluster-redundant sequences cannot straddle the split ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L87-L117), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L34-L47)). `load_saxs()` provides an orthogonal experimental check: SAXS-measured Rg values, deduplicated by sequence and averaged, so each unique protein contributes once ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L119-L127)).

All Rg comparisons use **Flory-normalized** units to remove trivial length dependence: true and predicted values are divided by the polymer scaling law `R0 · N^ν` with `ν=0.533`, `R0=2.420`, and the MLP's own length residual is added back via a degree-2 polynomial baseline in `log(N)` before normalization ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L36-L49), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L232-L239)). This means the evaluation metric — Spearman ρ, Pearson r, and MAE on normalized Rg — measures whether the model captures *compaction state relative to ideal-chain scaling*, not absolute size, which would otherwise be dominated by sequence length. Note one environment deviation from training: the ablation script batches inference at `TOKENS_PER_BATCH=8192` (versus 4096 during training) since no gradients are needed — a memory/throughput tradeoff discussed further in [Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management).

| Benchmark | Source | Split | Ground truth | Sequences used |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| IDRome | IDRome_DB.csv + Supplementary Table 3 | Held-out 20%, grouped by CD-HIT cluster, seed 42 | MD-derived Rg (Å) | Test partition only |
| SAXS | `all_comparison_data_WITH_STARTING.csv` | All (evaluation only) | Experimental Rg | Unique sequences, mean-aggregated |

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L87-L127), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L232-L245)

## The Cumulative Head Sweep

`run_sweep` is the dose-response experiment: for each `n` from 1 to 50, it ablates the top-*n* negative heads, the top-*n* positive heads, and the first-*n* heads of each of five pre-built random sequences, re-running full ESM-2 inference and MLP prediction at every step ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L291-L346)). The random sequences are constructed once before the loop: five `rng.choice` permutations (seeded at 42) of `candidate_heads` — every (layer, head) pair except the 100 targeted ones — so each random run is a coherent *consecutive prefix* ablation rather than resampling heads at every step, which would make the random curve non-cumulative and incomparable to the targeted curves ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L274-L289)). At each dose the script records Δ Spearman and Δ Pearson against baseline for all three conditions, including the random mean and standard deviation across the five runs. Because a full sweep is expensive, results checkpoint to CSV every 10 heads, and the final long-form DataFrame gains a random-condition ± standard-error band (`delta_upper`/`delta_lower`) before plotting the headline figure `figures/head_ablation_sweep_.svg` with red (negative), blue (positive), and gray-banded (random) trajectories ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L343-L377)).

A reading-the-code caveat: in the current committed state, the IDRome sweep call is **commented out** at the run block (`#run_sweep(idrome_proteins, ...)`), so executing the script as-is runs only the snapshot evaluations and the residualization analysis described below — re-enable that line to regenerate the dose-response curve ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L432-L441)).

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L263-L380)

## Snapshot Evaluation and Per-Protein Significance

Where the sweep asks *how much* damage accrues with dose, `run_eval` asks *what kind* of damage at the full 50-head dose.
