It computes baseline and ablated predictions per protein, then derives four per-protein quantities: the fraction of D/E and K/R residues (`frac_DE`, `frac_KR`), the MAE change `delta_mae` (ablated minus baseline error), and the signed prediction shift `bigger_or_smaller` (ablated minus baseline normalized Rg), all persisted to `data/figure_data/` as eight CSVs covering both head polarities on both benchmarks ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L386-L424), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L441-L450)). Significance is tested with a one-sample t-test of `delta_mae` against zero — asking whether mean per-protein error change differs from noise — supplemented by a "worse vs. better" tally, since a significant mean shift driven by a minority of proteins tells a different mechanistic story than a uniform degradation ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L418-L422)). The `frac_DE`/`frac_KR` columns are deliberately carried into the outputs: they feed the composition-confound analysis below and any downstream regression of ablation damage on charge content.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L386-L424)

## Residualization: Isolating Signal Beyond Composition

The final analysis confronts the study's central confound: D/E-attention heads are selected *because* they respond to charge composition, so any degradation they cause could reflect nothing more than the MLP having lost access to raw composition counts. The script's residualization protocol (its design is spelled out in a block comment: regress embedding on DEKR, residualize, re-predict, and attribute any residual gap to "some other electrostatics" beyond composition — [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L452-L460)) works as follows. Each of the 1,280 embedding dimensions is separately regressed via OLS on `frac_DE` (for negative heads) or `frac_KR` (for positive heads), producing *residualized* baseline and ablated embeddings with linear composition dependence removed ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L512-L525)). Four prediction conditions then enter a 2×2 matrix — baseline/ablated × original/residualized — and the quantity of interest is the **beyond-composition gap**: the difference between ablated-residual and baseline-residual prediction quality, which cannot be explained by composition since composition has been regressed out of both.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph ORIG["Original embeddings"]
        B1["Baseline ESM-2 emb"] --> P1["MLP → Rg (base)"]
        A1["Ablated ESM-2 emb"] --> P2["MLP → Rg (abl)"]
    end
    subgraph RES["Composition-residualized embeddings<br/>(OLS on frac_DE or frac_KR)"]
        B2["Baseline residual emb"] --> P3["MLP → Rg (base res)"]
        A2["Ablated residual emb"] --> P4["MLP → Rg (abl res)"]
    end
    P1 --> O["Raw ablation effect"]
    P2 --> O
    P3 --> G["Beyond-composition gap:<br/>Δ corr(res abl, true) −<br/>Δ corr(res base, true)"]
    P4 --> G
    G --> S["Paired bootstrap test<br/>5,000 resamples · 95% CI · two-sided p"]
```

Significance of the gap uses `bootstrap_gap_test`, a *paired* bootstrap over proteins: 5,000 resamples draw protein indices once and apply the identical resample to both baseline-residual and ablated-residual predictions, so the gap distribution reflects sampling variance in proteins rather than mismatched samples; the 95% CI comes from percentiles and the p-value is two-sided on the sign of the observed gap ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L462-L489)). The analysis runs for both Pearson and Spearman, for both negative and positive head sets on IDRome ([es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L553-L560)). A gap that survives residualization with tight bootstrap intervals is the strongest evidence this study can offer that electrostatic heads encode structured charge *relationships* (e.g., sequence-position-dependent interactions), not just residue frequencies.

> [!TIP]
> The pairing in the bootstrap is not decorative: because both prediction vectors are evaluated on the same resampled proteins, between-protein heterogeneity (length, composition outliers) cancels in the gap statistic. An unpaired test would inflate variance by the full between-protein spread, likely washing out a real but modest beyond-composition effect.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L452-L460), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L462-L560)

## Running the Study and Its Artifacts

Executing `python scripts/es_ablation2.py` requires: the committed `mlp_final.pt` and `data/attn_corr_norm_es.csv`, the IDRome supplementary table plus live network access to the IDRome database CSV, and the SAXS comparison file (external data acquisition is covered in [External Data Acquisition](3-external-data-acquisition)); a CUDA device is selected automatically when available. Inference regenerates embeddings live for every condition through `get_esm2_embeddings`, which mean-pools layer-33 representations over the true residue range (skipping `<cls>`, truncating at 1,022 tokens) ([attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L391-L420)). All result artifacts land in `data/figure_data/` and `figures/`, following the derived-data conventions described in [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility).

| Artifact | Type | Producer |
|---|---|---|
| `figures/DEKR_heatmaps.svg` | Layer×head attention heatmap (D, E, K, R) | Ranking diagnostics |
| `figures/head_ablation_sweep_.svg` | Dose-response curves + random ±SE band | `run_sweep` |
| `es_ablation_sweep_df_{label}_random_consecutive.csv` | Sweep results (+ checkpoint every 10 heads) | `run_sweep` |
| `results_df.csv` / `results_df_pos.csv` | IDRome snapshot: per-protein deltas, `frac_DE/KR` | `run_eval` |
| `saxs_results_df.csv` / `saxs_results_df_pos.csv` | SAXS snapshot, same schema | `run_eval` |
| Stdout: beyond-composition gap | 4-condition evaluation + bootstrap CI/p | `run_eval_residual` |

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L432-L450), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L391-L420)

## Where This Fits in the Pipeline

The ablation study is the hinge between the repository's observational and hypothesis-testing arms. Its head-ranking input inherits directly from [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics); its frozen predictor is documented in [MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor); and its findings feed the interpretive synthesis in [Electrostatics Hypothesis Testing](19-electrostatics-hypothesis-testing), which situates these causal results alongside the polarity-specific compaction behavior of IDRome sequences. For the memory-management implications of running 100+ full-model inference passes, see [Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management).


# Electrostatics Hypothesis Testing



This page documents the electrostatics hypothesis testing pipeline implemented in `scripts/es_ablation2.py`, the final causal-validation stage of the interpretability project. The script takes the observation that certain ESM-2 heads allocate disproportionate, occurrence-normalized attention to charged residues (D, E, K, R) and asks three nested questions: are those heads **charge-coherent** (do heads reading aspartate also read glutamate)? Are they **causal** (does zeroing them degrade MLP radius-of-gyration prediction beyond a random-head null)? And is that effect **more than composition** (does it survive when the linear contribution of charged-residue fraction is regressed out of the embeddings)? The script's own docstring states the intent directly: *"Ablate Heads of ESM-2 likely to be associated with electrostatics and evaluate ablation effect on MLP Rg prediction."*

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L12-L16)

## The Hypothesis Under Test

The analysis encodes a two-part hypothesis. The **representational claim** holds that ESM-2 maintains head populations specialized for charge sign — measurable as high correlation between (layer, head) attention heatmaps of same-charge residue pairs (D–E, K–R) and comparatively lower correlation across opposite-charge pairs (D–K, D–R, K–E, R–E). The **causal claim** holds that if these heads carry electrostatic information relevant to IDR dimensionality, removing their outputs should measurably shift Rg predictions, with the degradation pattern differing between charge signs. The critical confound is composition: IDRome sequences vary widely in D/E and K/R fraction, so any attention effect might simply re-encode `frac_DE`/`frac_KR` counts rather than electrostatic *interactions*. Stage 5 (residualization) exists precisely to separate these.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    H1["Representational:<br/>charge-coherent head populations"] --> H2["Causal:<br/>ablation degrades Rg prediction<br/>beyond random-head null"]
    H2 --> H3["Non-compositional:<br/>effect survives OLS residualization<br/>on charged-residue fraction"]
```

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L164-L177), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L452-L460)

## Pipeline Architecture

The script executes five sequential stages, each consuming the artifacts of the previous one. Note that in the current committed state, the expensive `run_sweep` call is commented out (line 438) — re-running the script as-is executes the snapshot evaluations and the residualization analyses, while the full sweep requires uncommenting.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["data/attn_corr_norm_es.csv<br/>660 head-layer combos × {D,E,K,R}"] --> B["Rank heads by mean<br/>occurrence-normalized attention"]
    B --> C["heads_neg_ranked (D/E)"]
    B --> D["heads_pos_ranked (K/R)"]
    C --> E["register_esm_ablation_hooks<br/>zero head slices before out_proj"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["run_sweep: cumulative n = 1…50<br/>Neg + Pos + 5×Random control"]
    F --> G["Δ Spearman/Pearson vs baseline<br/>+ Random ± SE confidence band"]
    E --> H["run_eval snapshot: top-50 heads<br/>IDRome test set + SAXS set"]
    H --> I["Per-protein Δ MAE<br/>one-sample t-test"]
    E --> J["run_eval_residual:<br/>OLS residualize embeddings on frac_DE / frac_KR"]
    J --> K["bootstrap_gap_test<br/>paired, 5000 resamples"]
```

| Stage | Function | Input heads | Output artifacts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Head identification | top-level ranking | `attn_corr_norm_es.csv` | `figures/DEKR_heatmaps.svg`, console correlations |
| Zero-ablation | `register_esm_ablation_hooks` | ranked lists | in-memory model hooks |
| Cumulative sweep | `run_sweep` | top-50 neg + pos | `data/figure_data/es_ablation_sweep_df_{label}_random_consecutive.csv`, `figures/head_ablation_sweep_.svg` |
| Snapshot evaluation | `run_eval` | top-50 neg / pos | `results_df.csv`, `saxs_results_df.csv` (+ `_pos` variants) |
| Residualization | `run_eval_residual` | top-50 neg / pos | console statistics (gap, CI, p) |

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L432-L450), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L559-L560)

## Stage 1 — Locating Charge-Specific Heads

The entry point is a **derived dataset**: `data/attn_corr_norm_es.csv` holds 2,640 rows — 33 layers × 20 heads × 4 charged amino acids — with columns `layer, head, aa, attn_occur_norm`. The commented-out block above the load shows its provenance: it was produced by `run_aa_analysis_head_layer(normalize='occurrence', model='original')`, which walks 22 precomputed attention-matrix chunks and, for every (layer, head) pair, sums attention received by each amino acid type and divides by that residue's occurrence count in each sequence (the *occurrence* normalization mode). This is the same statistical machinery documented in [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics); this page treats the CSV as a frozen input rather than recomputing it.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L118-L134), [data/attn_corr_norm_es.csv](/data/attn_corr_norm_es.csv#L1-L10), [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L313-L323)

From this table the script constructs two rankings. `mean_pos` averages `attn_occur_norm` over positively charged residues (R, K) per (head, layer); `mean_neg` does the same for negatively charged residues (D, E). Sorting descending yields `heads_pos_ranked` and `heads_neg_ranked` — ordered lists of the heads most attuned to each charge sign. These two lists are the entire "hypothesis-driven" selection mechanism; everything downstream is conditional on them.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L125-L134)

Before any ablation, the script produces **descriptive evidence** for the charge-coherence claim. A 2×2 figure grid renders one (layer × head) heatmap per amino acid (D, E, K, R) on a shared color scale, saved as `figures/DEKR_heatmaps.svg`. Then six Pearson correlations over the pivoted heatmap vectors quantify pattern similarity: `corr_DE` and `corr_KR` (same-charge pairs, expected high), versus `corr_DK`, `corr_DR`, `corr_KE`, `corr_RE` (opposite-charge pairs). The comparison logic is deliberate — same-sign pairs sharing a spatial attention pattern while cross-sign pairs diverge would indicate sign-selective, rather than generically "charged residue"-selective, heads.

| Correlation pair | Charge relationship | Coherence interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| D–E, K–R | Same sign | Shared (layer, head) pattern → sign-selective heads |
| D–K, D–R, K–E, R–E | Opposite sign | Decorrelated pattern → distinct populations per sign |

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L136-L177)

## Stage 2 — True Zero-Ablation Mechanics

The causal test requires removing a head's contribution from the live forward pass without disturbing the other 19. The script achieves this with a forward *pre*-hook on `self_attn.out_proj`, and the docstring is explicit about why this placement matters: the hook fires on the hook module's **input**, which is the concatenated per-head output `[Att_0(x), …, Att_19(x)]` *before* `out_proj` mixes heads together. Zeroing the h-th 64-dimensional slice (`h * head_dim` to `(h + 1) * head_dim`, with `HEAD_DIM = embed_dim / num_heads = 1280 / 20 = 64`) sets that head's output exactly to zero while every other head's slice passes through untouched, and the output projection then combines the surviving heads normally.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SDPA["Per-head outputs<br/>(64-dim each)"] --> C0["Head 0"]
    SDPA --> C1["Head 1"]
    SDPA --> CD["⋯"]
    SDPA --> C19["Head 19"]
    C0 --> X["concat:<br/>(tgt_len, bsz, 1280)"]
    C1 --> X
    CD --> X
    C19 --> X
    X --> Z["forward_pre_hook:<br/>x[:, :, h·64:(h+1)·64] = 0"]
    Z --> OP["out_proj mixes<br/>surviving heads"]
```

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L197-L226)

Engineering details worth noting: heads are grouped by layer into one hook per affected layer (so a 50-head target spanning many layers installs at most 33 hooks); the hook clones the input tensor before mutation (`args[0].clone()`); and `remove_hooks` strips every handle in a `finally` block, guaranteeing the model returns to its unmodified state even if embedding extraction raises. Hooks are never left installed across experimental conditions — each ablated embedding pass registers, extracts, and deregisters.

> [!TIP]
> Hooking `out_proj`'s *input* (a `register_forward_pre_hook`) rather than post-processing attention weights is what makes this a "true zero-ablation": the zeroed slice propagates through the nonlinearity of every subsequent layer, so downstream layers recompute in the actual ablated regime — unlike attention-map masking, which only reweights a post-hoc analysis.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L208-L230), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L296-L300)

## Stage 3 — Cumulative Sweep with a Random-Head Null

`run_sweep` is the dose-response experiment. For each cumulative head count `n` from 1 to `MAX_HEADS_ABLATE = 50`, it ablates the top-*n* negative heads, the top-*n* positive heads, and — critically — the first *n* heads from each of five **pre-shuffled random sequences**. The random control is constructed carefully: candidate heads exclude the entire targeted set (the union of top-50 neg and top-50 pos), each of the `N_RANDOM_RUNS = 5` permutations is drawn once up front from a seeded RNG (`SEED = 42`), and each run's prefix of length *n* is ablated — making the random condition cumulative and consecutive, exactly matched in structure to the targeted conditions at every `n`.

| Condition | Head source | Runs per *n* | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Negative (D/E) | `heads_neg_ranked[:n]` | 1 | Hypothesis arm: heads reading acidic residues |
| Positive (K/R) | `heads_pos_ranked[:n]` | 1 | Complementary arm: basic-residue heads |
| Random | shuffled non-targeted heads | 5 | Empirical null; mean ± SE band |

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L263-L291), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L310-L326)

Every ablated model state is evaluated through the identical measurement funnel: `get_esm2_embeddings` writes sequences to a temporary FASTA, batches them via `FastaBatchedDataset`, runs the (possibly hooked) ESM-2 forward pass, and mean-pools layer-33 representations per residue token (`representations[i, 1:truncate_len + 1].mean(0)`); `predict_rg` feeds these to the frozen `mlp_final.pt` MLP, applies the polynomial baseline correction, and Flory-normalizes both prediction and truth by `R₀·N^ν` (ν = 0.533, R₀ = 2.420); `evaluate` reduces each arm to Spearman ρ, Pearson r, and MAE. The sweep records **deltas against the un-ablated baseline** for all three conditions and persists results every 10 heads (`*_checkpoint_random_consecutive.csv`) so long GPU sweeps survive interruption.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L391-L429), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L232-L245), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L343-L350)

The final figure plots ΔSpearman versus number of heads ablated for all three conditions, with the random condition additionally drawn as a shaded ±SE band (`delta_spearman_random_se = std/√5`). The visual claim structure: a targeted curve falling below the random band at moderate *n* indicates the ablated heads matter more than equivalent volumes of arbitrary heads — the causal signature. The final sweep table is saved as `data/figure_data/es_ablation_sweep_df_{label}_random_consecutive.csv` for both `idrome` and `saxs` datasets.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L348-L379)

## Stage 4 — Fixed-Set Snapshot Evaluation

Where the sweep traces degradation curves, `run_eval` produces a **deep characterization at one operating point**: the top `OVERWRITE_NUM_HEADS = 50` heads of each ranking. It re-establishes baseline predictions, applies the ablation, and builds a per-protein results frame with `rg_true_scaled`, `rg_baseline_scaled`, `rg_ablated_scaled`, the charged-residue fractions (`frac_DE`, `frac_KR` via regex counting), and two derived columns: `delta_mae` (per-protein MAE increase from ablation) and `bigger_or_smaller` (signed prediction shift). Statistical support comes from a one-sample t-test of `delta_mae` against zero, plus the proportion of proteins made worse vs. better.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L386-L424)

The run block executes this four ways — negative-head and positive-head ablations, each on both evaluation sets: the IDRome held-out test split and the SAXS ensemble. The IDRome test proteins are the 20% cluster-grouped holdout from `GroupShuffleSplit(test_size=0.2, random_state=SEED)` over CD-HIT clusters, ensuring the ablation is scored on proteins never seen during MLP training; the SAXS set is deduplicated by averaging `saxs` values per unique sequence. Results are persisted as `results_df.csv`, `saxs_results_df.csv`, and their `_pos` counterparts under `data/figure_data/`.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L74-L113), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L432-L450)

## Stage 5 — Residualization: Separating Composition from Electrostatic Structure

The most methodologically distinctive stage addresses the composition confound head-on. The design comment in the script lays out the inference chain explicitly: residualize the baseline embedding against charged fraction, residualize the ablated embedding the same way, predict Rg from both residual embeddings — then *"any gap between them is NOT attributed to DEKR so has to come from some other electrostatics."* In other words, Stage 4's degradation could be trivially explained if the ablated heads merely tracked how many D/E residues a sequence has; Stage 5 asks what remains of the ablation effect once that linear count signal is subtracted.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    EB["Baseline embedding"] -->|"OLS: emb ~ frac_DE"| RB["Baseline residual emb."]
    EA["Ablated embedding"] -->|"OLS: emb ~ frac_DE"| RA["Ablated residual emb."]
    RB --> PB["Rg pred — baseline resid"]
    RA --> PA["Rg pred — ablated resid"]
    PB --> GAP["gap = corr(true, PA) − corr(true, PB)"]
    PA --> GAP
    GAP --> BT["Paired bootstrap<br/>(identical resample both arms)"]
    BT --> OUT["95% percentile CI + two-sided p"]
```

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L452-L460), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L491-L525)

Implementation is compact: for both the baseline and ablated mean-pooled embeddings (all 1,280 dimensions), `run_eval_residual` fits `sm.OLS(embedding, sm.add_constant(frac_col)).fit()` — one regression per embedding dimension, with `frac_KR` as the covariate for the positive-head condition and `frac_DE` for the negative-head condition — and keeps `model.resid` as the composition-orthogonalized embedding. The analysis then produces four Rg predictions (baseline, baseline-residual, ablated, ablated-residual), reports the **beyond-composition gap** (`abl_res_spearman − base_res_spearman` and its Pearson analogue), and subjects the gap to `bootstrap_gap_test`.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L512-L555)

The significance test is a **paired bootstrap**: 5,000 resamples of protein indices draw *the same* resample for both residual predictions in each iteration, compute `r_abl − r_base` per resample, and derive a two-sided p-value by checking which side of zero the bootstrap gaps fall on (with the direction chosen by the sign of the observed gap), plus a 95% percentile CI. Pairing is the statistically important choice — resampling both arms identically cancels protein-sampling variance shared between them, isolating the ablation-attributable difference. The test runs under both `pearson` and `spearman` correlation, and is executed for both the negative and positive head sets on IDRome.

> [!TIP]
> Because one OLS residualization is fit per embedding dimension on a single covariate, the residual embeddings retain any *nonlinear* relationship between charged composition and the representation — the procedure removes only the linear projection onto `frac_DE`/`frac_KR`. That is exactly the right null for "heads merely count charged residues," but a headline "beyond-composition" gap should still be read as *linear-composition-independent*, not composition-independent in general.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L462-L489), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L559-L560)

## Reading the Outcomes

The script's outputs are designed so that the hypothesis is adjudicated by three independent statistical instruments, each guarding a different failure mode. Use this decision matrix when interpreting a run:

| Observation | Instrument | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Same-charge correlations ≫ cross-charge correlations | Stage 1 `corr_DE/KR` vs `corr_DK/DR/KE/RE` | Heads are sign-selective, not generically charged-residue-selective |
| Targeted ΔSpearman drops below the Random ± SE band | Stage 3 sweep plot | Ablated heads carry non-redundant, above-null information |
| `delta_mae` t-test p < 0.05 with majority of proteins worse | Stage 4 per-protein t-test | Degradation is protein-wide, not driven by outliers |
| Bootstrap gap CI excludes 0 | Stage 5 paired bootstrap | Effect persists after linear composition removal → interaction-level electrostatic encoding |
| Residual gap CI contains 0 | Stage 5 paired bootstrap | Ablation effect is fully explained by charged-residue counts; no interaction evidence |

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L164-L177), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L418-L422), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L550-L555)

A practical asymmetry also exists between the two charge arms: the negative (D/E) and positive (K/R) rankings are independent head lists, and the positive condition uses `frac_KR` for residualization — so the two arms can in principle yield different conclusions, which is itself informative about which charge sign ESM-2 encodes more structurally. The `cohen_d` helper (pooled-SD effect size) is available in the script for effect-size reporting alongside the significance tests.

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L491-L496), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L247-L257)

## Artifacts, Seeds, and Reproducibility

Every stochastic element is pinned to `SEED = 42`: the cluster-grouped IDRome test split, the five random head permutations, and the bootstrap resampler all draw from seeds derived from it. Deterministic artifacts — the DEKR heatmap SVG, sweep CSVs with checkpoint variants, and the eight snapshot result frames — land under `figures/` and `data/figure_data/`. Runtime inputs not regenerated by this script include the derived `attn_corr_norm_es.csv` (reproducible via the commented `run_aa_analysis_head_layer` call, which requires the 22 attention-matrix chunks from [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction)) and the two Rg ground-truth sources (`Supplementary_Table_3.xlsx` and the remote IDRome DB CSV), which follow the acquisition flow described in [External Data Acquisition](3-external-data-acquisition).

| Artifact | Producing call | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `figures/DEKR_heatmaps.svg` | Stage 1 plotting | Per-AA (layer × head) attention heatmaps |
| `es_ablation_sweep_df_{label}_random_consecutive.csv` | `run_sweep` | Δρ/Δr per n, random mean/std/SE |
| `figures/head_ablation_sweep_.svg` | `run_sweep` | Three-condition degradation curves + null band |
| `results_df.csv` / `saxs_results_df.csv` (+ `_pos`) | `run_eval` | Per-protein scaled predictions, `delta_mae`, `frac_DE/KR` |

Sources: [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L20-L33), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L118-L123)

## Where to Go Next

This page is the payoff of a chain built across the Deep Dive section: the head-ranking input derives from [Amino Acid Attention Statistics](11-amino-acid-attention-statistics); the MLP being ablated is trained in [MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor); the general ablation methodology (head selection variants and non-electrostatic controls) is covered in [Attention Head Ablation Study](18-attention-head-ablation-study); and the memory-management techniques that make 50-head × full-dataset sweeps feasible on GPU are treated in [Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management). To regenerate the publication-quality versions of the sweep plots, follow the rendering pipeline in [Reproducing Paper Figures](4-reproducing-paper-figures).


# Large Tensor Memory Management



Every analysis stage in this repository materializes tensors whose sizes scale quadratically — or worse — with protein length: full attention tensors across 33 layers × 20 heads, categorical Jacobians of shape (L, 20, L, 20), and L×L rollout matrices held for thousands of proteins. Left unchecked, these artifacts would exhaust GPU memory within a single batch and exceed host RAM within a few hundred proteins. This page documents the *memory discipline* that makes the pipeline feasible on commodity hardware: a repeatable lifecycle of budget-bound batching, inference-mode guards, device demotion, explicit unbinding, and chunked disk persistence. It explains the engineering substrate beneath the scientific methods described in [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction), [Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm), and [Categorical Jacobian Contact Maps](14-categorical-jacobian-contact-maps).

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L40-L45), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L56-L74)

## The Tensor Arithmetic That Motivates Everything

The single number that governs this codebase's design is the size of a per-protein attention tensor. With `need_head_weights=True`, ESM-2 returns all layer-head matrices for a batch, and the extraction script immediately slices out each protein's (33, 20, L_pad, L_pad) matrix before moving it to host memory. At the model's 1022-residue context limit (padded to 1024), that single float32 array is 660 × 1024² × 4 bytes ≈ 2.8 GB — so even a batch of two saturates a modest GPU card, and 200 such proteins cannot coexist in RAM. The table below quantifies each artifact class; note how the Jacobian would grow to ~3.3 GB per protein at full length, which is precisely why the contact-map pipeline caps inputs at 160 residues.

| Artifact | Shape (per protein) | Dtype | Size @ L=160 | Size @ L=1022 | Producer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Raw attention tensor | (33, 20, L_pad, L_pad) | float32 | ~68 MB | ~2.8 GB | [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L54-L66) |
| Categorical Jacobian | (L, 20, L, 20) | float64 | ~82 MB | ~3.3 GB | [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L57-L74) |
| Contact map | (L, L) | float64 | ~0.2 MB | ~8.4 MB | [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L76-L86) |
| Attention rollout | (L, L) | float32 | ~0.1 MB | ~4.2 MB | [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L156-L218) |
| Mean-pooled embedding | (1280,) | float32 | ~0.5 KB | ~5.1 KB | [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L419-L423) |

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L45-L57), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L95-L107)

The architecture follows directly from this table: the pipeline never holds the full corpus of attention matrices in memory. Instead, each stage produces a *derived, compressed artifact* that downstream stages consume in bounded slices — the full-attention tensors (gigabytes per protein) exist only transiently and are reduced to rollouts and per-head statistics (megabytes) before any cross-protein analysis runs.

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L38-L56), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L350-L386)

## The Five-Stage Memory Lifecycle

All heavy scripts converge on the same five-stage discipline, executed once per batch: (1) tokenize under a budget, (2) forward under `torch.no_grad()`, (3) demote results from GPU to host, (4) unbind and collect, and (5) persist in chunks. The extraction script is the canonical implementation — every line of the loop maps to one stage of the lifecycle.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Stage 1: Budget-bound batching<br/>batch_size=2 · tokens_per_batch · chunk_size"] --> B["Stage 2: Inference-mode forward<br/>torch.no_grad() · model.eval()"]
    B --> C["Stage 3: Device demotion<br/>.cpu().numpy() · .to('cpu')"]
    C --> D["Stage 4: Deallocation<br/>del + empty_cache() · gc.collect()"]
    D --> E{"Buffer ≥ save_interval?"}
    E -- "No: next batch" --> A
    E -- "Yes" --> F["Stage 5: Chunked persistence<br/>joblib.dump(compress=3) · CSV append"]
    F --> A
```

This lifecycle is *composable*: the rollout stage re-enters it at stage 1 with joblib chunks as its input budget, and the MLP training loop applies a variant of it with a `DataLoader` over precomputed embeddings. The invariant across all instantiations is that no single stage ever materializes more than one batch's worth of unreduced GPU state.

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L47-L87), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L36-L54)

## GPU-Side Budgeting: The Four Knobs

The repository controls peak GPU memory through four independent knobs, each tuned to its workload's tensor shape. The extraction script fixes a sequence-count budget (`batch_size = 2` — annotated "Or whatever fits your memory budget") because attention tensors scale with the *longest* sequence in the batch. Embedding extraction instead uses a *token-count* budget (`tokens_per_batch`) via `FastaBatchedDataset.get_batch_indices`, which packs length-sorted sequences into batches of bounded total tokens — far more efficient when the corpus has mixed lengths. The Jacobian stage adds a third knob, `chunk_size`, that bounds how many mutated copies of a sequence enter one forward pass. The ablation sweep raises the token budget to 8192 because its per-protein output is only a mean-pooled 1280-dim vector, leaving ample headroom.

| Knob | Value(s) | Location | Bounds what |
|---|---|---|---|
| `batch_size` | 2 sequences | [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L45) | (33, 20, L_pad, L_pad) attention tensors |
| `tokens_per_batch` | 4096 / 8192 tokens | [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L383-L401), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L22) | transformer activations during embedding forward passes |
| `chunk_size` | 150 positions | [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L57) | mutated-copy batches for Jacobian computation |
| Input length caps | ≤ 160 (Jacobian) · 1022 (embeddings) · 1024 (perplexity) | [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L95-L107), [rg_mlp.py](scripts/rg_mlp.py#L32-L44), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L43-L68) | asymptotic size of every derived tensor |

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L401-L408), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L296-L318)

### Case Study: Chunking the Categorical Jacobian

The contact-map script contains a documented evolution from a memory-naive to a memory-aware implementation, and the delta illustrates the chunked-compute pattern in its purest form. The original `get_categorical_jacobian` tiles the tokenized sequence into 20 copies and loops over every residue position, issuing **one forward pass per position** — L sequential GPU round-trips, each cloning the tiled input. The optimized `get_categorical_jacobian_ln(seq, chunk_size=150)` instead precomputes wild-type logits once, then for each chunk constructs a (chunk_len × 20)-sequence batch via `x.repeat(chunk_len * 20, 1)` and scatters all point mutations simultaneously using advanced indexing before a single forward pass, reshaping the logits back into the preallocated host array `fx_h`.

| | Original `get_categorical_jacobian` | Optimized `get_categorical_jacobian_ln` |
|---|---|---|
| Forward passes per protein | L (one per residue) | ⌈L / 150⌉ |
| Peak GPU batch | 20 sequences × L passes | chunk_len × 20 sequences, transient |
| Host array | grown per-position (`fx_h[n] = f(x_h)`) | preallocated once, filled per-chunk |
| Transfer pattern | repeated small CPU↔GPU round-trips | one block per chunk: `.detach().cpu().numpy().reshape(chunk_len, 20, ln, 20)` |

> [!TIP]
> The chunked Jacobian is a deliberate memory-throughput trade: it reduces passes from L to ⌈L/150⌉ but inflates the transient GPU batch to 3,000 padded sequences per chunk (~486,000 tokens for L=160). Raising `chunk_size` beyond 150 trades host-array fill efficiency for quadratic activation growth inside the 33-layer forward pass — the default is the sweet spot for the pipeline's ≤160-residue cap.

Sources: [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L33-L54), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L56-L74)

## Host-Side Hygiene: Demotion, Unbinding, and Collection

Once a batch's results exist, the pipeline moves them off the GPU immediately and never round-trips them back. Demotion is consistently expressed as `.cpu().numpy()` (attention slices, Jacobian chunks, wild-type logits) or `.to("cpu")` (per-layer representations), so the GPU frees its copy at the earliest possible moment and only plain NumPy arrays accumulate on the host. Extraction of scalar results follows the same principle — the perplexity script collapses the masked-LM loss via `outputs.loss.item()` inside `torch.no_grad()`, releasing the graph-free tensor as soon as the float is extracted.

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L61-L66), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L60-L72), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L409-L417), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L64-L68)

Deallocation is performed in three complementary layers, because PyTorch's caching allocator and Python's cyclic GC each hold memory the others cannot see. First, explicit `del` unbinds batch-scope names (`results`, `attentions`, `batch_tokens`, and per-iteration objects like `traj`, `jac`, `md_df`). Second, `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` returns the freed blocks to the CUDA driver rather than hoarding them in PyTorch's cache. Third, `gc.collect()` runs at chunk boundaries — after joblib dumps, and crucially inside `safe_load`, which wraps every joblib load in the streaming consumers so that garbage from the *previous* chunk is swept before the next multi-gigabyte file is read.

| Layer | API | Scope of effect | Where used |
|---|---|---|---|
| Name unbinding | `del obj` | drops last reference → frees host tensor | [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L263-L270), [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L49-L54) |
| Allocator release | `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` | returns cached GPU blocks to driver | [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L74) |
| Cycle collection | `gc.collect()` | breaks reference cycles across interpreter | [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L82), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L249-L253) |

> [!TIP]
> The extraction script's deletion loop iterates `for obj in [...]: del locals()[obj]`. This only works because the script runs at *module scope*, where `locals()` returns the live module `__dict__` (i.e., globals) — deletion genuinely unbinds the name. Inside a function body, `locals()` returns a snapshot dict and this idiom would silently free nothing; use plain `del name` statements there instead.

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L70-L82), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L263-L276), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L249-L253)

## Chunked Persistence and Streaming Consumers

Because no single process can hold the corpus, persistence itself is chunked at production time: the extraction script flushes its in-memory `all_results` dictionary to `attention_matrices_chunks/attention_matrices_labeled_{n}_original.joblib` (with `compress=3` — essential, since a chunk of 200 full-length proteins would occupy hundreds of gigabytes uncompressed) every `save_interval = 200` proteins, then resets the buffer and increments the chunk counter. The contact-map pipeline applies the same idea to tabular results with `save_every = 500`: correlation rows and upper-triangle contact frames are appended to per-batch CSVs with explicit header/mode logic, then the buffers are `.clear()`ed so Python's small-object arenas stay bounded.

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L42-L43), [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L76-L87), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L240-L262)

The chunk layout defines the consumption contract for every downstream stage. `get_esm2_attention_rollout.py` iterates `range(0, 22)` — 22 chunks × 200 proteins ≈ 4,400 proteins — loading exactly one joblib file at a time through `safe_load`, converting each protein's matrix to a CPU tensor, computing its (L, L) rollout, and deleting per-protein and per-chunk references as it goes. The result shrinks the corpus from gigabytes-per-protein to megabytes-per-protein, which is why the final combined rollout file can be loaded in one shot by the figure-generation stage. Per-head amino-acid statistics follow the identical streaming protocol over the same chunks, deleting both the loaded chunk and each of the 33 × 20 = 660 per-head slices as they are consumed.

```mermaid
graph LR
    A["get_esm2_attention_matrices.py"] -- "joblib chunks ×22<br/>(33,20,L,L) per protein" --> S[("attention_matrices_chunks/")]
    A -- "incremental CSVs<br/>save_every=500" --> C2[("jacobian correlation CSVs")]
    B["get_contact_maps.py"] -- "flushes" --> C2
    S -- "safe_load 1 chunk at a time" --> C["get_esm2_attention_rollout.py"]
    S -- "safe_load 1 chunk at a time" --> D["run_aa_analysis_head_layer<br/>(attention_functions.py)"]
    C -- "combined rollout joblib<br/>(L,L) per protein" --> R[("attention_rollout_comb_original.joblib")]
    R --> E["attention_rollout_analysis.py"]
    D -- "precomputed CSV" --> F["es_ablation2.py"]
    E -- "embeddings via<br/>get_esm2_embeddings" --> A2["rg_mlp.py"]
```

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_rollout.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_rollout.py#L36-L56), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L362-L386), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L39-L40)

Two supporting hygiene practices complete the picture. Embedding extraction writes sequences to a `NamedTemporaryFile` FASTA and removes it in a `try/finally` block, and the contact-map script deletes downloaded trajectory temp files immediately after `md.load` — so scratch storage, like tensors, follows a strict allocate-consume-release lifecycle. Meanwhile, the rollout math itself defaults to `device='cpu'`, keeping 33 sequential L×L matmuls off the GPU entirely; since rollout output is two orders of magnitude smaller than its input, this placement avoids competing with the extraction job's GPU budget.

Sources: [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L383-L401), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L421-L426), [attention_functions.py](scripts/attention_functions.py#L156-L218)

## Pattern Trade-offs

The four memory patterns are not interchangeable — each buys bounded memory by spending something else, and the pipeline's correctness depends on pairing each workload with the right pattern. Understanding the exchange rates below is what allows the knobs in the table earlier to be retuned safely on different hardware.

| Pattern | Buys | Costs | Failure mode if abused |
|---|---|---|---|
| Budget-bound batching (`batch_size`, `tokens_per_batch`) | O(batch) peak GPU memory | launch overhead per small batch | OOM on long-sequence batches if budget raised blindly |
| Chunked compute (`chunk_size=150`) | bounded transient Jacobian batch | redundant prefix computations per chunk; repeated host↔GPU transfers | activation blow-up if chunk exceeds forward-pass capacity |
| Chunked persistence (`save_interval=200`, `compress=3`) | recovery points; bounded resident corpus | CPU compression time; N-file load orchestration downstream | RAM exhaustion if consumers load all chunks eagerly |
| Eager demotion + `del`/`empty_cache`/`gc.collect()` | earliest-possible release on both devices | minor CPU-sync latency; code verbosity | stale references keep GPU blocks cached after "freeing" |

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L45-L87), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L56-L74)

## Tuning Guidance and Pitfalls

When porting this pipeline to new hardware, retune in a fixed order: start with the input length caps (they set asymptotic bounds no other knob can recover), then the batch/token budgets (verify against the GPU memory the script itself prints at startup), and only then the chunk intervals (they trade RAM against file count). Three pitfalls recur in practice. First, watch *padded* length, not sequence length — attention tensors are sized by the batch's padded dimension, so one 1022-residue protein dominates a batch's cost regardless of its partner. Second, respect dtype: the Jacobian array is NumPy float64 by default, doubling every footprint in the arithmetic table, while PyTorch outputs are float32. Third, remember that `np.copy` guards in `do_apc`/`get_contacts` and the `args[0].clone()` in ablation hooks are deliberate — in-place aliasing across those transformations would silently corrupt downstream statistics.

The natural next readings are [Attention Head Ablation Study](18-attention-head-ablation-study) for how hook-based mutation interacts with this budget (the `try/finally` around every ablated forward pass guarantees hook cleanup even when a pass OOMs), and [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility) for why the ablation sweep consumes a precomputed attention CSV rather than re-running the 660-slice-per-protein analysis live.

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L19-L32), [get_contact_maps.py](scripts/get_contact_maps.py#L76-L86), [es_ablation2.py](scripts/es_ablation2.py#L296-L318)

## Where to Go Next

This page covered the *how* of memory-bound engineering; the *what* and *why* live elsewhere in the catalog. For the scientific content flowing through these tensors, proceed to [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction) and [Attention Rollout Algorithm](9-attention-rollout-algorithm), then [Categorical Jacobian Contact Maps](14-categorical-jacobian-contact-maps) and [MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor) for the two consumers that define the Jacobian and embedding memory contracts. For the adjacent engineering practice of keeping the corpus lean in the first place — which directly reduces the number of chunks the lifecycle must process — see [Dataset Curation and CD-HIT Clustering](21-dataset-curation-and-cd-hit-clustering).

# Dataset Curation and CD-HIT Clustering



This page explains the engineering practices that turn raw database dumps into statistically defensible input sets for the `plm_interp` analyses. It covers two coupled mechanisms: **rule-based dataset curation** in `define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py` (deduplication, length filtering, length-distribution matching) and **sequence-similarity clustering via CD-HIT**, which is executed externally and whose `.clstr` output files drive leakage-safe, cluster-grouped train/test splits in the attention, Rg prediction, and ablation pipelines. For how the curated sequences feed into embeddings and attention extraction, see [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction); for the raw-download mechanics, see [External Data Acquisition](3-external-data-acquisition).

## Why Curation Exists: The Homology Leakage Problem

Both protein databases used in this repo are *living databases*: PDB sequences are updated weekly and DisProt has no version-pinned URL, so a download performed today will not match the July 2025 snapshots used in the paper. The repo's answer is to commit the **derived** sequence files (`data/protein_input_sets.csv`, `data/pdb_disprot.fasta`, `data/clustered_input.fasta`, `data/clustered_input.fasta.clstr`) so that reproduction never depends on re-deriving from a moving target. The curation scripts remain in the repo so you can audit every transformation between the raw dump and the committed artifact.

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](/scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L8-L27), [README.md](/README.md#L55-L66)

The second motivation is subtler: protein databases are full of near-duplicate homologs, fragments, and isoforms. If two 95%-identical sequences land one in training and one in testing, a model or statistical test can score well by memorizing family-level signatures rather than learning generalizable structure. CD-HIT clustering at a **40% sequence identity threshold** partitions sequences into homolog families, and those cluster labels become the *grouping key* for every split in the repo — sequences from the same cluster are never separated across a split boundary.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](/scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L168-L177), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L190-L203)

## Stage 1: Rule-Based Curation in `define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py`

The curation script applies a parallel filter chain to the disordered (DisProt) and ordered (PDB) sets so that downstream group comparisons are not confounded by trivial artifacts. DisProt sequences are loaded via the `read_fasta` helper, deduplicated on the exact sequence string, and restricted to the 50–1023 residue window (1024 is ESM-2's positional limit including special tokens). The PDB branch adds one extra rule: sequences containing ambiguous or non-canonical residues (`X`, `U`, `O`) are dropped, since these tokens are unrepresentable in ESM-2's vocabulary.

| Filter | DisProt branch | PDB branch |
|---|---|---|
| Source | `data/disprot.fasta` (release 2025_06) | `pdb_seqres.txt.gz` (RCSB derived data) |
| Deduplication | `drop_duplicates(subset='Sequence')` | `drop_duplicates(subset='sequence')` |
| Length window | `50 < seq_len < 1024` | `50 < seq_len < 1024` |
| Residue alphabet | — | Drop sequences matching `X\|U\|O` |
| Group label | `'Disprot'` | `'PDB'` |

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](/scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L16-L35), [attention_functions.py](/scripts/attention_functions.py#L28-L37)

The most consequential step is **length-distribution matching**. Disordered proteins skew long, so a naive comparison of PDB vs DisProt attention could just be measuring sequence-length effects. The script bins DisProt lengths into 20 equal-width bins spanning the DisProt range, assigns each PDB sequence to a bin via `np.digitize`, then subsamples PDB per bin — sampling with `random_state=42` when supply exceeds demand, taking all candidates otherwise — until the ordered set mirrors the disordered length histogram. Every curated sequence then receives a synthetic identifier (`disprot_protein{i}` / `pdb_protein{i}`) that permanently replaces database IDs; all later scripts and outputs key off these `ProteinID` strings.

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](/scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L37-L64)

> [!TIP]
> The length-matching loop iterates over `bin_counts.items()` — the *DisProt* bin occupancy — not the PDB bins. This asymmetry is deliberate: DisProt defines the target distribution, PDB is subsampled to match it, so any cross-group difference in attention statistics cannot be explained by length composition.

## Stage 2: External CD-HIT Clustering and the `.clstr` Contract

CD-HIT is never invoked from Python — both pipelines write a plain FASTA file, pause with a comment showing the exact shell command, and expect the operator to run it externally. The PDB/DisProt branch writes `data/pdb_disprot.fasta` inside `attention_rollout_analysis.py`; the IDRome branch writes `data/idrome.fasta` inside `rg_mlp.py`. Both use identical parameters: `-c 0.40` (identity threshold) and `-n 2` (word size).

| Invocation site | Input FASTA | Cluster output | Command |
|---|---|---|---|
| `attention_rollout_analysis.py` | `data/pdb_disprot.fasta` | `data/clustered_input.fasta` + `.clstr` | `cd-hit -i pdb_disprot.fasta -o clustered_input.fasta -c 0.40 -n 2` |
| `rg_mlp.py` | `data/idrome.fasta` | `data/idrome_clustered.fasta` + `.clstr` | `cd-hit -i idrome.fasta -o idrome_clustered.fasta -c 0.4 -n 2` |

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](/scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L139-L147), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L161-L165)

The Python side consumes only the `.clstr` file, and the parsing logic (duplicated verbatim in three scripts) encodes CD-HIT's output grammar: a `>Cluster N` header switches the current cluster, then each member line carries the member index, its length in `aa`, the FASTA ID wrapped in `>` and `...`, and either `*` for the cluster representative or `at XX.XX%` for the identity to that representative. The parser extracts the ID by splitting on whitespace, stripping the leading `>` and trailing `...`, and builds a flat `seq_id → cluster` dictionary.

| `.clstr` line fragment | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `>Cluster 7` | Cluster identifier header |
| `2    956aa, >disprot_protein1124... *` | Representative (centroid) sequence, 956 aa |
| `1    162aa, >disprot_protein1967... at 43.21%` | Member at 43.21% identity to representative |
| `1    405aa, >disprot_protein1123... at 100.00%` | Member identical over the aligned region |

Sources: [clustered_input.fasta.clstr](/data/clustered_input.fasta.clstr#L1-L40), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](/scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L150-L163)

> [!TIP]
> Although `define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py` already deduplicated exact sequences, the committed `.clstr` still contains members at `100.00%` — these are sequences identical over a shared region but of different lengths (e.g., a 69 aa fragment inside a 929 aa protein). The 40% threshold is precisely what catches these containment relationships that exact-string dedup cannot.

> [!TIP]
> The `-n 2` word size is not optional tuning: CD-HIT's documentation requires word size 2 for identity thresholds in the 40–50% band. Using the default `-n 5` (for ≥80% thresholds) at 40% identity would shatter clusters and silently reintroduce homolog leakage into every grouped split downstream.

## Stage 3: Cluster Labels as Grouping Keys in Downstream Splits

Three independent analyses consume the cluster dictionaries, each translating them into a different scikit-learn grouping strategy:

| Consumer script | Cluster file | Split mechanism | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `attention_rollout_analysis.py` | `clustered_input.fasta.clstr` | `GroupKFold(n_splits=5)` with `groups=cluster` | Leakage-safe 5-fold CV for the ordered-vs-disordered logistic classifier |
| `rg_mlp.py` | `idrome_clustered.fasta.clstr` | Two nested `GroupShuffleSplit`s (80/20, then 90/10) | Cluster-disjoint train/val/test for the Rg MLP |
| `es_ablation2.py` | `idrome_clustered.fasta.clstr` | `GroupShuffleSplit(test_size=0.2)` | Cluster-disjoint hold-out set for head-ablation evaluation |

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](/scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L165-L177), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L166-L199), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L93-L116)

In the attention analysis, the parsed clusters are merged back onto the embedding frame via `ProteinID` and cast to integers, then passed as the `groups` argument to `cross_val_score` with `GroupKFold` — the printed summary explicitly reports accuracy "over N clusters" to make the effective sample size transparent. In the Rg pipeline, the same cluster column feeds a two-stage split: an outer 80/20 train-holdout split followed by an inner 90/10 train-validation split, both grouped by cluster, so no homolog family ever straddles a boundary while the MLP trains on mean-pooled ESM-2 embeddings.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](/scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L165-L177), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L185-L203)

## The Full Curation-to-Clustering Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph RAW["Living database snapshots (July 2025)"]
        DP["data/disprot.fasta<br/>DisProt release 2025_06"]
        PDB["pdb_seqres.txt.gz<br/>RCSB PDB"]
    end

    subgraph CURATE["define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py"]
        D1["Dedup + 50 ≤ len < 1024"] --> D2["Length-bin subsample<br/>20 bins · seed 42<br/>PDB matches DisProt histogram"]
    end

    DP --> D1
    PDB --> D1
    D2 --> CSV["data/protein_input_sets.csv<br/>Sequence · ProteinID"]

    CSV --> FA1["attention_rollout_analysis.py<br/>writes data/pdb_disprot.fasta"]
    FA1 --> CH1["Shell: cd-hit -c 0.40 -n 2"]
    CH1 --> C1["data/clustered_input.fasta.clstr"]
    C1 --> CV["GroupKFold(5) · cluster-grouped CV"]

    IDR["IDRome DB + Supplementary Table 3"] --> FA2["rg_mlp.py<br/>writes data/idrome.fasta"]
    FA2 --> CH2["Shell: cd-hit -c 0.4 -n 2"]
    CH2 --> C2["data/idrome_clustered.fasta.clstr"]
    C2 --> SPL["GroupShuffleSplit · rg_mlp.py<br/>GroupShuffleSplit · es_ablation2.py"]
```

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](/scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L16-L64), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](/scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L139-L177), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L156-L199)

## Re-running Curation Versus Using the Committed Sets

Because the raw sources drift weekly, the repo supports two workflows. To reproduce paper numbers, skip `define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py` entirely and use the committed derived files (`data/protein_input_sets.csv`, `data/pdb_disprot.fasta`, both `.clstr` files) — this is the default path, and `clinvar_expanded.py` exposes the analogous `derived=True` flag for its dataset. To refresh the datasets against current database contents, download the raw dumps via `esm2_interp_data.py`, re-run curation, re-run CD-HIT with the documented parameters, and commit the new derived artifacts as a snapshot. The trade-off between these modes — and the snapshot-vs-live decision framework — is treated in depth in [Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility](22-derived-versus-live-data-reproducibility).

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](/scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L20-L34), [esm2_interp_data.py](/scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L240-L246), [README.md](/README.md#L25-L29)

## Where to Go Next

The curated, clustered sets are the substrate for every analysis in this repo: the attention matrices are extracted from `protein_input_sets.csv` in [Attention Matrix Extraction](8-attention-matrix-extraction); the cluster-grouped classifier that consumes `clustered_input.fasta.clstr` is analyzed in [Ordered Versus Disordered Comparison](12-ordered-versus-disordered-comparison); the cluster-split Rg MLP is detailed in [MLP Radius of Gyration Predictor](17-mlp-radius-of-gyration-predictor), with its cluster-hold-out evaluation extended in [Attention Head Ablation Study](18-attention-head-ablation-study).

# Derived Versus Live Data Reproducibility



Every scientific repository faces a tension: committing data makes results reproducible but bloats the repository, while fetching data live keeps the repo lean but exposes results to upstream drift. `plm_interp` resolves this tension with an explicit, two-regime architecture: **derived snapshots** are frozen into the repo at filter boundaries, while everything downstream of expensive GPU compute or unstable external sources remains **live** and must be recomputed. This page explains how that split is implemented, where the runtime switch points live, and how to choose the correct reproduction path for your goals.

## The Two Data Regimes

The repository's `data/` directory serves a dual role, stated directly in the README: it holds raw data inputs to analyses *as well as* summary data generated by scripts. The critical architectural insight is that not all committed files are equal — some are **frozen provenance snapshots** (the exact filtered sequences used in the paper), some are **staging buffers** for runtime intermediates, and some raw inputs only materialize after running the download orchestrator. Meanwhile, the highest-volume artifacts — attention matrices serialized as joblib chunks — are categorically excluded from version control and must be regenerated on GPU hardware.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L18-L19), [README.md](/README.md#L29-L34), [README.md](/README.md#L44-L46)

The codebase organizes every data artifact into one of four tiers, each with distinct guarantees:

| Tier | Examples | Committed? | Reproducibility guarantee |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Frozen derived snapshot** | `protein_input_sets.csv`, `clinvar_sequences.csv`, `pdb_disprot.fasta`, `idrome_clustered.fasta.clstr` | Yes | Byte-identical inputs to the paper |
| **Raw external source** | `variant_summary.txt.gz`, `pdb_seqres.txt.gz`, `Supplementary_Table_3.xlsx` | No | Drifts with upstream updates (weekly for PDB/ClinVar) |
| **Live compute output** | `attention_matrices_chunks/*.joblib`, `mlp_final.pt` | No | Deterministic given seeds + fixed inputs, but requires GPU re-run |
| **Runtime intermediate** | `data/figure_data/*.csv`, `data/idrome.fasta` | No | Regenerated by analysis scripts before figure rendering |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L18-L19), [esm2_interp_data.py](/scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L2-L34), [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](/scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L76-L78)

## The Derivation Dependency Graph

Understanding reproducibility in this repo means understanding the direction of data flow. Raw external databases flow through **derivation scripts** (filtering, length-binning, clustering) to produce the committed snapshots; the snapshots then flow into **analysis scripts**, which consume both committed inputs and live-computed tensors to emit the runtime intermediates that `figures.py` finally renders. Notice the asymmetry: attention matrices flow from live compute *sideways* into analysis, never through a committed boundary.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Living external databases (drift risk)"
        PDB["RCSB pdb_seqres.txt.gz<br/>updated weekly"]
        CLINVAR["ClinVar variant_summary.txt.gz<br/>updated weekly"]
        IDROME["IDRome_DB.csv<br/>fetched from URL at runtime"]
    end

    subgraph "Derivation scripts (one-time, frozen)"
        D1["define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py<br/>filter + length-bin subsample"]
        D2["clinvar_expanded.py (derived=False)"]
        D3["CD-HIT -c 0.4 (external tool)"]
    end

    subgraph "Committed derived snapshots (data/)"
        S1["protein_input_sets.csv"]
        S2["clinvar_sequences.csv"]
        S3["idrome_clustered.fasta.clstr"]
    end

    subgraph "Live GPU compute (not committed)"
        L1["get_esm2_attention_matrices.py<br/>→ attention_matrices_chunks/*.joblib"]
        L2["attention_rollout_analysis.py<br/>→ data/figure_data/*.csv"]
    end

    PDB --> D1
    D1 --> S1
    CLINVAR --> D2
    D2 --> S2
    IDROME --> D3
    D3 --> S3
    S1 --> L1
    S1 --> L2
    S2 --> L2
    S3 --> L2
    L1 -.->|"joblib.load"| L2
    L2 --> FIG["figures.py<br/>reads only figure_data/*.csv"]
```

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](/scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L16-L64), [clinvar_expanded.py](/scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L63-L137), [attention_rollout_analysis.py](/scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L36-L101), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L56-L145)

The cleanest illustration of this separation is the figure-rendering stage: `figures.py` contains no computation of scientific quantities at all. It reads pre-aggregated CSVs from `data/figure_data/` (`umap_df.csv` at line 60, `disorder_comp_concat.csv` at line 89, `si_examples.csv` at line 113, `mean_aa_attn.csv` at line 142) and handles only matplotlib layout. This means the expensive, nondeterminism-prone pipeline can be separated from the cheap, purely deterministic figure assembly.

Sources: [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L56-L145)

> [!TIP]
> Notice that `data/figure_data/` does not appear in the repository tree — it is created by `attention_rollout_analysis.py` at runtime. If you clone the repo and run `figures.py` directly, it will fail. The correct order is: run the analysis scripts first (they write the intermediates), then render figures.

## The `derived` Flag: A Runtime Switch Between Regimes

The ClinVar pipeline implements the derived-versus-live boundary as an explicit boolean at the top of the script. When `derived = True`, the script skips all gathering and filtering and simply loads the committed snapshot; when `derived = False`, it reads raw external downloads (`variant_summary.txt.gz`, `gene2refseq`, `GRCh38_latest_protein_copy.faa`), applies the full filtering cascade — single nucleotide variants only, pathogenic classifications only, length bounds of 50–1024 residues, ambiguity-character exclusion, and genes mapping to multiple sequences — and then **overwrites** `data/clinvar_sequences.csv` with the freshly derived set.

Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](/scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L20-L22), [clinvar_expanded.py](/scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L63-L137)

| Aspect | `derived = False` (live) | `derived = True` (frozen) |
|---|---|---|
| Input | Raw NCBI downloads in `data/` | `data/clinvar_sequences.csv` (committed) |
| Compute cost | Full filter cascade (~6 stages) | Single CSV read |
| Output stability | Matches today's ClinVar release | Matches paper exactly |
| Side effect | Overwrites committed snapshot | Read-only |
| Use case | Extending the study to new data | Exact paper reproduction |

Sources: [clinvar_expanded.py](/scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L20-L22), [clinvar_expanded.py](/scripts/clinvar_expanded.py#L63-L137)

The PDB/DisProt pipeline encodes the same choice structurally rather than via a flag. `define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py` is the *only* producer of `data/protein_input_sets.csv`: it deduplicates both sources, applies the same 50–1024 length bounds, excludes ambiguous residues from PDB, then performs the scientifically critical step — subsampling ordered proteins per length bin so that the PDB set mirrors the DisProt length distribution, using `random_state=42` for reproducible sampling. The docstring-level contract in `esm2_interp_data.py` states that if you wish to reproduce the paper, you skip this script entirely and use the committed snapshot instead.

Sources: [define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py](/scripts/define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py#L16-L59), [esm2_interp_data.py](/scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L20-L27)

## Living Databases and the Snapshot Policy

The download orchestrator opens with a blunt warning: five of its sources are "living databases with no version pinned in the URL," and files downloaded today *will* differ from those used in the study. PDB and ClinVar update weekly; `GRCh38_latest` is explicitly not version-pinned; DisProt is release-based. The script documents an access date for each source (PDB: July 16, 2025; ClinVar/gene2refseq/GRCh38: Feb 3, 2026; DisProt: July 28, 2025) and annotates which committed derived file each raw download feeds into.

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](/scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L8-L34), [esm2_interp_data.py](/scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L120-L151)

| Source | Update cadence | Snapshot date | Committed fallback |
|---|---|---|---|
| PDB sequences | Weekly | July 16, 2025 | `protein_input_sets.csv`, `pdb_disprot.fasta` |
| ClinVar | Weekly | Feb 3, 2026 | `clinvar_sequences.csv` |
| gene2refseq | Regular | Feb 3, 2026 | embedded in `clinvar_sequences.csv` (via NM→NP mapping already resolved) |
| GRCh38 latest protein | Not version-pinned | Feb 3, 2026 | embedded in `clinvar_sequences.csv` |
| DisProt | Release-based | release 2025_06 | `disprot.fasta`, `protein_input_sets.csv` |
| IDRome Supplementary Table 3 | Static | stable | — (fetched fresh, deemed safe) |
| STARLING/SAXS CSV | Static | stable | — (fetched fresh, deemed safe) |

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](/scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L38-L76), [esm2_interp_data.py](/scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L193-L214)

The main block of the orchestrator encodes this risk assessment as executable policy: the four volatile downloaders (`download_pdb`, `download_clinvar`, `download_gene2refseq`, `download_grch38`) are **commented out**, while the two stable ones (`download_idrome_supplementary`, `download_starling`) run by default. This means a default invocation of `python scripts/esm2_interp_data.py` only fetches data whose drift risk is negligible, and deliberately does not tempt you into silently replacing the frozen snapshots.

Sources: [esm2_interp_data.py](/scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L219-L233)

> [!TIP]
> One residual live dependency survives the snapshot policy: both `rg_mlp.py` (line 156) and `es_ablation2.py` (line 89) fetch `IDRome_DB.csv` directly from a GitHub raw URL at runtime, with no caching or committed copy. Because this URL serves a versioned research dataset from the KULL-Centre repo it is treated as stable, but if it ever moves, the Rg pipeline breaks at data-load time — the failure mode is immediate and obvious rather than silent.

## Determinism Controls for Live Compute

For the tier of data that *must* be recomputed, the repository applies a layered determinism strategy. The most voluminous live artifact — attention rollout for the full input set — is produced by `get_esm2_attention_matrices.py` from the committed `protein_input_sets.csv` and serialized in 200-protein chunks. Since ESM-2 inference in `eval()` mode is deterministic for fixed weights and inputs, and the input set is frozen, re-running this step on the same hardware class converges to the same tensors.

Sources: [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](/scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L34-L55), [get_esm2_attention_matrices.py](/scripts/get_esm2_attention_matrices.py#L76-L80)

Downstream of model inference, every nondeterministic consumer pins its random state explicitly. `attention_rollout_analysis.py` sets `SEED = 42` across `random`, `numpy`, and `torch` (CPU and all CUDA devices), and additionally disables cuDNN autotuning and TF32 matmuls before UMAP and downstream statistics — the operations whose results genuinely vary run-to-run without these guards. `rg_mlp.py` applies the identical seed block at import time and threads `random_state=SEED` into both `GroupShuffleSplit` calls, ensuring the cluster-grouped train/val/test partition is stable. `esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py` goes one level finer, re-seeding inside the per-sequence perplexity function because masked-LM perplexity involves stochastic masking.

Sources: [attention_rollout_analysis.py](/scripts/attention_rollout_analysis.py#L72-L80), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L51-L56), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L190-L199), [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](/scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L40-L42)

Two further pinning mechanisms protect against *silent* rather than *statistical* drift. The perplexity script loads ESM-2 weights from Hugging Face with `local_files_only=True`, refusing to pull a potentially-updated checkpoint from the hub; and `es_ablation2.py` consumes the Rg predictor not by retraining but by loading the committed `mlp_final.pt` state dict — meaning the trained model itself is treated as a frozen derived artifact, with training weights persisted by `rg_mlp.py` whenever validation loss improves.

Sources: [esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py](/scripts/esm2_ppl_by_disorder.py#L24-L29), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L79-L82), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L285-L288)

## Choosing Your Reproduction Path

The README's "Reproducing Results" table distills all of this into per-figure command chains. Interpreting those chains through the derived-versus-live lens clarifies what each command actually contributes: the Figure 3 chain begins with `esm2_interp_data.py` only because the ClinVar conservation regression needs the manually-provided `9606_database.json`; the Figure 5 chain needs it only for the two static downloads. The committed snapshots short-circuit the volatile stages in both chains.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L66-L84), [esm2_interp_data.py](/scripts/esm2_interp_data.py#L237-L247)

| Your goal | Strategy | What you run | What you skip |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reproduce paper figures exactly | Frozen path | Analysis scripts reading committed snapshots | `define_pdb_disprot_datasets.py`, `clinvar_expanded.py` re-derivation, raw DB downloads |
| Re-derive from current databases | Live path | `esm2_interp_data.py` (uncomment volatile downloaders) → derivation scripts with `derived = False` | Expect results to differ from the paper |
| Reproduce attention analyses | Live compute + frozen inputs | `get_esm2_attention_matrices.py` → `get_esm2_attention_rollout.py` → `attention_rollout_analysis.py` | Nothing (GPU required; matrices never committed) |
| Render figures from existing analysis | Intermediate path | `figures.py` alone | All analysis — but only if `data/figure_data/` already exists on your machine |
| Retrain Rg predictor | Live compute + frozen clusters | `rg_mlp.py` (re-saves `mlp_final.pt`) → `es_ablation2.py` | CD-HIT clustering (committed `.clstr` file is read, not regenerated) |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L66-L84), [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L161-L167), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L56-L145)

One subtlety deserves emphasis: running `rg_mlp.py` regenerates `data/idrome.fasta` on every invocation and expects the CD-HIT output `idrome_clustered.fasta.clstr` to already exist — the script documents the exact external command (`cd-hit -i idrome.fasta -o idrome_clustered.fasta -c 0.4 -n 2`) in a comment but deliberately does not shell out to it. External binary-tool artifacts are frozen into the repo rather than re-executed, because tool version differences would alter clusters and thus the grouped train/test splits.

Sources: [rg_mlp.py](/scripts/rg_mlp.py#L161-L167)

This tiered design trades repository size for a precise, documented reproducibility contract: sequences are frozen because they define *what was studied*, model checkpoints are frozen because they define *what was learned*, and everything voluminous or upstream-volatile is recomputed under explicit seed control. To understand how these inputs were constructed in detail, continue to [Dataset Curation and CD-HIT Clustering](21-dataset-curation-and-cd-hit-clustering); for the mechanics of regenerating the largest live artifacts, see [Large Tensor Memory Management](20-large-tensor-memory-management); for how the derived intermediates become publication-ready visuals, see [Publication Figure Styling](23-publication-figure-styling).

# Publication Figure Styling



This page explains how `plm_interp` turns raw analysis numbers into journal-ready vector figures. The entire styling system lives in two places: a 15-line matplotlib style sheet at the repository root (`publication.mplstyle`) and a short "theme" block at the top of `scripts/figures.py` that loads it and adds project-specific conventions. Everything downstream — every panel in the paper — inherits from these two files, so if you are a beginner, understanding them is the fastest way to make your own plots look identical to the published ones. We will cover the theming architecture, the color strategy, a millimeter-based panel sizing system, layout discipline for fixed canvases, vector output conventions, and finally a step-by-step recipe for building a new figure.

Sources: [publication.mplstyle](/publication.mplstyle#L1-L15), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L22-L53)

## Why a Separate Styling Layer Exists

The repository follows a strict separation between **analysis** and **presentation**. Analysis scripts (for example `es_ablation2.py` and `rg_mlp.py`) compute statistics and write tidy CSV files into `data/figure_data/`; they import matplotlib but never load the style sheet and never produce final artwork. Only `figures.py` reads those CSVs, applies the shared theme, and writes SVGs into `figures/final/`. This means the look of every paper figure is controlled in exactly one file — change the theme once, and every figure changes with it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Analysis scripts<br/>(es_ablation2.py, rg_mlp.py, ...)"] -->|write CSVs| B["data/figure_data/*.csv"]
    B -->|pd.read_csv| C["figures.py"]
    D["publication.mplstyle<br/>(15 rcParams)"] -->|plt.style.use| C
    E["Code-level overrides<br/>(color cycle, svg.fonttype)"] -->|rcParams| C
    C -->|plt.savefig, dpi=300| F["figures/final/*.svg"]
```

Sources: [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L59-L62), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L85), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L1-L21), [es_ablation2.py](/scripts/es_ablation2.py#L460-L557)

## The Two-Layer Theming Architecture

Styling is applied in two layers with clear precedence. Layer one is the declarative style sheet `publication.mplstyle`, loaded with `plt.style.use(f'{BASE_PATH}/publication.mplstyle')`, where `BASE_PATH` is derived from the script's own location so the style loads correctly no matter which directory you run from. Layer two is a small set of code-level overrides applied immediately after, which handle things a style sheet cannot: the categorical color cycle and the SVG text handling. Later settings always win, so the code overrides take precedence over the file.

Sources: [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L6-L7), [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L26-L28), [publication.mplstyle](/publication.mplstyle#L1-L15)

The style sheet itself is deliberately tiny — it only contains settings that every single figure should share. Here is what each line means for someone new to matplotlib:

| Setting | Value | Plain-language meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `pdf.fonttype` | `42` | Embed TrueType fonts in PDFs so text stays editable (not converted to outlines) |
| `font.family` | `Arial` | The sans-serif font most journals expect |
| `font.size` | `6` | 6 pt base font — small, because figures are designed at true print size (see panel sizing below) |
| `axes.linewidth` | `0.5` | Thin 0.5 pt axis lines |
| `axes.spines.top` / `.right` | `False` | Remove the top and right box borders (the "open" scientific look) |
| `xtick.major.width` / `ytick.major.width` | `0.5` | Thin 0.5 pt tick marks |
| `xtick.major.size` / `ytick.major.size` | `2` | Short 2 pt tick marks |
| `xtick.labelsize` / `ytick.labelsize` | `6` | 6 pt tick labels |
| `legend.fontsize` | `6` | 6 pt legend text |
| `legend.frameon` | `False` | No box drawn around legends |
| `lines.linewidth` | `1` | Default 1 pt line width for plotted curves |

Sources: [publication.mplstyle](/publication.mplstyle#L1-L15)

The code-level overrides add three things the style file cannot express. First, the default categorical color cycle is replaced with a **colorblind-safe palette** (the hex codes `#56B4E9`, `#E69F00`, `#CC79A7`, `#009E73`, `#F0E442`, `#0072B2`, `#D55E00`, `#000000` — the widely used Okabe–Ito scheme), so any plot that uses matplotlib's automatic color rotation is readable by color-vision-deficient readers. Second, `mpl.rcParams['svg.fonttype'] = 'none'` tells matplotlib to keep text as real `<text>` elements in SVG output rather than converting glyphs to paths — essential when a journal asks you to edit labels in Illustrator or Inkscape. Third, the `group_color_map` dictionary establishes the project's core semantic colors used by many figures.

Sources: [figures.py](/scripts/figures.py#L26-L29)

> [!TIP]
> Because `publication.mplstyle` is loaded by absolute path built from `Path(__file__).resolve().parent`, the figures never depend on your current working directory. If you copy this pattern into a new repo, keep the style sheet at the repo root and recompute `BASE_PATH` the same way.

## Color Strategy: A Default Cycle Plus Semantic Maps

The project uses two complementary color mechanisms. The **default cycle** (the Okabe–Ito palette above) handles "whatever colors matplotlib picks automatically." **Semantic color maps**, by contrast, are plain Python dictionaries that assign a fixed meaning to each category, so a reader can compare colors across different figures in the paper. The main examples, all defined as module-level dictionaries in `figures.py`:

| Dictionary | Mapping | Used for |
|---|---|---|
